question_text: A female patient with a body mass index of 30 kg/m2 presents to you with a lesion on the neck, as shown below. Which of the following conditions is the most likely to be suffering from?
explanation:
Explanation

  • The image demonstrates acanthosis nigricans, characterized by velvety, hyperpigmented thickening of the skin on the neck.
  • This change is strongly associated with insulin resistance, especially in obese patients (BMI ≥30).
  • Insulin resistance is a central feature of metabolic syndrome, which also includes obesity, hypertension, and dyslipidemia.

Pathophysiology

  • Chronic hyperinsulinemia stimulates keratinocyte and dermal fibroblast growth.
  • This leads to the development of thickened, pigmented skin folds (acanthosis nigricans).
  • Represents a cutaneous marker of underlying metabolic disturbance.

Clinical Features of Metabolic Syndrome

  • Central obesity with BMI ≥30 or waist circumference above threshold.
  • Acanthosis nigricans and skin tags.
  • Hypertension, dyslipidemia (elevated triglycerides, low HDL).
  • Increased risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

Metabolic Syndrome and Acanthosis Nigricans

question_text: Find the incorrect statement regarding the condition shown in the image below:
option_a: Pressure-bearing area are most commonly affected
option_b: Often associated with moisture and hyperhidrosis
explanation:
Pitted keratolysis is a skin disorder characterized by crateriform pitting that primarily affects the pressure-bearing aspects of the plantar surface of the feet

The manifestations of pitted keratolysis are due to a superficial cutaneous bacterial infection.

Pitted keratolysis is caused by a cutaneous infection with Micrococcus sedentarius

Under appropriate conditions (ie, prolonged occlusion, hyperhidrosis, increased skin surface pH), these bacteria proliferate and produce proteinases that destroy the stratum corneum, creating pits

It is a common problem among athletes, as heat, sweat, and humidity cause changes in the skin microbiome.

Skin swab and culture is not done becaue the causative bacteria are commensals and any positive findings do not confirm the cause/diagnosis

Skin biopsies are not performed routinely because the diagnosis of pitted keratolysis can be made easily by means of visual examination and recognition of the characteristic odor.

Management: Limit the use of occlusive footwear and reduce foot friction by wearing properly fitted footwear. Absorbent cotton socks must be changed frequently to prevent excessive foot moisture.

Twice-daily applications of erythromycin, clindamycin, or fusidic acid are effective

A 72-hour-old newborn, bundled up with blankets, is noted to have a vesicular rash on the face and neck, as shown below. These vesicles can be easily ruptured.

What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Miliaria crystallina is a self-limiting eccrine gland disorder due to blockage of sweat glands.

Miliaria crystallina is usually seen in infants under 1 week of age.

Overclothing and excessive blanket use lead to excessive sweating and occlusion of the ducts at the stratum corneum level. This results in the buildup of sweat, leading to vesicles.

It results in very superficial vesicles that easily rupture. The most common sites affected are the upper trunk, neck, and head.

It usually occurs within 24 hours and is self-limiting, resolving quickly.

question_text: Which of the following is the correct order of layers of epidermis from deep to superficial?
option_a: S.basale, S. granulosum, S. spinosum, S. corneum
option_b: S. corneum, S. granulosum, S. spinosum, S. basale
option_c: S. basale, S. spinosum, S. granulosum, S. corneum
option_d: S. corneum, S. spinosum, S. granulosum, S. basale
explanation:
Explanation:

The correct order of epidermal layers from deepest to most superficial is:

  1. Stratum basale-single layer of mitotically active keratinocytes
  2. Stratum spinosum-cells with desmosomal "spines"
  3. Stratum granulosum-keratohyalin granules present
  4. Stratum corneum-outermost layer of dead, keratinized cells

Epidermal layers (deep to superficial):

  • S.basale: Stem cell layer, melanocytes, Merkel cells
  • S.spinosum: Thickest living layer, Langerhans cells
  • S.granulosum: Granular layer, barrier formation
  • S.lucidum: Present only in thick skin (palms, soles)
  • S.corneum: Anucleate keratinized layer providing protection

question_text: Which layer of epidermis is underdeveloped at birth in the VLBW infants ?
explanation:
• During development of the epidermis, first layer to form is S. Basale and subsequently, layers form from below upwards.
  • Thus, stratum corneum is the last layer to develop and is underdeveloped (only 2-3 layers) in preterm/ very low birth weight (VLBW) infants in initial one week.
  • In these babies, stratum corneum is thin and permeable, leading to more fluid/heat losses. It becomes similar to the adult and full term infant after 2 to 3 weeks postnatal maturation.

question_text: The Malpighian layer refers to the living, mitotically active portion of the epidermis responsible for continuous regeneration of keratinocytes. It is composed of two specific layers of the epidermis. Which of the following correctly identifies the Malpighian layer?
explanation:
Explanation:

The Malpighian layer includes the stratum basale and stratum spinosum, the two deepest layers of the epidermis. These layers contain actively dividing cells, melanocytes, Langerhans cells, and desmosome-rich keratinocytes.

Malpighian layer:

  • Stratum basale: Single row of stem cells, continuous mitosis
  • Stratum spinosum: Several layers of keratinocytes connected by desmosomes
    Together, they form the "germinative" portion of the epidermis.

Key features:

  • Responsible for cell renewal
  • Melanin synthesis occurs here
  • Contains Langerhans cells (immune surveillance)

question_text: A neonate presents with persistent seizures and lesion on face. Which of the following is true regarding this condition?
option_a: Sturge Weber syndrome is the most likely diagnosis
option_b: The image reveals Port wine stain
option_c: CT brain will reveal Tram track calcification
explanation:
Image : Port wine stain

Patients with Sturge-Weber syndrome may present with cerebral symptoms without facial findings.

Sturge-Weber syndrome (SWS) is a neurocutaneous syndrome characterized by involvement of the face, choroid, and leptomeninges.

The facial capillary vascular malformation is also known as "port-wine stain" or "nevus flammeus" and usually is seen in the territory of the trigeminal nerve, commonly along the ophthalmic or maxillary segment (forehead, cheeks). It is typically unilateral, present at birth, and does not change with the age of the patient.

A seizure is usually the first neurological manifestation of Sturge-Weber syndrome. Infantile spasms are seen in approximately 90% of affected patients in the first year of life, present on the contralateral side

A child with a facial port-wine stain has a 10% to 35% risk of brain involvement. If there is involvement of both upper and lower eyelids, then the risk of glaucoma increases up to 50%. Glaucoma is almost always ipsilateral to the facial port-wine stain.

Reference: Rook's dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 73, Page 2

question_text: A 35 year old obese female with hirsutism presents with lesions as shown. She is not responding to isotretinoin and antibiotics. What is the next step ?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The patient's acne is not responding to standard treatments (e.g., isotretinoin and antibiotics), which is a sign that the acne might be hormonally driven.
  • The presence of hirsutism, obesity, and acne predominantly on the lower face (U-shape) strongly suggests hormonal acne, which is commonly associated with hyperandrogenism.
  • Hyperandrogenism can be evaluated by testing for elevated levels of androgens such as testosterone, dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS), and dihydrotestosterone (DHT), all of which stimulate sebaceous gland activity and sebum production, contributing to acne.
  • Other signs of hyperandrogenism include hirsutism, seborrhea, alopecia, menstrual irregularities, and infertility. Conditions that lead to hyperandrogenism include polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), late-onset congenital adrenal hyperplasia, or, rarely, tumors in the ovaries, adrenal glands, or pituitary.

Incorrect Answers:

  • A. Look for antibiotic resistance: This step is unnecessary given that the acne appears to be hormonally driven and not due to bacterial infection, which would respond to antibiotics.
  • B. Look for triggering drugs: Although drug-induced acne can occur, this patient's clinical picture (obesity, hirsutism, lower face acne) points more strongly to a hormonal cause.
  • C. Look for dietary triggers: While diet may influence acne, the clinical signs of hirsutism, obesity, and lower face acne suggest a hormonal cause rather than dietary triggers.

Key Takeaway:

  • In cases of acne that do not respond to typical treatments, especially with accompanying signs of hirsutism and obesity, it is important to evaluate for hyperandrogenism, often associated with conditions like PCOS.

question_text: A 25-year-old man of Southeast Asian descent is started on a new anticonvulsant for seizures. One week later, he develops widespread targetoid lesions and the severe mucosal involvement shown in the image. Which of the following HLA alleles is most strongly associated with an increased risk for this specific drug-induced reaction?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's clinical presentation with widespread targetoid lesions and severe hemorrhagic mucositis (crusting of lips) is classic for Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS).

HLA-B*1502 is a specific HLA allele is a powerful pharmacogenomic predictor of SJS and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) induced by aromatic anticonvulsants, particularly carbamazepine and phenytoin, especially in individuals of Southeast Asian descent (e.g., Han Chinese, Thai, Malaysian). The presence of this allele is now considered a contraindication for the use of these drugs in at-risk populations.

Explanation of Other Options:

HLA-B*5801 (Option B): This allele is strongly associated with severe cutaneous adverse reactions (including SJS/TEN) induced by allopurinol.

HLA-DQ2 (Option C): This allele, along with HLA-DQ8, is strongly associated with celiac disease.

HLA-DR4 (Option D): This allele is associated with an increased risk for several autoimmune diseases, most notably rheumatoid arthritis and type 1 diabetes mellitus.

Key Takeaways: High-Yield HLA Associations

Reference: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 119, Page 14.

question_text: A 7 year old child presented with asymptomatic lesions on the trunk as shown in the picture. The histopathological report shows perifollicular granulomas. What is the diagnosis ?
explanation:
Lichen scrofulosorum (LS) is a rare tuberculid that presents as a lichenoid eruption of minute papules in children and adolescents with TB. The lesions are usually asymptomatic, closely grouped, skin-colored to reddish-brown papules, often perifollicular, and are mainly found on the abdomen, chest, back, and proximal parts of the limbs. The eruption is usually associated with a strongly positive tuberculin reaction

Histology shows non-caseating, epithelioid cell granulomas in upper dermis and around dermal appendages. Tubercle bacilli are almost never seen in the histology specimen, neither can they be cultured.

question_text: A patient of LL Leprosy on treatment presents with painful lesions on the body as shown in the image. On palpation, painful thickened ulnar and common peroneal nerve are found. What is the drug of Choice:
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient has Lepromatous Leprosy (LL) and presents with painful skin lesions along with painful, thickened ulnar and common peroneal nerves. This clinical picture is characteristic of Type 1 lepra reaction (reversal reaction) when occurring in borderline disease, or Type 2 reaction (ENL - Erythema Nodosum Leprosum) in LL patients, especially when lesions are painful, tender, and accompanied by systemic features.

LL is characterized by numerous symmetric lesions like macules, papules, nodules, and diffuse infiltration. These patients often have extensive bacterial load, and during treatment, they frequently develop ENL, a painful inflammatory reaction presenting with tender nodules, fever, malaise, and painful neuritis. The presence of painful thickened nerves signals active neuritis, which poses a high risk for irreversible nerve damage.

In such situations, the drug of choice is systemic corticosteroids, because steroids rapidly suppress the intense inflammatory response, reduce nerve edema, and prevent permanent sensory-motor deficit. Prednisolone is used in moderate to severe ENL to control painful skin lesions, nerve pain, systemic symptoms, and internal organ involvement.

While thalidomide (Option B) is highly effective for ENL due to its strong TNF-α inhibitory effect, it is not the first-line drug in acute, painful neuritis. Corticosteroids remain the DOC because they act quickly on nerve inflammation, which is the most urgent issue in this patient.

Thus, Steroids (Option A) are the drug of choice.

Clofazimine (Option C): Part of MDT and has anti-inflammatory properties, but not first-line for acute ENL.

Dapsone (Option D): Core MDT drug; no role in treating ENL reactions.

Key Takeaways:

Acute ENL with systemic signs, corticosteroids are drug of choice; thalidomide reserved where indicated.

question_text: What is the clinical condition in the following image?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image shows a red, indurated, swollen lesion with multiple pustular openings discharging pus on the nape.

This is classical for a carbuncle, a deep-seated infection of multiple hair follicles forming interconnected abscesses and draining sinuses.

Commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

Treatment:

  • Systemic antibiotics active against S. aureus (e.g., cloxacillin, cephalosporins, clindamycin).
  • Incision and drainage for large carbuncles.
  • Control of underlying risk factors (e.g., strict glycemic control in diabetics).
  • Supportive care with analgesics, warm compresses, and hygiene.

Explanation of Other Options:

  • Follicular abscess (Option B): Localized single abscess around one follicle (furuncle); no multiple sinuses.
  • Cellulitis (Option C): Diffuse, ill-defined, spreading infection of dermis and subcutis; no localized multiple discharges.
  • Erysipelas (Option D): Superficial infection with bright red, raised, sharply demarcated borders; commonly on face/legs, not with multiple draining points.

Key Takeaways:

  • Carbuncle = multiple furuncles with interconnecting sinuses + pus discharge.
  • Treatment requires antibiotics + incision and drainage + risk factor control.
  • Differentiate from furuncle (single lesion), cellulitis (diffuse swelling), erysipelas (sharply demarcated erythema).

question_text: Which HPV subtype can cause following penile lesions?
explanation:
Anogenital warts / condyloma acuminatum.

Anogenital warts are common and are caused in 75% by HPV-6.The remainder are caused by HPV-11 or more unusual, low-risk HPVs. They are often asymptomatic, but may cause discomfort, discharge or bleeding. The typical anogenital wart is soft, pink, elongated and sometimes filiform or pedunculated. The lesions are usually multiple especially on moist surfaces, and their growth can be enhanced during pregnancy.

The commonest sites, the area of frenulum, corona and glans in men, and the posterior fourchette in women, correspond to the likely sites of greatest coital friction.

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, chapter 25, page 56

question_text: A patient presented with multiple warty sessile lesions. What is the diagnosis ?
explanation:
Condylomata acuminata refers to anogenital warts caused by human papillomavirus (HPV).

The most common strains of HPV that cause anogenital warts are 6 and 11.

HPV is a double-stranded DNA virus primarily spread through sexual contact.

Lesions are generally found in multiples and can coalesce into larger lesions.

Condyloma acuminata usually appear as raised, skin-colored, fleshy papules that range in size from one to five millimeters in diameter. They can be broad and flat, pedicled, or occasionally have a cauliflower-like appearance

Reference: Rook’s textbook of dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 25, Page 56

question_text: A patient presented with grouped fluid filled lesions around lips. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
• Herpes labialis is caused by Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), leading to painful, fluid-filled blisters around the lips and perioral area (cold sores).
  • This is a self-limiting condition, but it can recur due to latent virus in the trigeminal ganglion.
  • Common triggers for recurrence include stress, fatigue, or exposure to bright light.
  • Diagnosis can be confirmed by Tzanck smear, which shows multinucleated giant cells (MNGs).
  • Treatment: The drug of choice is aciclovir (oral or topical).

Explanation of the Incorrect Options:

  • (B) Impetigo:
    • A bacterial infection caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes, characterized by honey-colored crusted lesions, usually around the mouth but not typically in grouped fluid-filled vesicles.
  • (C) Pemphigus:
    • A rare autoimmune blistering disorder that leads to flaccid blisters on the skin and mucous membranes, typically affecting the mouth, not primarily the lips. It involves acantholysis, which is absent in herpes labialis.
  • (D) Herpes zoster:
    • Caused by Varicella-zoster virus and presents with a unilateral, painful rash along a dermatome, not around the lips. It also involves vesicles but in a more distinct distribution.

Key Takeaway:

Herpes labialis presents as grouped vesicles on the lips and is caused by HSV-1. It is a recurrent, self-limiting infection typically treated with aciclovir.

question_text: What is the probable diagnosis for a cauliflower-shaped mass on the foot of a farmer that appeared after a minor injury, with microscope revealing copper penny bodies?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The hallmark feature here is the presence of copper penny bodies (Medlar bodies) on microscopy, which are pathognomonic for chromoblastomycosis.
  • Clinically, the disease presents as a slow-growing, cauliflower-like verrucous lesion, typically on exposed areas like the feet after trauma with contaminated soil or vegetation.
  • It commonly affects farmers and individuals exposed to rural environments.

Chromoblastomycosis:

  • Causative organisms: Fonsecaea, Cladophialophora, Phialophora.
  • Risk factor: Minor trauma in agricultural workers.
  • Clinical appearance: Verrucous, cauliflower-like lesions that spread slowly but can become disfiguring if untreated.
  • Microscopy: Thick-walled, pigmented fungal cells called Medlar bodies or copper penny bodies.
  • Spread: Chronic, localized; lymphatic spread is uncommon.
  • Treatment: Prolonged antifungal therapy with itraconazole or terbinafine; surgical excision for localized severe disease.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

Blastomycosis (Option B): Caused by Blastomyces dermatitidis. Typically presents with pulmonary infection or ulcerative skin lesions. It does not produce verrucous cauliflower-like growths or Medlar bodies.

Sporotrichosis (Option C): Known as "rose gardener's disease," caused by Sporothrix schenckii. Characterized by nodular lesions spreading along lymphatic channels. It does not produce localized cauliflower-like masses or copper penny bodies.

Phaeohyphomycosis (Option D): Caused by dematiaceous fungi (darkly pigmented), but histology shows pigmented septate hyphae, not Medlar bodies. Clinical presentation is variable but not typically cauliflower-shaped verrucous growths.

Key Takeaway:
A cauliflower-shaped verrucous lesion on the foot of a farmer with copper penny bodies on microscopy is diagnostic of chromoblastomycosis. It is a chronic subcutaneous mycosis caused by pigmented fungi, managed with prolonged antifungal therapy and, in some cases, surgery.

question_text: A Patient from Uttarakhand presented in September with fever and myalgia. Patient started on IV Ceftriaxone given but it didn't help, later noticed cutaneous lesions on examination. What is your diagnosis?
explanation:
Scrub typhus is an acute, febrile, infectious illness that is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi. obligate intracellular gram-negative bacterium

O tsutsugamushi, the pathogen that causes scrub typhus, is transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected chigger, the larval stage of Leptotrombidium mites.

The bacteria multiply at the inoculation site, and a papule forms that ulcerates and becomes necrotic, evolving into an eschar, with regional lymphadenopathy

Elements brought out in the history may include the following:

  • Travel to an area where scrub typhus is endemic
  • Chigger bite (often painless and unnoticed)
  • Incubation period of 6-20 days (average, 10 days)
  • Headaches, shaking chills, lymphadenopathy, conjunctival injection, fever, anorexia, and general apathy
  • CNS signs and symptoms
  • Rash: a small, painless, gradually enlarging papule, which leads to an area of central necrosis and is followed by eschar formation

Current treatment for scrub typhus is based on antibiotic therapy - doxycycline is the DOC

The diagnosis points to neurofibromatosis 1

The earliest clinical finding usually seen in children with NF1 is multiple café-au-lait spots. These may be present at birth or may appear over time, frequently increasing in size and number throughout childhood.

Axillary or inguinal freckles are rarely present at birth, but appear during childhood through adolescence. Also known as "Crowe sign" , they are the pathognomic finding

Subcutaneous or cutaneous neurofibromas appear over time in older children, adolescents, and adults. Histopathologically, they correspond to schwannomas.

Other signs and symptoms may include the following:

  • High blood pressure (potentially from renal artery stenosis or pheochromocytoma)
  • Bone abnormalities - Sphenoid dysplasia or typical long-bone abnormalities such as pseudarthrosis 
  • Optic nerve tumors
  • Lisch nodules
  • Learning disabilities; Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder; Autism spectrum disorder
  • Larger than average head size
  • Short stature

question_text: A 63-year-old male presents with the erythematous scaly skin lesions on the trunk since 4 -5 years. A skin biopsy was done and the findings are shown below. Which further test will help establish the diagnosis?
option_a: Immunohistochemistry for clonal rearrangement of the T-cell receptor genes.
explanation:
Primary cutaneous lymphomas are the second most common extranodal non-Hodgkin Lymphomas. They may be of either T cell, B cell, or NK cell origin.

Cutaneous T Cell lymphomas (CTCL), Mycosis fungoides is the most common type of CTCL. It is a cutaneous lymphoma that originates in the peripheral epidermotropic T-cells, specifically the memory T-cells (CD45RO+).

It is more common in adults over 50 years of age,

Chronic indolent course, fatal disease

Mycosis fungoides tumor cells are characterized by epidermotropic peripheral T lymphocytes whose phenotype is CD2+, CD3+, CD4+, and CD5+.

Clinically - 3 stages

Patch stage: The earliest lesion seen in mycosis fungoides is an erythematous, or brownish scaly patch,

Plaque stage: In the plaque stage, lesions now appear larger and raised with evident infiltration, along with the appearance of new lesions

Tumor stage: In the tumor stage, erythematous-purplish papules or nodules of larger diameter are seen.

The frequency of lymph nodal or visceral dissemination increases as the lesions progress from the patch stage to the plaque stage and finally the tumor stage.

Sezary syndrome is the final end stage and is characterized by a triad of manifestations: erythroderma with pruritus, lymphadenopathy, and atypical circulating lymphocytes (referred to as Sezary or Lutzner cells). The syndrome is understood as a leukemic phase of T-cell cutaneous lymphoma.

HPE - Intra-epidermal lymphocytic Pautriers microabscess, cutaneous epidermotropism

Treatment

the main goals of therapy are long-term disease control, prompt symptom relief, and management of life-threatening (aggressive) disease

Early stage - total skin electron beam therapy (TSEBT), treatment of choice

For more extensive disease, combinations of skin-directed therapies and systemic therapies are used. The various systemic options available include methotrexate, bexarotene, targeted immunotherapy (such as alemtuzumab), polychemotherapy, etc

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, chapter 140, page 140.5

question_text: The epidermis contains multiple specialized cell types with distinct functions, locations, and embryological origins. Understanding where each cell type resides is essential for dermatology and pathology. Which of the following statements about skin structure is NOT true?

option_b: Melanocytes are present in stratum basale.
option_c: Stratified squamous epithelium with hallmark keratin intermediate filaments.
option_d: Merkel cells are present in stratum basale.
explanation:
Explanation:

Langerhans cells do originate from bone marrow, but they are primarily located in the stratum spinosum, not the granular layer.
Key epidermal cell types and their locations:

  • Langerhans cells: Antigen-presenting dendritic cells derived from bone marrow; mostly in stratum spinosum.
  • Melanocytes: Neural crest-derived pigment cells; found in stratum basale.
  • Merkel cells: Mechanoreceptors involved in touch sensation; located in stratum basale.
  • Keratinocytes: Main epidermal cells with abundant keratin intermediate filaments, forming stratified squamous keratinized epithelium.

question_text: A newborn had reddish swelling over upper eyelid and the swelling regressed spontaneously at about one year of age. What is the diagnosis:
explanation:
Salmon patch (Nevus Simplex)

  • Salmon patches are small, pale pink, ill- defined, vascular macules that occur most commonly on the glabella, eyelids, upper lip, and nuchal area of 30-40% of normal newborn infants.
  • These lesions, which represent localized vascular ectasia, persist for several months and may become more visible during crying or changes in environmental temperature.
  • Most lesions on the face eventually fade and disappear completely.
  • The salmon patch is usually symmetric, with lesions on both eyelids and both sides of midline.
  • Port-wine stains are often larger and unilateral, and they usually end along the midline

Reference: Rook's dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 103, Page 9

question_text: Which among the following organism causes Buruli ulcer ?
explanation:
Buruli ulcer, caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans, is a chronic, debilitating, necrotizing disease of the skin and soft tissue.

Buruli ulcer is an emerging infectious disease and is the third most common mycobacterial disease of the immunocompetent host, after tuberculosis and leprosy.

Buruli ulcers generally begin as a painless dermal papule or subcutaneous edematous nodule, which, over a period of weeks to months, breaks down to form an extensive necrotic ulcer with undermined edges.

Treatment includes a prolonged course of antibiotics and surgical debridement.

Early identification and treatment are key, as lesions heal with scarring that can be a significant source of morbidity

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th edition, chapter 27, page 36

question_text: Which of the following lesions are not seen in leprosy?
explanation:
1. Leprosy skin lesions can be single or multiple, usually hypopigmented/reddish.
  2. A variety of skin lesions may be seen but macules (flat), papules (raised), or nodules are common.
  3. Sensory loss is a typical feature of leprosy, the initial sensation to go is thermal.
  4. Thickened nerves, mainly peripheral nerve trunks constitute another feature of leprosy, accompanied by other signs as a result of damage to the nerve.
  5. These may be loss of sensation in the skin and weakness of muscles supplied by the affected nerve.
  6. Positive SSS: Modified Ziehl Nielson staining - Rod-shaped, red-stained leprosy bacilli, which are diagnostic of the disease.

A person presenting with skin lesions or with symptoms suggestive of nerve damage, in which the cardinal signs are absent or doubtful should be called a 'suspect case' in the absence of any immediately obvious alternate diagnosis.

Reference: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page Number-10.

question_text: 32-year-old female patient, with no remarkable medical history, presents with a six-month history of a recurrent, itching rash of the face. Her work is mostly outdoor. On examination, there is erythema and wheal formation. What is the underlying mechanism for this condition?
explanation:
• Solar urticaria, a chronic acquired photosensitivity disorder, consists of recurrent episodes of urticaria rash developed on areas of the skin that are exposed to sunlight.
  • It is an immediate hypersensitivity reaction, which might be IgE-mediated, occurring after exposure to the sun.
  • This induces the degranulation of mast cells, releasing histamine and resulting in lesions of urticaria. The rash is associated with a sensation of itching or burning.
  • Sun exposure avoidance is recommended to decrease the Ig-E mediated reaction, as well as the use of broad-spectrum sunscreens and dark clothing photoprotection.

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 42, page 3

Lichen planopilaris is an inflammatory, primaryly lymphocytic cicatricial alopecia. Like lichen planus, the etiology of lichen planopilaris is not known.

The scalp lesions may be single or multiple, focal or diffuse, and occur anywhere on the scalp. Hair follicles around the margins of the bare areas show perifollicular erythema and perifollicular scale, in contrast to discoid lupus erythematosus, where follicular plugging is in the center of the active bare patch.

Cutaneous, nail, and mucous membrane lichen planus may occur before, during, or after the onset of scalp involvement.

The most characteristic trichoscopic feature of active lichen planopilaris is perifollicular scaling.

question_text: Which of the following is used as chemical peels in melasma
explanation:
Chemical peeling is the application of a chemical agent to the skin, which causes the controlled destruction of a part or of the entire epidermis, with or without the dermis, leading to exfoliation and removal of superficial lesions, followed by the regeneration of new epidermal and dermal tissues.

Chemical peels are a well-known modality of treatment for melasma. The basic mechanism of the action of chemical peels in melasma is the removal of unwanted melanin by causing a controlled chemical burn to the skin. Glycolic acid peel is the most commonly used alpha hydroxy peel.

Other peels - Salicylic acid(Beta hydroxy peels), Mandelic acid, trichloro acetic acid, Jessner's solution, Tretinoin peels

question_text: This clinical finding is caused by
explanation: Green nails, also known as chloronychia or green nail syndrome, are characterized by green discoloration of the nail plate (greenish-yellow, greenish-brown, greenish-black), proximal chronic non-tender paronychia, and distolateral onycholysis. The cause is Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection of the nail plate in persons whose hands are constantly exposed to water, soaps, and detergents or are subject to mechanical trauma, especially in the elderly. Green or black coloration of the nails should raise suspicion for Pseudomonas infection and be treated with an oral quinolone (ciprofloxacin), particularly in aged patients.

question_text: A 35-year-old woman presents to you with hair loss for the past three months. She tested positive for COVID-19 eight months ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation

  • The clinical history shows hair loss beginning 3 months ago, following a COVID-19 infection 8 months earlier, which is a known trigger for telogen effluvium.
  • The timing fits the classic pattern: hair shedding starts 2-3 months after a systemic stressor.
  • The diffuse, non-scarring nature of the hair loss with normal scalp appearance is typical of telogen effluvium.
  • The condition is temporary and resolves spontaneously within 6-12 months.

Pathophysiology

  • Normally, about 10% of scalp hairs are in the telogen (resting) phase.
  • Stressful events push a higher proportion of hairs prematurely into telogen, leading to diffuse shedding.
  • No scarring or follicular destruction occurs, making it reversible.

Clinical Features

  • Diffuse, non-scarring hair loss.
  • Sudden onset after a stressor (2-3 months delay).
  • Shedding more than 100 hairs per day, often noticed during combing or washing.
  • Normal scalp examination without inflammation or scaling.

Course and Prognosis

  • Self-limiting; regrowth occurs within 6-12 months.
  • Reassurance is the mainstay of management; no aggressive therapy needed.

Key Features of Telogen Effluvium

Explanation of Incorrect Options

Tinea capitis (Option A): Produces patchy alopecia with scaling, black dot hairs, or inflammatory boggy lesions, not diffuse shedding.

Trichotillomania (Option C): Characterized by irregular patches of broken hairs due to repetitive pulling, often with uneven lengths of hair.

Female-pattern androgenetic alopecia (Option D): Presents with gradual thinning over the central scalp, without sudden diffuse shedding or relation to a stress event.

Key Takeaway
Telogen effluvium is a diffuse, non-scarring hair loss condition that arises 2-3 months after a physical or emotional stressor, such as COVID-19, and resolves spontaneously.

question_text: A 20 year old girl presents with recurrent episodes of swelling on the face associated with abdominal cramps. She has tried multiple over the counter medicines but no relief. Which of these can be used as a treatment?

Associated with mutation in SERPING1 gene, which provides instructions for making a protein called C1 inhibitor.

Types I and II HAE are inherited as an autosomal dominant trait on chromosome 11q 12.1.

Type III HAE - Gain of function mutations of F12

All types of HAE are aggravated by Oestrogen in contraceptive and hormone replacement therapies

Clinical features

Treatment -

Agents used in the treatment of acute attacks of HAE include the following

C1-INH concentrate:

Kallikrein inhibitor - ecallantide

Selective bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist: Icatibant

Androgen analogues like danazol and tranexamic acid can be used for prophylaxis

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 43, page 5

question_text: The clinical finding is commonly seen in
explanation:
Symptomatic dermographism, also known as dermographism urticaria, or urticaria factitia, is an urticarial eruption upon pressure or trauma to the skin. The literal meaning is "to write on the skin." Downward pressure on the skin produces a linear wheal in the shape of the applied external force. Dermatographism is the most common type of inducible/physical urticaria, occurring in approximately 2% to 5% of the population.

Dermographism is essentially an exaggeration of this triple response. It has been postulated that it usually develops within five minutes of stroking the skin and persists for 15-30 min in contrast to the normal triple response of Lewis that subsides in less than 5-10 min

question_text: An 30 year old soldier presented with fever and dyspnea and skin lesions as shown in the image. CXR showed bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Which of the following organism is the causative agent?

Erythema multiforme is an acute, immune-mediated condition affecting the skin and mucosal surfaces.

By definition, less than 10% of the body surface area is affected. The disease is typically self-limiting.

The most common causes include infection such as herpes simplex and mycoplasmal infection (> 90% of cases), autoimmune conditions and medications.

question_text: Benign familial chronic pemphigus has the following features except-

Hailey-Hailey disease (HHD), also known as benign familial pemphigus, is a rare autosomal dominant genodermatoses

HHD is characterized by impaired keratinocyte adhesion resulting in widespread intraepidermal acantholysis.

Mutations in the ATP2C1 gene suggested a role of a Ca2+ dependent signaling pathway in regulating cell-to-cell adhesion and epidermal differentiation

Primary lesions are grouped, flaccid vesicles and blisters on an erythematous base or normal skin.

Lesions present a symmetrical, bilateral distribution Sites: usually occur in friction or intertriginous areas, including the sides and back of the neck, axillary, inguinal, and perineal folds (scrotum, vulva).

Tzanck smear - acantholytic cells

question_text: A Fish tank worker presented with lesions on hand as shown. What is the causative organism?
explanation:
Explanation:

Mycobacterium marinum is an environmental mycobacterium acquired from fish tanks, aquaria or contaminated water and is the classic cause of cutaneous infections in fish-tank workers.

Lesions typically appear after an incubation period of ~2-3 weeks (occasionally up to 9 months) as a solitary nodule, pustule, ulcer or verrucous plaque on the hand or fingers and may show sporotrichoid spread (proximal nodular extension along lymphatics).

The organism grows optimally at 30-33°C, is a slow mycobacterium of Runyon group I, and cultures are positive in ~70-80% of cases when incubated at the lower temperature; Ziehl-Neelsen stains are only rarely positive because organism numbers are low.

These clinical, epidemiological (fish-tank exposure) and microbiological features point to M. marinum as the causative agent.

Sporothroix schenckii (Option A): fungal cause of sporotrichosis that can produce a nodular lymphangitic (sporotrichoid) pattern and is a differential diagnosis but is not the classic fish-tank mycobacterial pathogen described in the stem.

Mycobacterium kansasii (Option B): Primarily a pulmonary pathogen; cutaneous disease is rare and typically occurs in immunocompromised patients or after trauma. It grows optimally at 37°C and is epidemiologically associated with tap water and urban/occupational exposures, not classically fish-tank infections.

Mycobacterium ulcerans (Option C): Causes Buruli ulcer, a painless, undermined ulcer acquired in tropical wetlands with long incubation and characteristic mycolactone-mediated necrosis; it is not the usual organism causing nodular hand lesions after fish-tank exposure.

Key Takeaways:

  • Fish-tank/aquarium exposure + nodular/ulcerative hand lesions +/- sporotrichoid spread: Mycobacterium marinum.
  • marinum grows best at ~30-33°C; inform the lab so cultures are incubated at the correct temperature.
  • Differentials include sporotrichosis, other NTM (e.g., M. kansasii, M. chelonae) and fungal infections; epidemiology and culture conditions help distinguish them.

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 30, page 22

question_text: A patient presented with hypopigmented rash with satellite lesions as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image shows hypopigmented patches with satellite lesions around the main lesion.

Satellite lesions are characteristic of Borderline Tuberculoid (BT) leprosy.

Lesions are hypopigmented, well-defined, and often asymmetrically distributed.

BT is part of the borderline spectrum in Ridley-Jopling classification, with features intermediate between TT and BL.

Nerve involvement is common, with sensory loss over lesions.

Explanation of Other Options:

  • Borderline Lepromatous (BL) (Option B): Shows numerous, ill-defined, symmetrically distributed lesions, often infiltrated, without the classical satellite lesion pattern.
  • Lepromatous Leprosy (LL) (Option C): Diffuse, symmetric lesions, nodules, leonine facies; no clear hypopigmented patches with satellites.
  • Tuberculoid Leprosy (TT) (Option D): Single or few, large, well-defined hypopigmented patches with sensory loss; no satellite lesions.

Key Takeaways:

  • Satellite lesions = hallmark of BT leprosy.
  • TT: Few, well-demarcated patches.
  • BL/LL: Multiple, diffuse, symmetric lesions.

question_text: The rarest form of Leprosy is :
explanation:
BB leprosy is the immunologic midpoint in the clinical spectrum of the leprosy.

It is the most unstable and uncommon form.These patients upgrade or downgrade to a more stable clinical form at the earliest.

Cutaneous lesions are characteristically annular plaques with sharp interior and exterior border – inverted cup saucer appearance

Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9th edition Chapter 28, page 10

question_text: All of the following are diagnostic criteria for tuberculid except ?
option_b: Absence of M. tb in skin culture
explanation:
Tuberculids are a manifestation of cutaneous tuberculosis (TB), resulting from delayed hypersensitivity reactions to Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M. tb) or mycobacterial antigens in individuals with strong cell-mediated immunity. The diagnostic criteria include tuberculoid granuloma on histopathology, strongly positive Mantoux test, absence of M. tb in smear and culture, and resolution of skin lesions with antituberculosis therapy (ATT).

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th edition, chapter 27, page 25

question_text: A 5-year-old child presents with a hypopigmented patch on her face with fine scaling. There is a history of atopy in the family. What is the clinical diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Pityriasis alba presents with:

  • Hypopigmented, slightly scaly patches
  • Most commonly on the face of children
  • Strong association with atopy and dry skin
  • More noticeable in summer due to tanning of surrounding skin

Pityriasis alba:

  • A mild form of eczema
  • Often seen in atopic children
  • Lesions: poorly defined, hypopigmented patches, fine scaling
  • No anesthesia or loss of sensation (helps differentiate from leprosy)
  • Treatment: emollients, mild topical steroids if needed

Indeterminate leprosy (Option A): Has reduced sensation, dry hair loss, not typical fine facial scaling in children

Pityriasis rosea (Option B): Presents with Herald patch and Christmas-tree pattern on trunk, not facial hypopigmentation

Pityriasis versicolor (Option D): Causes hypopigmented or hyperpigmented patches with fine branny scales, usually on trunk and back, not commonly isolated to face in children

question_text: This clinical picture is seen in?

Leonine facies: a face that resembles that of a lion

Leonine facies are seen in

question_text: A 24-year-old unmarried woman presents with lesions on face, upper back and shoulders for 2 years. The drug of choice for her treatment.
explanation:
Isotretinoin

question_text: Which of the following is incorrect regarding Type 1 Lepra reaction?
option_b: Systemic symptoms like uveitis, orchitis, hepatitis are seen
option_c: Existing lesions of Leprosy get inflammed
option_d: Occurs within the first year of starting the treatment
explanation:
Sudden changes in immune-mediated response to Mycobacterium leprae antigen are referred to as leprosy reactions. The reactions manifest as acute inflammatory episodes

Leprosy reactions can occur at any time before, during, or after the treatment.

Type 1 reaction is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction. It mostly occurs in borderline patients

The existing lesions show signs of inflammation, but no new lesions occur. Previously unnoticed or invisible patches may become prominent.

The lesions are often accompanied by edema and neuritis in the extremities. Edema in the hands and feet may be sometimes the main symptom Nerve thickening and pain may occur and preexisting peripheral neuropathy may become prominent (sensory, motor, or autonomic).

The main goal of treatment in type 1 reaction is to suppress the cellular immunity. Prevention of nerve damage required early diagnosis and early institution of anti-inflammatory medications.

MDT must be continued during the reactions.

Corticosteroids are the most effective drugs used to treat reversal reaction.

Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9th edition, Chapter 28, page 12

question_text: A male child presented with bleeding gums, arthralgia and skin condition shown below. Which of the following deficiency is associated with this ?
explanation:
Scurvy is a clinical syndrome resulting from vitamin C deficiency. Vitamin C is essential for the growth and repair of skin, cartilage, bone, and teeth.

Vitamin C is water-soluble and gets absorbed in the distal ileum

patients with scurvy experience oral and skin symptoms such as bleeding gums, easy bruising, skin rashes, fragility, delayed wound healing, and bone and joint aches.

Corkscrew strands, characterized by twisted or coiled hair shafts, result from impaired collagen synthesis and are considered pathognomonic for scurvy.

Perifollicular hemorrhages are often localized to the lower extremities

Painful joint swelling, hemarthroses, and subperiosteal hematomas result from vascular fragility caused by impaired collagen formation.

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th edition, chapter 63, page 20

question_text: A patient presents with Ludwing grade 2 hair loss. In which alopecia is this grading done ?
explanation:
Ludwig scale is used to classify female-pattern baldness, i.e. female androgenic alopecia.

In women, Hair generally is lost diffusely over the crown, seen clinically as widening of the central parting. females tend to retain their frontal hairline while experiencing diffuse hair thinning on top, causing a broader appearance of the anterior part of the hair.

Reference: Rook's Textbook Of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 89, Page 17

question_text: "Bamboo hair" as shown in the image below is seen in ____
explanation:
1. Netherton's syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive genodermatosis
  2. This syndrome is caused by mutation in the Spinks gene, which is located on the long arm of Chromosome 5
  3. Netherton's syndrome is characterized by the triad of ichthyosis linearis circumflexa, trichorrhexis invaginata (bamboo hair) and an atopic diathesis
  4. classical cutaneous lesions of ichthyosis linearis circumflexa in the form of recurrent crops of erythematous annular and polycyclic scaly patches with double-edged scales. 
  5. Trichorrhexis invaginata is pathognomonic of Netherton's syndrome
  6. Trichorrhexis invaginata, also called bamboo hair, occurs by invagination of the distal hair shaft into the proximal hair shaft creating a ball in a cup appearance. It manifests as brittle, sparse, and short scalp and eyebrow hair.

Reference: Rook's Textbook Of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 89, Page 53

question_text: A 17 year old patient presents with lesions on face. Which of the following is not a causative factor of this disease?
explanation:
The disease in the picture is acne vulgaris as comedone, papules are visible on the forehead of this young girl.

There are 4 main factors that contribute to acne

  1. Follicular hyperkeratinization: Increased proliferation of keratinocytes leads to obstruction of the follicle, essentially plugging the pilosebaceous unit - forming a comedone
  2. Seborrhoea: Stimulation of sebaceous gland secretion by androgens
  3. Propionibacterium acnes within follicle: An anaerobic bacteria that thrives in the lipid-rich environment of sebum. Colonization of P. acnes triggers the immune system and leads to perifollicular inflammation.
  4. Inflammation: Acne progression often happens due to inflammation. Main mediator - IL - 1 alpha

Reference: Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 90, Page 2

question_text: A patient present with 5 days fever and painful erythematous lesions on face and biopsy revealed neutrophilic infiltrate. What is a most probable diagnosis.
explanation:
Neutrophilic dermatoses consist of a group of non-infectious disorders that are characterized by neutrophilic infiltration of the skin (epidermis, dermis, or hypodermis)

Sweet syndrome characteristically demonstrates the sudden onset of well-defined tender plaques or nodules accompanied by fever, arthralgias.

Sweet syndrome may be idiopathic, which is most common, or may be associated with an underlying condition. It may follow:

  1. Inflammatory bowel disease (e.g. ulcerative colitis or Crohn disease)
  2. Rheumatoid arthritis
  3. Myeloproliferative disorders - leukaemia (most often acute myelogenous leukaemia or myelodysplastic syndromes).

In Sweet disease there is a sudden appearance of red tender lumps (plaques) on the skin usually of the limbs or neck, sometimes elsewhere.

DOC - steroids, dapsone, colchicine

Reference: Rook's dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 148, Page 6

question_text: The following image shows-
explanation:
Plantar warts are cutaneous lesions on the plantar aspect of the foot that are caused by the infection of keratinocytes with the human papillomavirus (HPV).

Plantar warts may appear as a singular, rough, flesh-colored to yellow or grey-brown, hyperkeratotic papule.

Visualization of thrombosed capillaries (black dots) and pinpoint bleeding along with the loss of normal dermatoglyphics differentiate a plantar wart from other cutaneous lesions, such as calluses or corns.

On palpation, plantar warts feel rough and are tender when squeezed along the sides.

Reference: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 25, Page Number-47.

question_text: A 28-year-old female has asymptomatic lesions on face from past 2 months and similar lesions also present in 3 -year-old daughter. What is the causative agent of the lesions?
explanation:
Molluscum contagiosum virus causes characteristic skin lesions consisting of single or, more often, multiple, rounded, dome-shaped, umbilicated papules that are 2-5 mm

Molluscum contagiosum virus is an unclassified member of the Poxviridae family.

The molluscum contagiosum virus may be inoculated along a line of minor skin trauma (eg, from shaving), resulting in lesions arranged in a linear pattern - PseudoKoebners.

Reference: Rook’s textbook of dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 25, Page 12

question_text: A 60 year old patient presented with lesions as shown below. Which of the following is the principal antigen involved?
explanation:
Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is the most common autoimmune subepidermal blistering disorder, representing 80% of subepidermal immunobullous cases.

The immunological role comprise autoantibodies against 2 parts of the basal keratinocyte hemidesmosomal proteins BP antigen 230 (BPAG1) and BP antigen 180 (BPAG2 or type XVII collagen). The principal antigen is BPAG 2. These antigens play an essential part in the adhesion complexes that promote epithelial-stromal adhesion.

Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 50, Page 11

question_text: A 45-year-old male had multiple hypo anesthetic mildly erythematous large plaques on trunk and extremities. His ulnar and lateral popliteal nerves on both sides were enlarged. The most probable diagnosis is:
explanation:
The lesions of BT leprosy are often hypopigmented hypo-aesthetic macule/plaques. Slowly, the lesions enlarge by peripheral spread, and the margins become elevated. Then the central area becomes atrophic and depressed. Although any peripheral nerve may be enlarged, most commonly affected are ulnar, posterior auricular, peroneal and post-tibial.

Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9th edition, Chapter 28, page 10

question_text: A patient presented with itchy lesions and he applied steroids on it. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Tinea incognito is a type of dermatophyte infection modified by corticosteroid (systemic or topical) and other immunosuppressive agents.

Corticosteroid is prescribed for pre-existing disease or given mistakenly for the treatment of misdiagnosed tinea.

The history is quite characteristic; the patient is often initially satisfied with the treatment, but the eruption relapses, with varying rapidity once the drug is stopped.

he clinical manifestation of tinea incognito varies greatly, makes its diagnosis difficult and can easily lead to misdiagnosis, preventing prompt an appropriate treatment

question_text: A 25 year old man with multiple episodes of GTCS was prescribed phenytoin by the treating physician. After 7 days, he presents with mutliple targetoid lesions on the body and mucosal findings shown in the image. Which of the following will predispose to the condition shown here?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation (targetoid lesions, mucosal involvement, onset after phenytoin) is suggestive of Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS).

Phenytoin/fosphenytoin is contraindicated in individuals with the "HLA-B*1502-positive" allele due to significantly increased risk of phenytoin-induced cutaneous adverse reactions of Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN).

Explanation for the other options:

  • HLA B5801 is associated with a severe cutaneous reaction (SJS/TEN) induced by allopurinol.
  • HLA DQ2, DR3, DR4 are associated with various autoimmune disorders (e.g., Celiac disease, Type 1 Diabetes).
  • HLA DR4 is associated with rheumatoid arthritis and other conditions.

Key Takeaways:

The presence of the HLA-B*1502 allele in certain populations (especially South East Asian) significantly predisposes individuals to SJS/TEN when taking aromatic anticonvulsants like phenytoin or carbamazepine.

question_text: A 6-year-old boy presents to the OPD with clinical image as shown and and eyes that rapidly dart side-to-side. The patient most likely has a defect in which enzyme?
explanation:
• The patient's presentation is most consistent with oculo-cutaneous albinism (OCA).
  • The presence of white skin, white hair and nystagmus, noted as "eyes that rapidly dart from side-to-side," is sufficient to suspect albinism.
  • OCA, type 1a is caused by a tyrosinase gene mutation. Tyrosinase is imperative for melanin production, and individuals with OCA are melanin deficient.
  • Because melanin is the major photoprotective pigment in the skin, hypomelanotic individuals are at increased risk for solar-damage and UV-associated malignancies, such as squamous cell carcinoma

Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 70, page 6

question_text: 5 year old male child with multiple hyperpigmented macules over trunk. On rubbing the lesions with a back of pen, following finding is noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Mastocytosis is a disorder characterized by mast cell accumulation, commonly in the skin, bone marrow, gastrointestinal (GI) tract, liver, spleen, and lymphatic tissues.

Urticaria pigmentosa (UP) is the most common cutaneous mastocytosis in children, but it can form in adults as well. It is considered a benign, self-resolving condition that often remits in adolescence.

UP is caused by several activating mutations in the KIT gene

UP has small, monomorphic tan to brown macules or papules distributed mainly on the trunk and classically spares the central face, palms, and soles.

Darier's sign is the formation of a wheal upon stroking or rubbing skin lesions and suggests the diagnosis of cutaneous mastocytosis. The wheal forms due to the release of mast cell mediators, which can contribute to the systemic symptoms that may occur after stroking the lesion.

The hallmark finding histologically for UP is having an increased amount of mast cells in the dermis. Mast cell nuclei are rounded with surrounding ample cytoplasm, producing a 'fried egg' appearance.

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 46, page 4

question_text: The clinical image as shown below is characteristic of which disease?
explanation:
Clinical features of linear IgA bullous disease/ CBDC:

Location:

May occur anywhere on the body

In children, usually found on the lower abdomen, thighs, and groin.

In adults, the limbs, face, and truck are more commonly affected.

Approximately 50% of people have blisters and ulcers on the lips and inside the mouth.

Presentation:

Round or oval filled with clear fluid

Small (vesicles) or large (bullae)

May arise from normal, red flat, or elevated patches of skin

Typically found in rings (annular lesions) in children - new blisters tend to arise in a ring around an existing blister known as the 'string of beads' sign

Groups of small blisters may be described as a 'cluster of jewels' or 'crown of jewels'.

Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition Chapter 50, Page 33

question_text: Which of the following is false about DRESS syndrome ?
option_a: Phenytoin and carbamezapine are most common drugs
explanation:
Drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) syndrome is a distinct, severe, idiosyncratic reaction to a drug characterized by a prolonged latency period. It is followed by a variety of clinical manifestations, usually fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, and a wide range of mild-to-severe systemic presentations.

DRESS syndrome is a complex syndrome with a broad spectrum of clinical features.

The clinical manifestations are not immediate and usually appear 2 to 8 weeks after introduction of the triggering drug.

Common features consist of fever, rash, LAP, hematological findings (eosinophilia, leukocytosis, etc.), and abnormal liver function tests, which can mimick viral hepatitis.

The cutaneous manifestations typically consist of an urticarial, maculopapular eruption.

Visceral involvement (hepatitis, pneumonitis, myocarditis, pericarditis, nephritis, and colitis) is the major cause of morbidity and mortality in this syndrome.

Many cases are associated with leukocytosis with eosinophilia (90%) and/or mononucleosis (40%). Atypical lymphocytes are also seen.

Antiepileptic medications, such as phenytoin and Phenobarbital, are thought to be the predominant cause of DRESS syndrome.

DRESS syndrome must be recognized promptly and the causative drug withdrawn.

Treatment is largely supportive and symptomatic; corticosteroids are often used

Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9th edition, Chapter 119, page 4

question_text: What is the causative organism of this asymptomatic lesion on the palm?
explanation:
Tinea nigra is an uncommon superficial dermatomycosis usually caused by Hortaea werneckii.

Tinea nigra is characterized by the presence of a painless brown-to-black macule. The macule appears insidiously as a small dark spot.

The lesions are typically solitary, typically located on the palmar surfaces of the hands or plantar surfaces of the feet, and they may extend to the fingers or toes.

Reference: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 32, Page 14

question_text: Pseudo Darier sign is seen in
explanation:
Congenital smooth muscle hamartoma is defined as a rare asymptomatic benign skin defect detected in newborns and young children. Clinically it manifests as a hyperpigmented or skin-colored plaque where prominent vellus hairs may be observed. The condition is characterized by the proliferation of smooth muscle bundles in the dermis, which can reach the hypodermis where a connection to the hair follicle may occur A diagnostic clue in our case was the pseudo-Darier's sign, which is present in 50% of cases of smooth muscle hamartoma. It appears after rubbing the lesion, due to the contraction of the piloerector muscle, and is characterized by skin indentation, piloerection, and color accentuation in a fleeting way.

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 75, page 20

question_text: Pseudo bubo formation is seen in :
explanation:
Granuloma Inguinale

Genital ulcerative disease caused by the intracellular gram-negative bacterium Klebsiella granulomatis (formerly known' as Calymmatobacterium granulomatis)

  • Painless, slowly progressive ulcerative lesions on the genitals or perineum without regional lymphadenopathy, subcutaneous granulomas (Pseudo buboes)
  • Lesions are highly vascular (beefy red appearance) and bleed on touch

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 30, page 25

question_text: A patient presented with multiple red, purple, flesh-colored, or colorless papules on the right arm. He is known to be HIV positive. These lesions are caused by:
explanation: Bacillary angiomatosis, a treatable opportunistic infection, was initially reported as atypical subcutaneous infection in patients with advanced HIV disease and as epithelioid angiomatosis. The agents causing this infection, initially designated as Rochalimaea, have been reclassified as Bartonella. The term bacillary angiomatosis is being replaced by Bartonella infection because the infectious agents causing this condition have been identified as two species of Bartonella - B. henselae and B. Quintana. Bartonella henselae is most often transmitted through a cat scratch or bite, though ticks and fleas may also act as a vector. Bartonella quintana is usually transmitted by lice. It can manifest in people with AIDS and rarely appears in those who are immunocompetent.

question_text: A 8-year old boy presented with given clinical condition. Which of the following is incorrect statement regarding the diagnosis?
option_b: Most common form of cutaneous Tuberculosis in children
explanation:
Explanation:

Lesions of endogenous cutaneous tuberculosis arise from the breakdown of skin over a subcutaneous focus of M. tuberculosis.

Scrofuloderma (tuberculosis colliquativa cutis) results from direct spread of infection from underlying lymph nodes, bone, or joints to the overlying skin.

It begins as a painless, red-brown, firm nodule that becomes indurated and subsequently breaks down to form discharging sinuses releasing watery, purulent, or caseous material.

These lesions commonly occur at prominent lymph node sites such as the neck, axillae, chest wall, and groin, and represent the most common form of cutaneous tuberculosis in children in India.

A more recent proposal emphasizes the mycobacterial load as a useful conceptual framework. Tuberculosis can be classified into:

  • Multibacillary forms: conditions with abundant mycobacteria, such as scrofuloderma, tuberculous chancre, and acute miliary tuberculosis.
  • Paucibacillary forms: conditions in which mycobacteria are difficult to isolate, such as lupus vulgaris and tuberculosis verrucosa cutis.

Within this classification, tuberculids represent the extreme end of the paucibacillary spectrum.

question_text: Which of the following statements is not true regarding Pityriasis Rubra Pilaris:
option_a: Isolated patches of normal skin are found
explanation:
The classic sequence of signs in Pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP)begins with a diffuse fine scale seen on the scalp.

Within weeks to months, lesions increase , coalescing into patches and plaques that progress in a cephalocaudal manner appear.

Characteristic orange-red hyperkeratotic follicular papules are prominent both within the patches of erythema and within adjoining areas of uninvolved skin. Various terms including "nutmeg grater" or "exaggerated gooseflesh" have been used to describe these follicular-based papules.

Involved skin is often sharply demarcated from adjacent uninvolved skin producing a very characteristic phenomenon coined "islands of sparing" or "skip areas."

At times, the disease may even evolve in to diffuse orange-red erythroderma. 

Another characteristic finding, also notable in children, is a unique red-orange waxy palmoplantar keratoderma (PPK) so-called "sandal-like" PPK

PRP occurs worldwide with no predilection for gender or ethnicity.

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 36, page 3

question_text: A 5 years old boy presented with lesions on the face for the last 3 months. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Molluscum contagiosum virus causes characteristic skin lesions consisting of single or, more often, multiple, dome-shaped, pearly white umbilicated papules.

Molluscum contagiosum is a viral disease caused by a Molluscipox virus, dsDNA poxvirus

Lesions arranged in a linear pattern -pseudokoebners phenomena

In adults, molluscum contagiosum most commonly is a sexually transmitted disease and more severe in HIV infected patients or chemotherapy/transplant patients

T/t - self-limited and heals spontaneously in 6-9 months

Although treatment is not required, it may help to reduce autoinoculation or transmission to close contacts and improve clinical appearance - cryotherapy or curettage

Reference: Rook’s textbook of dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 25, Page 12

question_text: A patient of lichen planus complains of nail deformities as shown. What is the clinical finding here?
explanation:
Explanation:

Discrete violaceous papules in the nail bed may lift and split the overlying nail plate longitudinally and split lateral edges angle forward to give a pup tent appearance. This has been referred as pup tent sign

Pterygium unguis is the hallmark of severe nail disease in lichen planus. It results from a focal destruction of the nail matrix with subsequent scar formation. As the nail plate is not formed at the affected site, the epithelium of the proximal nail fold attaches itself directly to the nail bed epithelium and both grow distally together to produce a wing-like deformity (Option C)

Tin-tack sign - scaly sign seen in Discoid lupus erythematosus (Option A).

Parrot beak nails are a benign deformity of the nail plate characterized by excessive, symmetric forward curvature (Option D).

question_text: Which of the following cutaneous tuberculosis is analogous to ghon focus in the lungs ?
explanation:
Cutaneous tuberculosis (CTB) manifestations are typically categorized based on the mechanism of propagation: exogenous, endogenous, or hematogenous

Analogous to how the Ghon complex is a key finding of primary pulmonary TB, the complex of the tuberculous chancre and regional adenopathy may serve as the cutaneous counterpart. These lesions typically occur after a local trauma,. A tuberculous chancre initially presents as a reddish-brown firm and nontender papulonodular lesion accompanied by lymph node enlargement. The lesion rapidly grows, then erodes to result in a painless, well-demarcated ulceration with a coarse granular base and , bluish margins, and undermined edges.

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th edition, chapter 27, page 6

question_text: Phrynoderma is NOT due to deficiency of:
explanation:
Phrynoderma

Phrynoderma characterized by spiny hyperkeratotic follicular papules

  • Distribution of lesions is bilateral and symmetrical in 70% of patients
  • Disease is localized elbows, knees, extensor extremities, and/ or buttocks
  • Deficiencies of vitamins A and E, B complex vitamins, and essential fatty acids have all been implicated in the etiology
  • Phrynoderma is associated with nutritional deficiencies
  • Often occurs as a result of malabsorption due to surgical or medical causes, such as small-bowel bypass surgery, colectomy and pancreatic insufficiency

question_text: A dermatology referral was called for a newborn baby. Which of the following is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Collodion baby refers to a newborn with a parchment-like membrane covering the entire body surface. The collodion baby is not a disease entity but phenotype common to several disorders. Collodion membrane at birth is gradually shed over 2 to 4 weeks usually revealing an ichthyosis phenotype.

A total of 60%-80% of children born with a collodion membrane eventually develop ichthyosis either nonbullous ichthyosiform erythroderma or lamellar ichthyosis

Ichthyosis vulgaris- baby is normal at birth

question_text: Ichthyosis vulgaris is inherited as:
explanation:
1. Ichthyosis is characterized by roughness, dryness and scaling of the skin.
  2. The essential defect in ichthyosis is abnormal keratinisation
  3. Inheritance: AD
  4. It may be subdivided into three subtypes on genetic and clinical grounds viz. ichthyosis vulgaris (autosomal dominant), ichthyosis nigricans (X-linked recessive) and Harlequin ichthyosis (autosomal recessive).

question_text: What is a key differentiating factor between pemphigus and bullous pemphigoid?
explanation:
• Pemphigus and pemphigoid both have an autoimmune component, but they differ in their immunopathology.
  • Immunofluorescence will demonstrate linear IgG deposits along the basement membrane in pemphigoid while IgG deposits are seen in the intercellular and transmembrane domains of keratinocytes in pemphigus Circulating IgG antibodies target hemidesmosomes in pemphigoid and desmosomes in pemphigus.
  • Mucous membrane involvement occurs in both pemphigus and pemphigoid. Lesions in Management of both conditions consists of immunosuppressive and immunomodulatory therapy to control host autoimmune reaction.

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th Edition, chapter 50, page 10

question_text: A patient presents with itchy lesions as shown. The causative organism is most likely to be:
explanation:
• The image: annular lesion with scaling, vesicles, pustules - Tinea
  • Tinea caused by dermatophytes (Trichophyton/ Microsporum/ Epidermophyton)
  • Trichophyton rubrum - MC cause of tinea corporis/cruris
  • Sporothrix causes linear nodules and sinuses along lymphatics;
  • Candida usually causes white creamy lesions for eg in oral cavity or erythematous itchy lesions in skin folds/on glans.

question_text: A 50 year old man presented with skin lesions as seen in the image below. On examination, painful swollen fingers were noted along with an the inflamed wrist joint. What is the most likely diagnosis ?
explanation:
The majority of patients have psoriasis prior to the onset of arthritis. In 70% of patients, the skin features of psoriasis develop prior to joint disease, in 20% of patients, the joint disease presents fi rst and in 10% the skin and joints are affected concurrently There is an association between more severe cutaneous psoriasis and the development of psoriatic arthritis. The prevalence of psoriatic arthritis is also increased in patients with nail and scalp psoriasis [ Early morning back stiffness may be the only clinical feature of sacro-iliitis or cervical spondylitis. Heel pain (a manifestation of enthesitis of the Achilles tendon) or plantar fasciitis may also be a presenting feature. Clinical examination may reveal evidence of dactylitis (sausage fingers) or swollen or tender joints. This may affect one joint in an asymmetric pattern or several joints simultaneously.

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 35, page 43

question_text: Satellite lesion is seen in which type of leprosy :
explanation:
Borderline tuberculoid leprosy (BT) presents with single or a few lesions only, but margin of the lesion is not so sharply demarcated from the surrounding normal skin, and there may be a few satellite lesions around the main lesions.

question_text: A patient presents to you for evaluation of lesions on face since 6 months. The lesions have a white adherent scales and keratotic plugging. What is the best course of action for this patient at this time?
option_d: Wide surgical excision with regional lymph node dissection
explanation:
1. Plaques with depigmented scarring in the centre, white adherent scaling and keratotic plugging , presents on photo-exposed areas like face -s/o - The patient has discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) or chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus.
  2. It is characterized by discrete lesions most often on the face, scalp, or ears.
  3. The lesions are usually erythematous papules or plaques with a thick white adherent scale that occludes hair follicles(keratotic plugging).
  4. Carpet tack sign /tin tack sign - positive
  5. The lesions persist for years and grow slowly.
  6. Treatment consists of topical or intralesional glucocorticoids.
  7. Systemic therapy with an aminoquinoline antimalarial - hydroxychloroquine may be indicated in extensive lesions.

Human herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8) is present in all forms of Kaposi sarcoma

Clinically, Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular lesion, and presents as a violaceous pink to purple plaque on the skin or mucocutaneous surfaces.

question_text: The most common premalignant tumour of skin is-
explanation:
Actinic keratosis/Solar keratosis/ Keratosis senilis -

Actinic keratoses are premalignant cutaneous lesions that may progress to squamous cell carcinoma. These lesions commonly appear on sun-exposed areas of the skin in individuals with a history of cumulative sun exposure.

Common locations for actinic keratoses include the face, scalp (bald or thinning hair), back of the arms, and dorsal aspect of the hands.

individuals with actinic keratosis may present with irregular, red, scaly papules or plaques on sun-exposed regions of the body

question_text: A HIV positive adult male presented with hilar lymphadenopathy and lung involvement presented with lesions on face as shown. CBNAAT was negative. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
In a HIV patient, there can be many differentials of umbilicated lesions on skin.

However, Umbilicated lesions on the skin + pulmonary complaints points towards a diagnosis of histoplasmosis.

Histoplasmosis is a granulomatous infection caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus.

Pulmonary involvement is the most common clinical presentation.

Cutaneous manifestations are reported to occur in 10% to 25% of AIDS patients with disseminated histoplasmosis.

The skin lesions are polymorphic papules, plaques pustules, nodules, mucosal ulcers.

Characteristic and often confusing lesions - lesions resembling molluscum contagiosum, umbilicated papules

Reference: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 31, 32, Page 32.82, 31.26

question_text: Maximum suppression of cell-mediated immunity occurs in:
explanation:
1. Lepromatous leprosy - Extensive cutaneous involvement and bilaterally symmetric lesions. Variable skin lesions, include macules, nodules, plaques, or papules. The borders of the lesions are ill defined
  2. Diffuse infiltration of the dermis between discrete lesions, and apparently normal skin usually contains bacilli(SSS+ from both lesions and normal skin).
  3. Loss of the lateral portions of the eyebrows (madarosis) is common and later on the skin of the face and forehead becomes thickened and corrugated (leonine facies), and the earlobes become pendulous (Buddha ear). Septal perforation and nasal collapse leads to saddlenose
  4. Nasal stuffiness and epistaxis, are common early symptoms.
  5. Anterior portion of the eye can be involved - keratitis and iridocyclitis.
  6. In men, infiltration and scarring of the testes lead to sterility. Gynecomastia is common.
  7. Glove and stocking anaethesia Is seen, No lesional anaesthesia.
  8. Histological examination - diffuse granulomatous reaction with macrophages, large foam (Virchow or lepra) cells with intracellular bacilli. Globi+ Grenz zone+

question_text: A patient presents with multiple anogenital warts. The biopsy of these lesions showed squamous atypia. Which of the following human papillomavirus types are considered high-risk?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The image and history indicate condyloma acuminata (anogenital warts), most caused by HPV types 6 and 11.
  • The biopsy showing squamous atypia raises concern for progression to high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL) or malignancy, which is associated with high-risk HPV types.
  • Among the listed options, HPV 18 is a high-risk oncogenic strain. Along with HPV 16, it is strongly linked to cervical, anal, penile, vulvar, and oropharyngeal cancers.
  • HPV 18 is particularly associated with cervical adenocarcinoma.

HPV and oncogenic potential:

  • Low-risk types (HPV 6, 11): Cause benign anogenital warts and recurrent respiratory papillomatosis.
  • High-risk types (HPV 16, 18, 31, 33, 45): Cause cervical intraepithelial neoplasia and cancers of the cervix, vulva, anus, penis, and oropharynx.
  • HPV 2: Associated with common cutaneous warts (verruca vulgaris), not anogenital warts.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

HPV 2 (Option A): Causes common skin warts (verruca vulgaris). It is not linked to anogenital warts or malignancy.

HPV 6 (Option C): A low-risk HPV type causing benign anogenital warts. It does not carry malignant potential.

HPV 11 (Option D): Another low-risk type, associated with genital warts and recurrent respiratory papillomatosis. It is not linked to cancer.

Key Takeaway:
HPV types 16 and 18 are the most important high-risk oncogenic strains, associated with cervical and other anogenital cancers. In contrast, HPV types 6 and 11 are low-risk and cause benign genital warts. Biopsy showing atypia in genital lesions should raise suspicion for infection with a high-risk strain such as HPV 18.

question_text: Topical antifungal therapy is the first-line therapy for uncomplicated cases of oral candidiasis. A patient on immunosuppressives develops white lesions on the tongue which cannot be rubbed off. What is the causative agent?

    • Seen mostly on the lateral margin of the tongue.

question_text: This appearance on KOH scaring is seen in:
explanation:
Pityriasis Versicolor

  • Pityriasis versicolor, is a frequent, benign, superficial fungal infection of the skin.
  • Pityriasis versicolor is caused by Malassezia, a dimorphic lipophilic fungus, also known as Pityrosporum. It is a component of normal skin flora
  • The main species: Malassezia furfur, Malassezia globose
  • Malassezia can cause pityriasis versicolor when it converts to its pathogenic filamentous form.
  • CF: multiple, well-demarcated, oval, finely scaling patches. Skin lesions may be hypopigmented, hyperpigmented
  • The diagnosis is confirmed by microscopic examination of scales soaked in potassium hydroxide examination, which demonstrates the typical grape-like clusters of yeast cells and long hyphae
  • Woods lamp: pale yellow fluorescence
  • Topical & oral medications used. Antifungal agents include imidazole (clotrimazole 1%, ketoconazole 2%, econazole, isoconazole, miconazole), ciclopirox olamine 1%, oral azoles. Some nonspecific antifungal agents (sulfur plus salicylic acid, selenium sulfide 2.5%, and zinc-pyrithione) also used.
  • Terbinafine and griseofulvin not used.
