question_text: Identify the condition in the image.
explanation:
Contact leukoderma occurs due to the destruction of melanocytes following exposure to specific chemicals. Common culprits include:

  • Monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone (MBEH): Found in rubber gloves treated with this compound.
  • Para-tertiary butyl phenol (PTBP): Used in adhesives like bindi glue.
  • Para-phenylenediamine (PPD): Found in hair dyes and a leading cause of cosmetic-related leukoderma.

These chemicals trigger a toxic reaction, resulting in depigmentation of the skin.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

(A) Vitiligo:

An autoimmune condition causing melanocyte destruction but not due to chemical exposure. It has a progressive course and often symmetrical distribution.

(B) Piebaldism:

A rare genetic condition characterized by stable, congenital hypopigmented patches due to melanocyte migration defects. Typically present since birth.

(C) Albinism:

A genetic condition resulting in a lack of melanin production in the skin, hair, and eyes. Unlike contact leukoderma, it is systemic and not due to external exposure.

Key Takeaway: Contact leukoderma is an acquired depigmentation caused by chemical exposure, unlike autoimmune or genetic conditions like vitiligo, piebaldism, and albinism.

Explanation:

Acne Excoriee (AKA excoriated acne and picker's acne) is an excoriation disorder in which patients have a conscious, repetitive, and uncontrollable desire to pick, scratch, or rub acne lesions.

Obsessive-Compulsive (OCD) and Related Disorders are usually underlying in patients presenting with such a diagnosis.

Excoriated lesions vary in size (millimetres to several centimetres) and shape (linear/angular to circular/oval). Ultimately, the repeated picking results in erosions, ulcerations, and long-term scarring with hyper or hypopigmentation.

It is essential first to identify any underlying psychological disorder that could account for skin-picking behaviour.

question_text: A 22 yr Male Developed Pigmentation over upper chest for the last 2 years as shown in image. What is the diagnosis?

The most common sites involved are the shoulder, scapular area, and the upper arms

question_text: A 7 years old child presents with freckles, telangiectatic spots, photosensitivity, microcephaly. Sibling also suffers from similar symptoms. The diagnosis is:
explanation:
Explanation:

Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is a rare autosomal recessive genodermatosis that results due to mutations in nucleotide excision repair.

The nucleotide excision repair system is capable of removing ultraviolet-induced damage to DNA, such as pyrimidine dimers and pyrimidines 6-4 pyrimidones. The progression of xeroderma pigmentosum is due to the accumulation of unrepaired DNA damage

All patients with xeroderma pigmentosum will present with skin changes secondary to severe sun sensitivity. Patients may also present with oral, ophthalmologic, and/or neurologic manifestations of the disease.

The condition characteristically demonstrates severe photosensitivity, skin pigmentary changes, malignant tumor development, and occasionally progressive neurologic degeneration

Characteristic features include:

  • Severe photosensitivity
  • Freckles and pigmentary changes
  • Telangiectatic patches
  • Early-onset skin cancers
  • Neurologic and ophthalmologic involvement in some cases

The presence of photosensitivity, freckles, neurologic signs (microcephaly), and sibling involvement strongly support XP.

Cockayne syndrome (Option B): Photosensitivity is present but lacks UV-induced skin cancers and pigmentary freckles typical of XP.

Bloom's syndrome (Option C): Features include growth retardation and photosensitivity but has butterfly rash and chromosomal instability, not classical XP features.

Neurofibromatosis type II (Option D): Characterized by bilateral vestibular schwannomas; no severe photosensitivity.

Key Takeaways:

  • XP = defect in nucleotide excision repair.
  • Presents with early photosensitivity, freckling, pigmentary changes.
  • High risk of skin cancers in childhood.

question_text: A patient has a history of severe sunburn after only a few minutes of sun exposure. They also have freckles in sun exposed areas, dry skin and changes in pigmentation. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Patients with Xeroderma pigmentosa develop severe sunburns after minimal sun exposure, leading to early onset of freckling, multiple actinic keratoses, and various skin cancers (SCC, BCC, melanoma) at a young age. Other features can include dry skin (xerosis) and pigmentary changes (hypo- and hyperpigmentation). Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is a rare autosomal recessive genetic disorder characterized by an extreme sensitivity to ultraviolet (UV) radiation due to a defect in DNA repair mechanisms, specifically nucleotide excision repair (NER).

  • Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER): A critical DNA repair pathway that fixes damage caused by UV radiation (e.g., pyrimidine dimers). In XP, this pathway is deficient.
  • Photosensitivity: An abnormal or exaggerated reaction to sunlight.
  • Poikiloderma: A combination of atrophy, telangiectasias, and pigmentary changes (both hypo- and hyperpigmentation) often seen in chronic sun-damaged skin or certain genetic disorders.

Explanation of other options:

Bloom syndrome (Option B): Bloom syndrome is another rare genetic disorder with photosensitivity, but its classic presentation includes characteristic facial features (telangiectatic erythema, photosensitivity, microcephaly), growth retardation, and increased risk of various cancers, not typically the severe sunburn and extensive freckling pattern described.

Warts (Option C): Warts are benign skin growths caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. They are not associated with generalized severe photosensitivity, dry skin, or widespread pigmentary changes.

Melanocytic nevus (Option D): A melanocytic nevus (mole) is a benign proliferation of melanocytes. While patients with XP will develop numerous nevi (and melanomas), a single nevus or even multiple nevi do not explain the severe sunburns, dry skin, or diffuse pigmentary changes.

Key Takeaways:

  • Xeroderma Pigmentosum is characterized by extreme photosensitivity and impaired DNA repair.
  • Clinical signs include severe sunburn, early onset of freckling, dry skin, and pigmentary changes.
  • Patients have a dramatically increased risk of skin cancer.

A lattice-like network of white lines called Wickham striae overlies the lesions but is most easily observed on the buccal mucosa where erosions can also be present

The majority of patients with cutaneous lesions spontaneously clear within 1 to 2 years after initial presentation and residual hyperpigmentation of the skin frequently results.

question_text: In epidermolysis bullosa acquisita, antibodies are present against antigens.
explanation:
Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (EBA) - rare, chronic autoimmune blistering disease that impacts both the skin and mucous membranes.

This condition arises due to autoantibodies targeting the NC1 domain of type VII collagen located within the lamina densa. The type VII collagen is a crucial component of anchoring fibrils within the dermal-epidermal junction and are responsible for attaching the epidermis to the underlying dermis.

When auto antibodies bind to type VII collagen, they cause the detachment of the epidermis, leading to subepidermal bullae.

The classic presentation involves a noninflammatory mechanobullous disease characterized by skin fragility, tense blisters, erosions, scarring, milia formation, and postinflammatory dyspigmentation. These findings are localized to trauma-prone sites and extensor surfaces, including the elbows, knees, dorsal hands, and feet.

Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 50, Page 41

question_text: A female patient with a history of fever, photosensitivity, rash sparing nasolabial fold presents to OPD. Identify the condition?
explanation:
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by:

  • Multisystem involvement: Skin, joints, kidneys, blood cells, and nervous system.
  • Classic symptoms: Fever, photosensitivity, and rash sparing the nasolabial fold (characteristic of the malar rash in SLE).
  • Demographics: More than 90% of cases occur in women, commonly of childbearing age.

The presence of fever, photosensitivity, and a malar rash sparing the nasolabial fold strongly suggests SLE.

Brief Explanation of Incorrect Options:

  • (B) Dermatomyositis:
    • Features include a heliotrope rash (violaceous rash on the eyelids) and Gottron's papules (over knuckles), which are not seen in this case.
    • Photosensitivity can occur, but joint pain and fever are less prominent.
  • (C) Melasma:
    • A pigmentary disorder presenting with brownish hyperpigmentation over sun-exposed areas.
    • It lacks systemic features such as fever, joint pain, or photosensitivity-related inflammation.
  • (D) Rosacea:
    • Typically presents with erythema, papules, and pustules on the face, sparing the nasolabial fold.
    • Photosensitivity is not a hallmark, and systemic symptoms like fever and joint pain are absent.

Key Takeaway:

When a woman of childbearing age presents with fever, photosensitivity, joint pain, and a rash sparing the nasolabial fold, always consider SLE as the primary diagnosis.

question_text: Among the drugs used for treating leprosy, which medication is most commonly associated with skin hyperpigmentation?
explanation:
Explanation:

Clofazimine is an antileprosy drug known to cause skin pigmentation ranging from red-brown to black, especially with long-term use. The pigmentation occurs due to deposition of the drug intracellularly. Other side effects of clofazamine are Ichtyosis and GI disturbances like nausea and vomiting.

Explanation of Other Options:

Rifampicin (Option A): Causes orange-red discoloration of body fluids (urine, sweat, tears), but not hyperpigmentation of skin.

Dapsone (Option B): Main adverse effects include hemolysis (especially in G6PD deficiency) and methemoglobinemia, hepatitis and hypersensitivity reactions not skin pigmentation

Ofloxacin (Option D): A fluoroquinolone used as a second-line drug in leprosy, adverse effects are mainly GI upset, tendonitis, CNS effects, not pigmentation

Key Takeaways:

  • Clofazimine → skin hyperpigmentation (brown-black discoloration).
  • Rifampicin → red-orange discoloration of body fluids.
  • Dapsone → hemolysis, methemoglobinemia.
  • Ofloxacin → fluoroquinolone side effects (GI, tendon, CNS).

question_text: What is the probable diagnosis for a 28-year-old pregnant woman who is experiencing brownish pigmentation on her face, as shown in the image?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The clinical scenario of a woman experiencing brownish pigmentation on her face is likely to be melasma.
  • also known as chloasma or the mask of pregnancy.
  • A commonly acquired skin disorder that presents as bilateral blotchy brownish facial pigmentation.
  • It is strongly associated with hormonal changes, particularly during pregnancy and with oral contraceptive use, and exacerbated by sun exposure.
  • With hormonal changes, increased levels of estrogen and progesterone stimulate an increase in melanin production.
  • Females are affected more than males.

Explanation of other options:

Melanoma (Option B):

A serious form of skin cancer that can appear as a new, changing, or irregular mole or pigmented lesion. While it can be brownish, it is usually asymmetrical, has irregular borders, varied color, a diameter greater than 6mm, and evolves over time (ABCDEs of melanoma). It is typically a solitary lesion and not a diffuse, symmetrical facial pigmentation as described for this pregnant woman.

Normal sun tan (Option C):

A normal sun tan results from increased melanin production in response to UV exposure, leading to a generalized darkening of the exposed skin. While sun exposure can exacerbate melasma, the specific pattern of brownish patches on the face in a pregnant woman is beyond a "normal" tan and points to a physiological hyperpigmentation disorder.

Basal cell carcinoma (Option D):

Most common skin cancer found in sun-exposed parts of the body. It often presents as a pearly nodule with telangiectasias, a sore that doesn't heal, or a scar-like lesion. It does not typically manifest as diffuse brownish facial pigmentation in this manner.

Key Takeaways:

  1. Melasma is a common cause of facial hyperpigmentation during pregnancy ("mask of pregnancy").
  2. It presents as symmetrical, brownish patches on sun-exposed areas of the face.
  3. Hormonal influences and sun exposure are key contributors to melasma development.

question_text: What are the associated symptoms of the disease which presents with
explanation:
Pellagra is a nutritional disorder caused by niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency, which leads to systemic disease with clinical manifestations affecting the skin, gastrointestinal tract, and nervous system.

The pellagra syndrome is historically characterized by the 4 D's:

  • Dermatitis
  • Diarrhea
  • Dementia
  • Death

The characteristic skin rash has a typical photosensitive distribution, with well-defined borders, mostly observed on the face, neck (forming the so-called Casal's necklace), the dorsum of the hands, and the extensor surfaces of the forearms.

Gastrointestinal involvement includes intractable diarrhea, stomatitis, and glossitis.

Neurocognitive impairment includes apathy, memory loss (dementia).

Niacin deficiency should especially be suspected in:

  • Corn/maize eaters
  • Chronic alcoholism
  • Malnutrition
  • Malabsorption
  • Hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis
  • Drugs like isoniazid, ethionamide, 6-mercaptopurine, estrogens
  • Carcinoid syndrome

Reference: Rooks Textbook of Dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 63, page 63.15

Incorrect Options:

  • B: Alopecia - While alopecia can be seen in certain conditions like iron deficiency anemia, it is not characteristic of pellagra.
  • C: Glossitis - Glossitis is seen in pellagra but it is a part of the gastrointestinal involvement, not the primary defining symptom.
  • D: None of the above - This is incorrect, as diarrhea is a hallmark symptom of pellagra.

Key Takeaway:

Pellagra is primarily caused by niacin deficiency and manifests with the 4 D's: dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia, and if untreated, death. The characteristic skin rash is photosensitive, often seen on the face, neck, and hands, while gastrointestinal symptoms such as diarrhea are commonly associated with the condition.

question_text: One year old child presents with eczematous dermatitis over face (Image shown). His mother has the history of bronchial asthma. Diagnosis?
explanation:
Atopic dermatitis is a chronic, non-contagious inflammatory skin condition commonly present in infants. It is strongly associated with a family or personal history of atopy (e.g., asthma, hay fever).

  • Clinical Features:
    • Eczematous dermatitis typically appears on the face in infants.
    • Severe itching, redness, oozing, and cracked skin are hallmark signs.
    • Symptoms are worsened by scratching, leading to an increased risk of secondary infections.
  • Cause:
    • Genetic factors (e.g., filaggrin deficiency).
    • Immune system dysfunction and skin barrier abnormalities.
    • Environmental triggers.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

  • (A) Infantile Eczematous Dermatitis:
    • A descriptive term, but it lacks specificity and does not encompass the atopic nature or association with family history of atopy.
  • (B) Seborrheic Dermatitis:
    • Presents with greasy scales on areas rich in sebaceous glands (e.g., scalp, face, neck). It is not related to atopy and does not typically cause severe itching or oozing lesions.
  • (C) Airborne Contact Dermatitis:
    • Caused by exposure to airborne allergens or irritants, affecting exposed areas like the face and neck in adults. It is uncommon in infants and does not have a strong association with atopy.

Key Takeaway:

Atopic dermatitis in infants commonly presents with eczematous lesions on the face and is associated with a personal or family history of atopy (e.g., asthma, hay fever). Recognizing the genetic and environmental triggers is crucial for management.

question_text: A patient presents with an itchy lesion in the infra-axillary region. He developed a similar rash at the same site every time he takes Cotrimoxazole. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Fixed drug eruption is a type of drug-induced reaction that recurs at the same site upon re-exposure to the same drug
  • It commonly appears as well-demarcated, erythematous, or bullous lesions followed by slate-brown pigmentation
  • Lesions often affect the mucosa, genitalia, perianal areas, or flexures like the infra-axillary region
  • It is strongly associated with drugs like Cotrimoxazole, NSAIDs, tetracyclines, and sulfonamides
  • The hallmark is the recurrence of lesions at the exact same location after repeated exposure
  • In this patient, the same itchy rash occurs at the same site after Cotrimoxazole, strongly suggesting a Fixed drug eruption

Explanation of Other Options:

Drug allergy (Option A) is a general term that includes many types of hypersensitivity reactions; it doesn't specifically explain recurrence at the same site, which is a hallmark of Fixed Drug Eruption (FDE).

Immunological drug reaction (Option C) is a broad category and does not fit the localized, recurrent nature seen in this patient.

Contact dermatitis (Option D) results from external allergen exposure and usually causes itchy, spreading rashes, but does not typically recur at the same site in response to an oral drug like Cotrimoxazole

question_text: A patient presented with blisters on the body. The bedside test findings are shown below. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Pemphigus Intra-epidermal bullous disorder characterised clinically by blisters and histologically by acantholysis.

  • The earliest change is intercellular edema with loss of attachments in the basal layer. Suprabasal cells separate to form clefts and blisters, while basal cells remain attached to the basement membrane, creating a "row of tombstones" appearance. Blister cavities contain acantholytic cells detectable on Tzanck smear. Clefting may involve adnexal structures. Eosinophilic spongiosis can precede blistering, and the superficial dermis shows a mild mixed inflammatory infiltrate, sometimes with eosinophils.
  • Diagnostic tests:
    • Tzanck smear: Show acantholytic cells
    • Biopsy of bulla:Split in supra-basal layer, floatingacantholytic cells

  • Cicatricial Pemphigoid (Option C): Blisters are subepidermal and tense
  • Dermatitis herpetiformis (Option D): Bedside tests do not show blister extension or easy rupture like pemphigus vulgaris

question_text: A 5-year-old child presents with intense itching and tense blisters on the body, as shown in the image. Direct immunofluorescence demonstrates a linear IgA band along the basement membrane zone. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Linear IgA Dermatosis (LAD) (Chronic bullous disease of childhood) is an immune-mediated subepidermal blistering disorder identified by uniform linear IgA deposition along the skin's basement membrane zone. It is distinct from dermatitis herpetiformis based on differences in immunopathology, immunogenetics, and absence of association with gluten-sensitive enteropathy.

  • LAD is more common after puberty. Its clinical features resemble dermatitis herpetiformis but with more pronounced blistering. Patients show combinations of annular or grouped papules, vesicles, and bullae arranged symmetrically on the trunk and limbs, including elbows, knees, and buttocks. The lesions are very itchy but usually less severe than in dermatitis herpetiformis.
  • Mucosal lesions are significant and may present as large, painless oral erosions or ulcerations, isolated oral disease, or widespread skin involvement with oral lesions similar to cicatricial pemphigoid. LAD is the same condition as chronic bullous disease of childhood (CBDC), a rare blistering disorder that mainly affects children under 5 years.
  • Circulating autoantibodies against different epidermal basement membrane antigens have been detected. LAD has been linked to medications such as vancomycin, lithium, phenytoin, sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim, furosemide, captopril, diclofenac, and others. There is a slight association with lymphoid malignancies and reports of coexisting ulcerative colitis.
  • Treatment includes dapsone or sulfapyridine, and many patients may also need low-dose prednisone. A gluten-free diet does not improve the condition. Chronic bullous disease of childhood presents with widespread blistering on the upper limbs and trunk in young children, with both tense and flaccid blisters arranged in groups and minimal surrounding inflammation.

question_text: Young female came with complaint of bizarre shaped lesion over hand as shown in the image. Diagnosis?
explanation:
Dermatitis artefacta is a condition in which skin lesions are solely produced or inflicted by the patient's own actions. This usually occurs as a result or manifestation of a psychological problem.The condition is also known as factitial dermatitis

  • Patients present with lesions that are difficult to recognise and do not conform to those of known dermatoses.
  • Lesions are often in bizarre shapes with irregular outlines in a linear or geometric pattern,
  • Lesions are usually clearly demarcated from surrounding normal skin.
  • The appearance of lesions varies depending on methods used to injure the skin.
  • Lesions may be produced by a variety of mechanical or chemical means, including fingernails, sharp or blunt objects, lit cigarettes and caustic chemicals.
  • Lesions do not evolve gradually but emerge almost overnight without any prior signs or symptoms.
  • They are usually found on sites that are readily accessible to the patient's hands, e.g. face, hands, arms or legs.
  • The patient will usually deny that the rash is self induced.

  • Intense pruritus
  • Often starts in early childhood
  • Atopic stigmata may be present (xerosis, Dennie-Morgan folds, allergic rhinitis, asthma)

question_text: A 22-year-old college student reports having small, depigmented skin patches that have persisted for more than two years, as shown in the accompanying image. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Vitiligo is an acquired disorder of pigmentation caused by the immune-mediated destruction of melanocytes in the basal layer of the epidermis. This loss of pigment-producing cells leads to sharply demarcated, chalk- or milky-white macules and patches. The disease can start at any age, although onset most often occurs in early adulthood and affects males and females equally, with some studies noting a slight female predominance.

Under a Wood's lamp, vitiligo lesions exhibit a characteristic bright white fluorescence, which helps distinguish them from other hypopigmented conditions. Electron microscopy further supports the diagnosis by demonstrating the complete absence of melanocytes.

A notable clinical feature is the Koebner phenomenon, where new depigmented lesions appear at sites of skin trauma.

MILKY WHITE INFLORESCENCE OF VITILIGO UNDER WOOD'S LAMP

Explanation for other options:

Melasma (Option A): Melasma is a common cause of facial hyperpigmentation, particularly in individuals with darker skin tones. It presents as symmetric, brown to gray-brown macules and patches, most often on sun-exposed areas of the face. Ultraviolet radiation and hormonal factors-such as the use of oral contraceptives or pregnancy-commonly aggravate the condition. Women are affected far more frequently than men.

Psoriasis(Option C): Psoriasis typically shows a bimodal age of onset, with peaks in late adolescence/early adulthood (around 16-22 years) and again in later adulthood (around 57-62 years). Patients often present with pruritic, well-demarcated erythematous plaques covered by silvery-white scales. A pale, ring-like halo known as the Woronoff ring may surround lesions during the healing phase. Common sites include the scalp, trunk, and extensor surfaces of the elbows and knees.

Dermatitis Herpetiformis (Option D): This chronic, intensely itchy dermatosis is closely associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathy (celiac disease). It usually begins in the fourth decade of life and characteristically involves extensor areas such as the elbows, knees, buttocks, and scalp. Lesions are grouped vesicles and papules that are often excoriated due to severe pruritus.

question_text: The given condition is seen in which micronutrient deficiency?
explanation:
Explanation:

Niacin (Vitamin B3) deficiency causes Pellagra, characterized by the classical "3 Ds":

  1. Dermatitis - photosensitive dermatitis on sun-exposed sites (face, neck, dorsum of hands, forearms). The rash is erythematous, later hyperpigmented with scaling. The Casal's necklace is a classical finding (hyperpigmented rash around the neck).
  2. Diarrhoea - due to gastrointestinal mucosal involvement.
  3. Dementia - due to neurologic impairment.

If untreated, Pellagra can progress to a 4th "D": Death. Flowchart: Pellagra Pathogenesis

Niacin deficiency → ↓NAD/NADP → Impaired cellular energy metabolism → Dermatitis (skin) + Diarrhoea (gut) + Dementia (CNS)

Explanation of Other Options:

Iron deficiency (Option A): Causes koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails), pallor, angular cheilitis, but not photosensitive dermatitis.

Copper deficiency (Option C): Leads to hypopigmented hair, anaemia, neutropenia, and neurological defects. Seen in conditions like Menkes disease. No pellagra-like dermatitis.

Selenium deficiency (Option D): Causes Keshan disease (cardiomyopathy), Kashin-Beck disease (osteoarthropathy). Dermatological findings are minimal, not pellagra-like.

The most fundamental and important step in combating atopic dermatitis (AD) is rehydration of the stratum corneum using emollients and moisturisers.

Topical steroids are gold standard in managing AD

Topical calcineurin inhibitors like tacrolimus, pimecrolimus are also useful in long term maintenance in AD and serve as non-steroidal altenatives

Crisaborole topical ointment 2% was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in December 2016 for mild-to-moderate atopic dermatitis in adults and children aged 2 years or older.

Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 41, page 30

question_text: Identify the incorrect statement regarding eczema.
option_a: All eczema is dermatitis, but not all dermatitis is eczema
option_c: Acute eczema is typically oedematous, vesicular and may be exudative
option_d: Chronic eczema shows spongiosis on histopathology
explanation:
Dermatitis is inflammation of the skin, typically characterized by itchiness, redness and a rash.

  • In eczema also, there is inflammation in skin and thus all eczema is dermatitis
  • But not all dermatitis is eczema
  • Pruritus is universally seen
  • Acute eczema is typically oedematous, vesicular and may be exudative, spongiosis is seen on histopathology
  • Chronic eczema shows dry lichenified lesions, which have acanthosis as primary finding in histopathology.

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th edition, chapter 39, page 3

question_text: A 55-year-old farmer with uncontrolled diabetes and hypertension presents with a widespread, severe, itchy rash on the face, arms, and legs. Which drug is most appropriate for treatment?
explanation:
Explanation:

In severe allergic contact dermatitis, systemic corticosteroids are usually the first-line treatment.

However, this patient has:

  • Uncontrolled diabetes-steroids worsen hyperglycaemia
  • Hypertension-steroids worsen blood pressure
    Therefore, steroids are contraindicated. (Option A)

Azathioprine is the safest and most appropriate immunosuppressive agent for severe allergic contact dermatitis when steroids cannot be used.

Management of severe allergic contact dermatitis:

  • Avoid allergen
  • Topical steroids for mild/moderate cases
  • Systemic steroids for severe cases, except when contraindicated
  • In steroid contraindication:
    • Azathioprine
    • Methotrexate
    • Cyclosporine (more nephrotoxic and riskier in uncontrolled hypertension) (Option D)

question_text: Interface dermatitis is seen in all of the following conditions except :
explanation:
Interface dermatitis includes conditions in which the primary pathology involves the "interface," i.e., the dermo-epidermal junction. The components of this "interface" include the basal layer of the epidermis, the dermo-epidermal junction, the papillary dermis.

Patho-physiologically, apoptosis/individual cell necrosis of keratinocytes is the most prominent feature in primary interface dermatitis. T-cell-mediated cytokine damage is the most likely mechanism resulting in these diseases.

Examples - Lichen planus, erythema multiforme, cutaneous LE, and acute graft vs host reaction, fixed drug eruptions

Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9th edition, Chapter 119, page 11

question_text: The microorganism associated with Seborrheic dermatitis is:
explanation:
Seborrheic Dermatitis

Seborrheic dermatitis (SD): inflammatory skin disease in areas rich in sebaceous glands, particularly the scalp, face, and body folds.

Pathogenesis: linked to the interplay of normal microscopic skin flora (especially Malassezia spp.), the composition of lipids on the skin surface and individual susceptibility.

The infantile (ISD) and adult (ASD) variants reflect the condition's bimodal occurrence.

infantile (ISD): firm, greasy scales on the crown and frontal regions of the scalp. It occurs in the first three months of life and is mild, self-limiting

ASD: Folliculocentric salmon-colored lesions with a yellowish greasy scale.

Sudden onset of severe SD should be a red flag for the presence of HIV-AIDS

Treatment:

  • Topical antifungals: Ketoconazole, Ciclopirox, Selenium sulphide
  • Topical steroids
  • Topical immunomodulators: Tacrolimus, Pimecrolimus

Reference: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 107, Page 1-2

question_text: A 5 year boy presented with itching and tense bullae on the body as shown in the image. The DIF shows linear IgA deposit in the BMZ. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
LINEAR IgA DERMATOSIS (LAD)

A rare, immune-mediated, subepidermal blistering skin disease defined by the presence of homogeneous linear deposits of IgA at the cutaneous basement membrane zone.

  1. It is clearly separate from dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) on the basis of immunopathology, immunogenetics, and lack of association with GSE.
  2. LAD most often occurs after puberty.
  3. Clinical manifestations are very similar to those of DH, but there is more blistering. Patients present with combinations of annular or grouped papules, vesicles, and bullae that are distributed symmetrically on trunk and extremities including elbows, knees, and buttocks. The lesions are very pruritic but less severe than those of DH.
  4. Mucosal involvement is important and ranges from large asymptomatic oral erosions and ulceration to severe oral disease alone, or severe generalized cutaneous involvement and oral disease similar to that in cicatricial pemphigoid.
  5. It is identical with chronic bullous disease of childhood(CBDC), which is a rare blistering disease that occurs predominantly in children <5 years.
  6. Circulating autoantibodies against various epidermal basement membrane antigens have been found.
  7. LAD has been associated with drugs: vancomycin, lithium, phenytoin, sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim, furosemide, captopril, diclofenac, and others.
  8. There is a small risk of lymphoid malignancies, and associated ulcerative colitis has been reported.
  9. Management: Patients respond to dapsone or sulfapyridine but in addition, most may require low-dose prednisone. Patients do not respond to a gluten-free diet.

Linear IgA dermatosis (chronic, bullous disease of childhood) Extensive blistering on the upper extremities and trunk in a 7-year-old child. As seen in the fig. blisters are both tense and flaccid. They are grouped and there is no notable inflammation.

Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 50, Page 33

question_text: Which of the following statements about lichenification is NOT true?
explanation:
Explanation:

Lichenification is characterized by thickened, leathery skin, not atrophy. Atrophy refers to thinning of the epidermis or dermis, which is the opposite of what occurs in lichenification.

Lichenification occurs due to chronic irritation or scratching, typically seen in:

  • Chronic eczema
  • Lichen simplex chronicus
  • Atopic dermatitis

  • Hyperpigmentation due to chronic inflammation
  • Hyperlinearity, where skin markings become prominent

question_text: What is the preferred drug of choice used in treating dermatitis herpetiformis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Dapsone is the drug of choice for treating a case of dermatitis herpetiformis.
  • Dapsone works in dermatitis herpetiformis by affecting neutrophil function and recruitment. It is used in doses of 25-150 mg/day and generally tolerated but may cause hematologic side effects such as hemolysis, methemoglobinemia, and agranulocytosis, requiring regular blood monitoring.
  • Non-hematologic reactions include dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome and peripheral neuropathy. Patients with G6PD deficiency are more prone to adverse effects, so G6PD testing is advised. Cimetidine can reduce dapsone toxicity.
  • Dapsone must be combined with a gluten-free diet, allowing dose reduction or withdrawal over time. Other useful sulphonamides include sulphamethoxypyridazine, sulphapyridine, and sulphasalazine. Systemic steroids offer little benefit, potent topical steroids help temporarily, colchicine has weak evidence, and JAK inhibitors may be beneficial.

question_text: Match the following diagnostic tests with their respective diseases.
explanation:
Explanation:

Patch Test → Contact Dermatitis (a-4):

  • Contact dermatitis is an eczematous condition and is a delayed type IV hypersensitivity to external allergens such as nickel, cosmetics, fragrances.
  • Patch testing is the gold standard investigation, where allergens are applied under occlusion and read after 48-96 hours to detect hypersensitivity reactions.

Slit Skin Smear → Leprosy (b-3):

  • Leprosy is a chronic granulomatous disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae, affecting skin and peripheral nerves.
  • Slit skin smear is performed from active lesions on ear lobes, fingers, toes, stained with Ziehl-Neelsen/Fite-Faraco, to demonstrate acid-fast bacilli (AFB). It helps in diagnosis, classification (multibacillary vs paucibacillary), and monitoring treatment response.

Biopsy → Lupus Vulgaris (c-1):

  • Lupus vulgaris is a form of cutaneous tuberculosis seen in individuals with high immunity.
  • It presents as slow-growing reddish-brown plaques with elevated borders and central atrophy.
  • The diagnosis is confirmed by skin biopsy, which typically reveals caseating granulomas, a hallmark of tuberculosis.

KOH Mount → Tinea Corporis (d-2):

  • Tinea corporis ("ringworm") is a superficial fungal infection caused by dermatophytes such as Trichophyton rubrum.
  • Lesions are annular, scaly, and sharply marginated.
  • The KOH mount is a rapid diagnostic test that dissolves keratin and demonstrates branching septate hyphae under microscopy.

Key Takeaway:

  • Contact Dermatitis → Patch Test (Type IV hypersensitivity)
  • Leprosy → Slit Skin Smear (AFB detection)
  • Lupus Vulgaris → Biopsy (granulomas with caseation)
  • Tinea Corporis → KOH Mount (branching fungal hyphae)

question_text: Which mineral deficiency leads to impaired wound healing, skin inflammation, diarrhoea, and hair loss?
explanation:
Explanation:

Zinc deficiency results in impaired wound healing, skin lesions, diarrhoea, and hair loss because of its essential role in cell growth, immunity, and tissue repair.

Explanation of other options:

Iron (Option A): Iron deficiency results in anaemia, tiredness, spoon-shaped nails, and glossitis, but not dermatitis or diarrhoea.

Calcium (Option B): Calcium deficiency causes tetany, muscle cramps, and osteomalacia, but does not result in hair loss or impaired wound healing.

Magnesium (Option C): Magnesium deficiency presents with neuromuscular hyperexcitability, tremors, and heart rhythm disturbances, but does not cause dermatitis or hair loss.

question_text: Dermatological manifestation of which of the following disease?
explanation:
• Pellagra is caused by a deficiency of niacin (vitamin B3), leading to a systemic condition that involves the skin, gastrointestinal system, and nervous system.
  • The hallmark clinical signs of pellagra are often referred to as the 4 D's: Dermatitis, Diarrhea, Dementia, and Death.
  • The dermatological manifestation of pellagra is characterized by a photosensitive rash, typically involving areas exposed to sunlight such as the face, neck (forming a "Casal's necklace"), the dorsum of the hands, and the extensor surfaces of the forearms.
  • In addition to skin involvement, pellagra also leads to gastrointestinal symptoms like diarrhea, and neurocognitive issues such as dementia.
  • Risk factors for pellagra include diets high in corn/maize (which is low in niacin), chronic alcoholism, malnutrition, malabsorption syndromes, and certain medications (e.g., isoniazid, ethionamide, 6-mercaptopurine).

Explanation of the Incorrect Options:

  • (B) Acrodermatitis enteropathica:
    • This condition is a zinc deficiency disorder, presenting with periorificial dermatitis, alopecia, and diarrhea. It is not associated with the same rash distribution or features seen in pellagra.
  • (C) Photodermatitis:
    • Photodermatitis refers to a skin reaction triggered by exposure to sunlight, but it is not a specific diagnosis. It can be seen in various conditions, including drug-induced photosensitivity and lupus, but it does not match the characteristic photosensitive rash seen in pellagra.
  • (D) Vitamin A deficiency:
    • Vitamin A deficiency can cause xerosis, night blindness, and keratomalacia, but it does not present with the photosensitive rash seen in pellagra. Instead, its dermatological manifestations are more related to dryness and scaling.

Key Takeaway:

Pellagra presents with photosensitive dermatitis, often in areas like the face, neck, and dorsum of the hands. It is typically caused by niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency and associated with diarrhea and dementia.

explanation:
Explanation:

Acrodermatitis enteropathica (AE) is a rare genetic disorder caused by a defect in zinc absorption, leading to severe zinc deficiency. It can also occur as an acquired condition due to inadequate zinc intake or malabsorption. The classic clinical triad of AE includes periorificial and acral dermatitis (rash around the mouth, anus, and on the hands/feet), alopecia (hair loss), and diarrhea. Zinc is an essential trace element crucial for numerous enzymatic functions, DNA synthesis, cell division, and immune function, hence its deficiency manifests with widespread systemic effects.

  • Genetic Acrodermatitis Enteropathica: Autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the SLC39A4 gene, which encodes for the zinc transporter protein ZIP4, primarily expressed in the intestine.
  • Acquired Acrodermatitis Enteropathica: Can be seen in conditions like malabsorption syndromes (e.g., Crohn's disease), alcoholism, bariatric surgery, or in infants on certain unsupplemented formulas or breastfed by mothers with low zinc levels.
  • Clinical Triad: Dermatitis, alopecia, and diarrhea.

Explanation of other options:

Iron (Option B): Iron deficiency leads to anemia (iron-deficiency anemia) and can cause symptoms like pallor, fatigue, pica, and koilonychia (spoon nails), but not acrodermatitis enteropathica.

Calcium (Option C): Calcium deficiency can lead to rickets/osteomalacia, tetany, and osteoporosis, but it does not cause acrodermatitis enteropathica.

Vitamin A (Option D): Vitamin A deficiency can cause night blindness, xerophthalmia (dry eyes), follicular hyperkeratosis (phrynoderma), and impaired immune function, but not acrodermatitis enteropathica.

Key Takeaways:

  • Acrodermatitis enteropathica is caused by zinc deficiency.
  • It presents with a classic triad of periorificial/acral dermatitis, alopecia, and diarrhea.
  • Zinc is critical for many physiological processes, explaining the diverse symptoms.

question_text: A malnourished man presents with photosensitive dermatitis over sun-exposed areas, chronic diarrhoea, and progressive memory disturbances. He also exhibits signs of apathy and glossitis. What is the most likely nutritional deficiency responsible for these symptoms?
explanation:
Explanation:

Niacin (Vitamin B3) deficiency causes pellagra.

Pellagra is characterised by the classic triad of symptoms:

  • Dermatitis
    • Bright red erythema in sun-exposed areas (face, ankles, feet)
    • Casal's necklace- ↑pigmentation around the neck
  • Diarrhoea, and
  • Dementia.

Causes of pellagra :

  • Dietary Deficiency- Maize and Sorghum-based diet
  • Impaired Tryptophan Metabolism
    • Factors Affecting Tryptophan to Niacin Conversion:
      • Vitamin B6 Deficiency
      • Medications: Isoniazid (INH), OCPs
      • Hormonal Influences: Estrogen metabolites hinder tryptophan metabolism.
      • Genetic Disorders: Inherited conditions like Hartnup disease can impede tryptophan absorption in the intestines and reabsorption in the kidneys
  • Carcinoid Syndrome
  • Other Contributing Factors:
    • Alcoholism: Interferes with nutrient absorption, including niacin and tryptophan.
    • Malabsorption Syndromes

Explanation of other options:

Riboflavin (Option B): Deficiency causes angular cheilitis, glossitis, and seborrheic dermatitis, but not the 3 Ds of pellagra.

Thiamine (Option C): Leads to beriberi (dry or wet) and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, involving cardiac and neurologic issues, not diarrhoea or dermatitis.

Biotin (Option D): Deficiency results in dermatitis, alopecia, and neurological symptoms, but not the classic triad of pellagra.

question_text: A patient got pricked by a rose thorn and after that, there are linear lesions along the lymphatics. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Linear lymphangitis starting from primary lesion by rose prick is suggestive of sporotrichosis.


Explanation of Other Options:

Chromoblastomycosis (Verrucous dermatitis) (Option B)

Causative agent: Pigmented (Dematiaceous fungi)

  • Fonsecaea pedrosoi
  • Phialophora verrucosa

Clinical feature: Rough warty, cauliflower like lesions over exposed (trauma prone) sites. MC on foot

Histopathology shows medlar/ sclerotic bodies/ copper penny bodies

Blastomycosis (Option C)

Caused by Blastomyces dermatitidis, a dimorphic fungus that primarily affects the lungs, causing symptoms similar to pneumonia.

Although it can cause skin lesions, these do not present as linear lesions along the lymphatics. It is not associated with rose thorn pricks and usually involves the lungs first.

Mucor rhizopus (Option D)

Caused by fungi such as Rhizopus, usually presents in immunocompromised patients and can affect the sinuses, lungs, or skin. However, it does not typically cause linear lesions along lymphatics, and it is not associated with trauma from rose thorns. Mucormycosis more commonly leads to necrotizing tissue infections.

Key Takeaway:

The lesions of sporotrichosis (lymphocutaneous type) typically begin as a painless papule or nodule at the site of inoculation, often progressing to an ulcer. Subsequently, a chain of similar, firm, red to purplish nodules or papules appears linearly along the lymphatic drainage pathway proximal to the initial lesion.

question_text: A 24-year-old male presents with asymptomatic, scaly lesions on the back, distributed symmetrically. Images of the lesions are shown below. Identify the disease and the pattern of lesions:
option_a: Collarette scale, Christmas tree pattern; Pityriasis rosea
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The image shows collarette scales with lesions arranged along the lines of Langer, producing the characteristic Christmas tree pattern, which is seen in pityriasis rosea.
  • Pityriasis rosea is an acute, self-limiting disorder of probable infective origin, commonly seen in children and young adults.
  • The disease typically begins with a herald patch - a large, sharply defined, red oval plaque with fine scale, most often on the trunk, neck, thigh, or arm.
  • After 5-15 days, multiple smaller lesions appear in crops, following Langer's lines in a Christmas tree pattern.
  • Lesions are pink, oval, with central clearing and a collarette of scale at the margins. Distribution is mainly on the trunk and proximal limbs, but may also involve the face, scalp, or rarely palms and genitalia.
  • Oral lesions occur in about 25% of cases. Symptoms are usually mild, with occasional pruritus, low-grade fever, malaise, or cervical lymphadenopathy.

Explanation of other options:

Wickham's striae; Lichen planus (Option B), Christmas tree pattern; Lichen planus (Option C): Lichen planus does not show the Christmas tree distribution. Instead, it is characterised by the classical six Ps: purple, polygonal, planar, pruritic, papules, and plaques. The diagnostic feature is Wickham's striae seen on the surface of the lesion.

Woronoff ring; Seborrheic dermatitis (Option D): Woronoff ring is seen in healing psoriasis, not seborrheic dermatitis. Seborrheic dermatitis involves seborrheic sites with greasy yellow scales, without collarette scaling or a Christmas tree pattern.

question_text: Which test out of the following will be positive in this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

Image shows erythematous plaques with singer scaling present over back suggestive of psoriasis vulgaris.

Bedside test for diagnosis of psoriasis:

  1. Gently scraping the lesion with a glass slide accentuates the silvery scales: positive Grattage test.
  2. Continued scraping reveals a glistening white adherent membrane called the Burkley'smembrane
  3. On removal of this membrane, punctate bleeding points are seen: positive Auspitz sign. Scraping removes the thin overlying epidermis, exposing and rupturing the dilated, superficial capillaries within the elongated dermal papillae

Explanation of Other Options:

Nikolsky sign (Option B)

Nikolsky sign is dislodgement of the intact superficial epidermis by a shearing force, indicating a plane of cleavage in the skin epidermal junctions. It is positive in pemphigus vulgaris, SJS-TEN, staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome.

Asboe Hansen test (Option C)

This "bulla spread sign" refers to the extension of a blister to adjacent unblistered skin when pressure is put on the top of the bulla. Seen in pemphigus vulgaris, bullous pemphigoid.

Patch test (Option D)

The patch test is used to diagnose allergic contact dermatitis, not psoriasis vulgaris. It helps identify specific allergens that may cause skin reactions.

Key Takeaway:

The Grattage test is used to diagnose psoriasis vulgaris. When the scales are scraped off, the Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding) is observed, which is characteristic of psoriasis. The test helps to distinguish psoriasis from other dermatological conditions.

question_text:
A patient presents with itchy papulovesicular lesions on the shoulder, back, arms and legs. The DIF results showed positivity for IgA deposits. What is the diagnosis?
20251129b47e9463-3461-4f37-9b27-efd1300c5aa7
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Granular IgA at the dermal papillae is characteristic of Dermatitis Herpetiformis (DH).
  • Dermatitis Herpetiformis is associated with subclinical gluten-sensitive enteropathy and HLA types B8/DRw3 and DQW2. It involves IgA autoantibodies directed against epidermal transglutaminase, with granular IgA deposits in the papillary dermis. Clinically, DH presents with extremely itchy, grouped papulovesicles over extensor sites such as elbows, knees, back, buttocks, scalp, and posterior neck. It usually occurs in the 2nd to 4th decades.
  • Histology shows subepidermal blisters with neutrophilic microabscesses at the tips of dermal papillae. DIF reveals granular IgA at the basement membrane zone. IgA deposits persist despite dapsone but reduce or disappear with a long-term strict gluten-free diet.
  • Linear IgA Disease (Option B): This condition shows linear IgA deposition along the basement membrane zone.
  • Herpes Gestationis (Option B): it is a pregnancy-associated autoimmune blistering disorder with linear IgG (not IgA) along the basement membrane zone.
  • Bullous Pemphigoid (Option D): Bullous pemphigoid also demonstrates linear IgG deposition at the basement membrane zone on DIF

question_text: A 3 year old female presented with skin lesions as shown in the image. There was a history of diarrhea. Which mineral deficiency can lead to this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image shows erythematous periorificial plaques. This distribution is suggestive of acrodermatitis enteropathica. Acrodermatitis enteropathica is a rare disorder associated with zinc deficiency. It presents with the classic triad of:

  • Peri-acral and periorificial dermatitis
  • Diarrhoea
  • Alopecia.

Explanation of Other Options:

Choice B: Selenium (Option B)

Selenium deficiency can cause various symptoms, such as muscle weakness and cardiomyopathy (Keshan disease), but it is not typically associated with skin lesions, especially in the context of diarrhea.

Niacin (Option C)

Niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency causes pellagra, which presents with the "3 D's": dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. Pellagra often causes a photosensitive rash.

Magnesium (Option D)

Magnesium deficiency can lead to muscle cramps, tremors, and seizures, but it does not typically cause skin lesions.

Key Takeaways:

Acrodermatitis enteropathica Presentation: Pediatric age

Zinc Defeciency

Classic triad of Peri-acral and periorificial dermatitis,Diarrhoea, Alopecia.

question_text: Which skin disease shows coral-red fluorescence under a Wood's lamp?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Erythrasma is a superficial skin infection caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum.
  • It presents as well-defined reddish-brown patches usually in groin or axilla region.
  • The characteristic feature of this condition is coral-red fluorescence under Wood's lamp, this is diagnostic clue for this condition.
  • This appearance is due to production of coproporphyrin III by the bacteria.

Explanation of Other Options:

Acanthosis Nigricans (Option B): It shows no immunoflourescence under woods lamp.

Allergic Contact Dermatitis (option C): no fluorescence under woods lamp, the charateristic lesion caused is eczema.

Cutaneous Candidiasis (Option D): No characteristic fluorescence under woods lamp.

question_text: A patient receiving anti-PD-1 immunotherapy (Nivolumab) presents with pruritus, eczema-like lesions, and urticarial rashes. Histopathological examination shows a subepidermal blister. Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) of the lesion demonstrates linear deposition of IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation and direct immunofluorescence findings are suggestive of bullous pemphigoid.

Bullous pemphigoid:

  • An IgG-mediated autoimmune disorder in which antibodies target the hemidesmosomes of the basement membrane zone (BMZ).
  • Unlike pemphigus, there is no acantholysis.
  • Clinically, it presents with tense, fluid-filled blisters, often associated with erythema, pruritus, and urticarial lesions.
  • A Tzanck smear may show eosinophilic infiltrates.
  • On histopathology, there is a subepidermal split, and the blister cavity contains numerous eosinophils (Image A).
  • Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) demonstrates linear deposition of IgG and C3 along the basement membrane (Image B).

Explanation of other options:

Dermatitis herpetiformis (Option A): Dermatitis herpetiformis is an IgA-mediated disorder which, on direct immunofluorescence, shows granular deposition of IgA in dermal papillae.

Pemphigus vulgaris (Option C): Pemphigus vulgaris is characterised by autoantibodies against desmoglein-3 and sometimes desmoglein-1. It presents with flaccid bullae, erosions. Histology shows a suprabasal blister with a row of tombstone appearances, and direct immunofluorescence demonstrates a fish-net pattern of intercellular IgG deposition.

Pemphigus foliaceus (Option D): Pemphigus foliaceus is due to autoantibodies against desmoglein-1 only. Histology shows a superficial intraepidermal split, and DIF reveals intercellular IgG deposition.

question_text: Darier's sign is positive in the following :
explanation:
• Darier's Sign :The skin characteristically urticates within minutes of gentle rubbing in children causing localized pruritus, redness and wheal, which subside within an hour.

It is not 100% specific for mastocytosis, since it has been described on rare occasions in juvenile xanthogranuloma and acute lymphoblastic leukaemia of neonates

question_text: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is seen in urticaria
explanation:
• Type I hypersensitivity is also known as an immediate reaction and involves immunoglobulin E (IgE) mediated release of antibodies against the soluble antigen. This results in mast cell degranulation and release of histamine and other inflammatory mediators.

Manifestations - anaphylaxis, urticaria, angioedema, food, and drug allergies

The allergens that result in a type I hypersensitivity - pollen, mites, or foods, drugs, etc

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 42, page 4

question_text: Acute urticaria resolves within:
explanation:
Acute urticaria resolves within 6 weeks. Urticaria longer than 6 weeks' duration is considered chronic.

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 42, page 5

question_text: A 17-year-old male presents to the clinic due to an intermittent rash as shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial medication for treating this patient's condition?
explanation:
• Prevention and avoidance of precipitating factors such as physical stimuli and stressors are important in managing urticaria. Most patients are asymptomatic, and pharmacotherapy should be restricted to symptomatic patients.
  • Choice therapy includes treatment with H1 antihistamines such as cetirizine or loratadine.

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 42, page 16

question_text: True about omalizumab is :
option_a: It is a chimeric monoclonal antibody against IgE
option_b: It is used in the treatment of chronic urticaria
option_d: Once a year dosing is enough
explanation:
• Omalizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody against human IgE.
  • It is given sub cutaneously every 2 to 4 weeks

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 42, page 18

question_text: Quincke's disease is:
explanation:
Angioedema

Giant Edema, Giant Urticaria, Hives, Nettle Rash, Quincke's disease

  • A vascular reaction, which involves subcutaneous or submucosal tissues so the skin overlying the swelling is normal in color & margins of swelling are indistinct
  • It commonly results in swelling of the lips, eyelids but may also affect pharynx, larynx

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 43, page 4

question_text: The condition shown in the following image is :
explanation:
• Angio-oedema is a deep, localized and self-limiting swelling of the skin and submucosal tissues due to a temporary increase in vascular permeability resulting from vasoactive mediators

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 43, page 4

question_text: A 7-year-old boy is brought by parents with abdominal pain, joint aches, and a rash on his legs and feet. He does not have a history of frequent nosebleeds, easy bruising, or other episodes of abnormal bleeding. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Immunoglobulin A vasculitis (IgAV), formerly Henoch-Schonlein purpura, involves the small vessels of the joints, kidneys, gastrointestinal tract, and skin.

The classic presentation of IgA vasculitis includes palpable purpura, gastrointestinal complaints, arthralgias, and renal involvement.

Reference: Rook's dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 102, Page 15

question_text: A patient with recurrent lip edema underwent Laboratory evaluation which shows decreased C4 and C1 INH (quantity and function) with normal C1q. The diagnosis is
explanation:
The 3 types of HAE can be differentiated with complement testing and, in the case of HAE with normal C1 inhibitor levels, genetic testing. Type I HAE is characterized by the following:

  • Low C1 esterase inhibitor (C1-INH) protein level
  • Low C4 level
  • Normal C1q level

Type II HAE is characterized by the following:

  • Normal or elevated, but dysfunctional, C1-INH level
  • Low C4 level
  • Normal C1q level

HAE with normal C1 inhibitor levels is characterized by the following:

  • Normal C1-INH level
  • Normal C1-INH functional assay
  • Normal C4 and C1q level
  • Factor XII mutation may be present

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 43, page 4

question_text: Which of the following statements is true regarding ACE inhibitor-induced angio-edema?
option_a: It occurs due to reduced bradykinin metabolism
option_b: Face and oropharynx are usually spared
explanation:
Angioedema is a localized swelling of deep dermis, subcutaneous, or submucosal tissue caused by the vascular extravasation of fluid into the interstitium.

Via bradykinin 2 receptors, bradykinin affects vascular permeability and stimulates the release of substance P, which is a peptide that causes vasodilation and fluid extravasation into tissues.

Inhibition of the angiotensin-converting enzyme and subsequent blockade of bradykinin degradation is thought to be a likely explanation for ACEI-induced angioedema.

Blacks, women, and smokers are at an increased risk for ACEI-induced angioedema.

Angioedema may occur at any time during treatment with ACEIs and may continue after the medication is discontinued.

Because ACEI-induced angioedema is not a histamine-mediated process, the role of antihistamines is unclear and they are usually used with minimal response

Switching to ARBs helps.

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 43, page 4

question_text: Most common type of Cutaneous mastocytosis is?
explanation:
Cutaneous Mastocytosis (CM)

  • Most cases of Pediatric mastocytosis are sporadic and appear during the first 2 years of life, especially on the trunk
  • Urticaria pigmentosa is the most frequent variant Three main forms of CM (defined by the WHO)
  • Urticaria pigmentosa (UP - Maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis MPCM)
  • Diffuse cutaneous mastocytosis (DCM)
  • Mastocytoma of skin

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 46, page 4

question_text: A 17-year-old female with no previous medical history presented with swelling of her lips, face and mouth area. She claims that she had four previous episodes over the past two months, each lasting two days. No recent insect bites or stings. She denies any itching or pain but feels a warm sensation around the mouth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Acquired angioedema occurs because of an acquired C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency. It is usually characterized by recurrent episodes of asymmetric swelling of the face and oral area, without urticaria or pruritis.
  • The disease is usually self limiting but laryngeal swelling can cause significant morbidity.
  • Patients with this disorder either have a total quantitative deficiency or a qualitative deficiency.
  • Although it is usually a clinical diagnosis, frequently along with a positive family history. Laboratory data to confirm diagnosis include serum C1INH, and C4.

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 43, page 4

question_text: A patient on anticonvulsant medication presented with rashes as shown in the image. What could be the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The image shows a well-demarcated, round to oval erythematous to dusky plaque with central violaceous discoloration.
  • This is classical of a Fixed Drug Eruption (FDE), which recurs at the same site on re-exposure to the offending drug.
  • Mainly caused by anticonvulsants, NSAIDs, sulfonamides, and tetracyclines.

Explanation of Other Options:

  • Urticaria (Option A): Transient pruritic wheals with central pallor and surrounding erythema, lasting <24 hours, migratory in nature.
  • Angioedema (Option C): Sudden deep dermal and subcutaneous swelling (lips, eyelids, genitalia), often associated with urticaria, not localized violaceous patches.
  • Cellulitis (Option D): Painful, erythematous, warm, and tender swelling with indistinct margins, usually associated with fever and systemic signs of bacterial infection.

Key Takeaways:

  • Fixed Drug Eruption = well-defined, dusky erythematous plaque, recurs at same site.
  • Differentiate from urticaria (transient wheals), angioedema (deep swelling), cellulitis (infective, painful).

question_text: Among the following conditions, which one is least likely to present with annular lesions?
explanation:
Explanation:

Urticaria is characterized by transient, edematous wheals that usually resolve within 24 hours.

Lesions are not annular but rather irregular, raised, and erythematous, caused by histamine mediated allergic reaction.

Explanation of Other Options:

Tinea corporis (Option A): A superficial dermatophyte infection caused by Trichophyton species. It typically produces annular, scaly lesions with central clearing and an active advancing margin.

Pityriasis rosea (Option B): A self-limiting papulosquamous disorder, often preceded by a herald patch that has an annular or oval shape with fine central scaling.

Porokeratosis (Option D): A keratinization disorder that manifests with annular plaques with a distinctive raised keratotic border (cornoid lamella).

question_text: A patient presents with rashes all over body with erosions of the lips and other mucosa since 2 days. What can be the triggering factor?
explanation:
• Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) is a potentially life-threatening dermatologic disorder characterized by widespread (> 30% BSA), erythema, necrosis, and bullous detachment of the epidermis and mucous membranes, resulting in exfoliation.
  • Mucous membrane involvement can result in gastrointestinal hemorrhage, respiratory failure, ocular abnormalities, and genitourinary complications.
  • TEN is most commonly drug-induced - antibiotics (sulfonamides), antiepileptic drugs (Phenobarbital, Phenytoin), nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), ampicillin, allopurinol, and the antiretroviral drugs (nevirapine, abacavir).
  • The mainstay of treatment is supportive care until the epithelium regenerates.

Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9th edition, Chapter 119, page 10

question_text: 27-year-old sexually active male develops an erosive lesion on the glans 2 days after taking a tablet for stomach upset. The lesion healed with hyperpigmentation. The most likely diagnosis is:
explanation:
1. Localized hyperpigmentation is seen as a side effect of several systemic medications, including those that produce fixed drug reactions (tetracyclines, sulfonamides, analgesics(NSAIDS), antimalarials).
  2. Fixed drug eruptions recur in the same location as circular areas of erythema that can become bullous and then resolve as hyperpigmented macules.
  3. Lesions can also appear on genitalia where they appaear as erosions.

The eruption usually appears within hours of administration of the offending agent, and common locations include the genitalia, extremities, and perioral region.

Other options

Behcets - recurrent oro-genital aphthae, no H/o drug. Other manifestations of behcets.

Herpes - grouped painful vesicles, lymphadenopathy. No H/o drugs

Pemphigus - wouldn’t present as a single erosion. No H/o drugs

Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9th edition, Chapter 118, page 11

question_text: A male aged 30 years presents a skin lesion over his body 1 week after taking NSAIDs. What appears to be the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Patient's intake of NSAIDS & morphology of lesion indicates that she is having fixed drug eruption.

Fixed drug eruptions emerge 7 to 14 days after first exposure.

The lesions can develop and are most frequently seen on the lips, feet, hands, face and genitalia. Mainly, they appear as edematous, annular, well-demarcated plaques. Single or even multiple lesions can develop. A central vesicle, denuded or bulla epidermis may be present.

The lesion(s) may fade over a number of days leaving residual hyperpigmentation after the discontinuation of the offending medication. Re-exposure to the offending medication leads to reappearance of the same lesion at the same site.

Following are the most common offending medications:

  • NSAIDs
  • Sulfonamides
  • Barbiturates
  • Tetracyclines
  • Carbamazepine

Explanation for the other options:

  • A. Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory disorder, not an acute drug reaction presenting 1 week after exposure.
  • B. Erythema multiforme typically presents with targetoid lesions, often triggered by infection (HSV), not classically an isolated fixed plaque.
  • D. SJS (Stevens-Johnson Syndrome) is a severe reaction involving mucous membrane erosion and widespread skin detachment, which is not suggested by the description of a single or multiple plaques.

Key Takeaways:

Fixed drug eruptions (FDEs) typically appear 7-14 days after first exposure and recur at the exact same site upon re-exposure to the offending drug. NSAIDs are a common cause.

question_text: The most commonly involved internal organ in DRESS Syndrome is _____
explanation:
Visceral involvement (hepatitis, pneumonitis, myocarditis, pericarditis, nephritis, and colitis) is the major cause of morbidity and mortality in this syndrome.

Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9th edition, Chapter 119, page 4

question_text: All the following are TRUE about erythema multiform EXCEPT :
option_a: Vesicle and bullae are not seen
option_c: Target lesion with bull's eye lesion seen over palms and soles
option_d: Associated with adverse reaction to drugs
explanation:
Erythema multiforme - manifests as very characteristic 1-2 cm circular lesions consisting of 3 concentric zones - a pinkish raised periphery, pallor in middle and a dark violaceous centre thickened to the iris of the eye or the target of the shooting range. Such a lesions are therefore called iris lesions or target lesions

  1. Some case may develop tense blister at the centre of the target lesions
  2. Approximately 90% of cases of erythema multiforme minor follow outbreaks of herpes simplex (HSV 1 infection)

question_text: Body surface area percentage involved in Stevens-johnson syndrome is :
explanation:
<10% - Stevens-johnson syndrome

10-30% - SJS-TEN complex

> 30% - Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN)

Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9th edition, Chapter 119, page 10

question_text: Which of the following drugs is most likely to cause a lichenoid eruption ?
explanation:
Medications commonly reported to trigger a lichenoid drug eruption include: Antihypertensives - ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, nifedipine, methyldopa. Diuretics - hydrochlorothiazide, frusemide, spironolactone. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), Tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-alpha inhibitors, and gold

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 37, page 3

question_text: A patient presented with painful oral ulcers since 3 months and flaccid bullae and painful erosions on the body since 1 month. He is planned for treatment with rituximab. Which of the following is the RA protocol for the administration of rituximab?
option_a: 1000mg IV of Rituximab given every 2 weekly
option_b: 1000mg IM of rituximab given every 2 weekly
explanation:
Dosage and administration of rituximab for the Food and Drug Administration-approved indications

Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma: RTX 375 mg/m2 is administered as an IV infusion once a week with four infusions over a month. It can be used either as monotherapy or combined with other chemotherapy regimens such as cyclophosphamide, hydroxydaunorubicin, Oncovin, and prednisone (CHOP regimen)

Rheumatoid arthritis: RTX 1 g is administered as an IV infusion. Two infusions, one on day 1 and the other on day 15, are given

Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 50, page 9

question_text: The Asboe-Hansen sign as applies to blister formation refers to:
option_a: Lateral slipping of the epidermis when perilesional is rubbed
option_b: Spread of blister when pressure is applied directly to a blister
option_c: Blister formation following stroking of the lesion
option_d: Blister induction with incised trauma to skin
explanation:
• The Asboe-Hansen sign as applies to blister formation refers to lateral dissection of the blister when pressure is applied directly to the blister.
  • This is also called, "bulla-spread phenomenon", because pressure on an intact bulla, gently forces fluid to wander under the skin away from the pressure site.

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th Edition, chapter 50, page 8

question_text: A patient developed bullae without erythema on elbows, knee & sacral area fib crust formation, scarring & milia. He had no photo sensitivity and negative family history for bullous diseases. On DIF IgG deposition at DEJ with no blood vessel involvement is seen probable diagnosis is:
explanation:
Epidermolysis Bullosa Acquisita (EBA)

  • Epidermolysis bullosa - congenital, present from birth
  • EBA is not inherited and usually presents in adult life
  • EBA is a rare disease in which tense blisters appear at sites of trauma
  • EBA blisters tend to be localized to areas that are easily injured such as the hands, feet, knees, elbows, and buttocks
  • Sometimes there is mucosal involvement with blisters forming in mouth, nose and eyes
  • EBA may mimic Bullous pemphigoid
  • Salt split immunofluorescence used to differentiate between EBA and BP

Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 50, Page 45

question_text: Drug-induced pemphigus is seen with all the following EXCEPT:
explanation:
1. Drugs causing pemphigus have most commonly produced pemphigus foliaceous

question_text: A 35-year-old lady with history of hair dye application presents with the following clinical picture. What is the allergen present in the hair dye

Explanation:

PPD allergy:

  • A type IV hypersensitivity reaction
  • Often triggered after repeated hair dye use
  • Clinical features:
    • Erythema, vesicles, crusting

    • May spread down neck or upper chest

Other important triggers:

  • "Black henna" tattoos (contain high PPD concentration)
  • Sticker bindis are made up of circular discs of polyvinylchloride (PVC) and the adhesive material contains para-tertiary butyl phenol (PTBP)
  • Textile dyes

Balsam of Peru: Common fragrance allergen (Option A)

Pollen: Causes allergic rhinitis/conjunctivitis (Option C)

Drug intake: May cause Fixed drug eruptions but not this characteristic distribution (Option D)

question_text: A 35 year old lady with a history of hair dye application presents with the following clinical picture. What is the cause ?
explanation:
Explanation:

Paraphenylenediamine (PPD) is the most common allergen causing allergic contact dermatitis from hair dyes.

  • This patient is presenting with allergic contact dermatitis, a Type IV hypersensitivity reaction, following hair dye application.
  • The most frequently implicated chemical in hair dye-induced dermatitis is paraphenylenediamine (PPD).
  • PPD is a coal-tar derivative used to achieve permanent black or dark-colored dyes.
  • When applied to the scalp, it can penetrate the skin and elicit an immune-mediated reaction in sensitized individuals.
  • Clinical features include:
    • Itching, erythema, and vesiculation at the site of application.
    • Involvement of face, ears, neck, and scalp margins (regions exposed to the dye).
    • Repeated exposure worsens symptoms.
  • Diagnosis is primarily clinical, but patch testing can confirm sensitivity.
  • Management involves discontinuing the offending agent, topical corticosteroids, and avoidance of future exposure.

Explanation of other options:

Balsam of Peru (Option A): This is a plant-derived substance used in perfumes and some topical products, which can cause contact dermatitis, but it is not commonly associated with hair dye reactions.

Pollen (Option C): Pollen causes respiratory allergies (e.g., allergic rhinitis), not contact dermatitis, and is unrelated to hair dye exposure.

Drug intake (Option D): Systemic drugs can lead to drug eruptions, but the localized nature of the lesions after direct exposure to hair dye supports contact dermatitis rather than a drug-related cause.

question_text:
Statement 1: Histopathological examination of a patient with flaccid bullae and painful erosions reveals a suprabasal blister with an inflammatory infiltrate in the blister cavity.
Statement 2: The row of tombstones is diagnostic of pemphigus vulgaris.
option_a: Statement 1 is false and Statement 2 is true
option_b: Statement 1 is true and Statement 2 is false
option_c: Both statements are true, but Statement 2 is not the conclusion of Statement 1
option_d: Both statements are true, and Statement 2 is the conclusion of Statement 1
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Flaccid bullae and painful erosions always suggest an intraepidermal pathology, most classically seen in the pemphigus group of disorders.
  • Because the bullae are flaccid, they rupture easily, producing erosions that tend to extend and show poor healing.

On histopathology:

  • Pemphigus foliaceus shows a superficial split in the epidermis due to autoantibodies against desmoglein-1.
  • Pemphigus vulgaris shows a suprabasal split caused by antibodies against desmoglein-3.

Fig: Histopathology of Pemphigus vulgaris showing suprabasal split

Thus, Statement 1 is correct.

  • In pemphigus vulgaris, the basal keratinocytes remain vertically attached to the basement membrane by hemidesmosomes, but are laterally detached from each other due to acantholysis. This gives the classical "row of tombstones" appearance under the microscope.
  • Therefore, Statement 2 is also correct, and it does not directly follow from Statement 1.

On direct immunofluorescence (DIF), there is IgG deposition within the epidermis in an intercellular pattern. This produces the classical fish-net appearance.

Histopathology in Lichen planus

question_text: Which of these is a known association with this disease?
explanation:
Pityriasis rosea is an acute self-limiting papulosquamous disorder. It is characterized by a herald patch followed by scaly oval patches on the trunk and proximal extremities in a "Christmas-tree" appearance.

The exact cause of pityriasis rosea is not known, but features like seasonal variation and clustering in communities suggest that it is an infectious disease. Infections like viruses, bacteria, spirochetes.

Recently, reactivation of latent human herpesvirus-6 and human herpesvirus-7 infection have been found as the possible etiologic agents. Pityriasis rosea-like eruptions have been reported after vaccinations such as Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG), influenza, H1N1, diphtheria, smallpox, hepatitis B, and Pneumococcus. Eruptions have also been seen with drugs like gold, captopril, barbiturates, D-penicillamine, and clonidine.

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 25, page 90

question_text: A patient presents with non-erythematous bullae over the elbows, knees, and sacral region, which heal with crusting, scarring, and milia. There is no photosensitivity, and there is no family history of blistering disorders. Direct immunofluorescence shows IgG deposits along the dermo-epidermal junction without involvement of blood vessels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given clinical scenario presents a case of Epidermolysis Bullosa Acquisita (EBA).

  • Unlike inherited forms of epidermolysis bullosa, which present at birth, EBA is an acquired blistering disorder that usually appears in adulthood.
  • It produces tense blisters at trauma-prone sites such as the elbows, knees, hands, feet, and buttocks.
  • Lesions frequently heal with scarring and milia, which is characteristic of EBA.
  • Mucous membranes may occasionally be affected, with blisters involving the mouth, nose, or eyes.
  • EBA can closely resemble bullous pemphigoid, so salt-split skin testing is used to differentiate the two.
  • In DIF, EBA shows IgG deposition at the dermo-epidermal junction (along the basement membrane).

question_text: Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) is expected to show immunoreactant deposition in all of the following disorders except:
explanation:
Explanation:

Dariers disease does not involve autoantibodies, so their DIF studies are negative.

  • DIF becomes positive when there are immune complexes (antibodies + antigens) deposited in the skin, which is characteristic of autoimmune blistering diseases.
  • In Darier disease (DD), mutations occur in the ATP2A2 gene, located on chromosome 12q24.1. This gene encodes the SERCA2 (sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca²⁺-ATPase type 2) pump, which is found in the endoplasmic reticulum.SERCA2 normally transports calcium ions back into the ER by using ATP. ATP binding and phosphorylation trigger a conformational change that moves Ca²⁺ into the ER lumen; after dephosphorylation, the pump resets and repeats the cycle.
  • The ATP2A2 gene contains 20-21 exons (depending on isoform) and produces a 4 kb transcript, generating four SERCA2 isoforms through alternative splicing.
  • conditions such as pemphigus vulgaris, IgA pemphigus (subcorneal pustular dermatosis), and herpes gestationis show positive DIF findings. (Options A, B, D)
  • In contrast, disorders caused by genetic defects in structural proteins, like Darier disease, Hailey-Hailey disease, congenital epidermolysis bullosa, or Grover disease, do not involve autoantibodies, so their DIF studies are negative.
