question_text: Identify the following lines in dermatology.
explanation:
Explanation:

The given image shows regularly arranged, horizontal lines without a wavy pattern, which are characteristic of relaxed skin tension lines.

Relaxed Skin Tension Lines (RSTL)

  • Also called Langer's lines or Cleavage lines.
  • Surgical incisions are ideally placed along these lines, as they reduce the risk of hypertrophic scar formation.
  • They correspond to the orientation of collagen fibres in the dermis.
  • Associated conditions:
    • Guttate psoriasis
    • Pityriasis rosea

Explanation of other options:

Blaschko lines (Option A): Blaschko lines represent embryologic lines of development. They appear V-shaped on the upper back, S-shaped on the abdomen, and spiral on the scalp. These lines are seen associated with conditions such as incontinentia pigmenti.

Marionette lines (Option B): Marionette lines are age-related facial lines. They run from the corners of the mouth down to the mandible and are formed due to contraction of the depressor anguli oris muscle.

Hinderers line (Option C): It is formed by the intersection of two reference lines: one drawn from the ala of the nose to the tragus of the ear, and the other from the lateral canthus. These lines mark the zones where fillers can be safely injected in aesthetic dermatology.

Reference: https://publishing.rcseng.ac.uk/doi/10.1308/rcsann.2018.0038

question_text: Koebner's phenomenon is not seen in:
explanation:
Explanation:

Koebner's phenomenon (isomorphic response) = Development of new lesions of an existing dermatosis at sites of cutaneous trauma.

Skin Trauma → Release of cytokines (IL-1, TNF-α) → Local inflammation → Activation of disease-specific pathways → Lesion appears at trauma site

It is classically seen in:

  • Psoriasis - lesions develop along lines of scratches, pressure, or surgical scars.
  • Lichen planus - violaceous papules appear in areas of trauma.
  • Vitiligo - depigmented patches appear following trauma.

Herpes simplex/zoster: lesions appear due to viral reactivation in dermatomal distribution, not due to trauma, hence no Koebnerization.


Explanation Of Other Options:

Vitiligo (Option A): Demonstrates true Koebnerization. Trauma → melanocyte destruction → depigmented macules at site.

Psoriasis (Option B): Prototype condition for the Koebner phenomenon. It is seen in 25-75% of patients. Mechanical trauma, tattoos, or surgery may induce plaques.

Lichen planus (Option C): Classically associated. Trauma → appearance of flat-topped violaceous papules.

question_text: Which nail finding is characteristic of psoriasis vulgaris as shown in image?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image shows thickening and accumulation of keratinous debris beneath the nail plate, termed as subungual hyperkeratosis.

  • It is a classic nail change in psoriasis, where proliferation of the nail bed keratinocytes and retention of keratin causes nail plate elevation distally.
  • Leads to discoloration, thickened nail, and brittle texture.
  • Subungual hyperkeratosis contributes to onycholysis in advanced cases.

Explanation of Other Options:

  • Auspitz sign (Option B): Refers to pinpoint bleeding seen on removal of psoriatic scales due to exposure of dermal papillary vessels; this is a skin finding, not a nail finding.
  • Oil drop sign (Option C): Refers to a translucent, yellow-red discoloration seen through the nail plate resembling a drop of oil; highly characteristic of nail psoriasis but not the one shown in this image.
  • Onycholysis (Option D): Refers to separation of the nail plate from the nail bed; often distal and associated with a whitish area; can occur in psoriasis but the image here shows subungual thickening instead.

Key Nail Changes in Psoriasis: Mnemonic - POisON

  • Pitting: Small, regularly spaced depressions on nail surface due to defective keratinization in nail matrix.
  • Oil drop/salmon patch sign: Translucent yellow-red discoloration beneath the nail plate.
  • Subungual hyperkeratosis: Keratinous debris under nail plate causing thickening and elevation.
  • Onycholysis: Distal nail plate separation.
  • Nail plate Dystrophy
  • Leukonychia and splinter hemorrhages may also be present.

question_text: Auspitz sign is seen in?
explanation:
Explanation:

Auspitz sign is a clinical finding characteristic of psoriasis. It refers to the appearance of pinpoint bleeding when the silvery scales of a psoriatic plaque are gently scraped or removed. This phenomenon is due to the thinning of the epidermis over the tips of the elongated dermal papillae, which contain superficial, dilated capillaries. When the scales (composed of parakeratotic stratum corneum) are removed, these fragile capillaries are exposed and rupture, leading to punctate hemorrhages.

  • Psoriasis Vulgaris: The most common form of psoriasis, characterized by well-demarcated, erythematous plaques covered with silvery scales, typically on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, scalp) and the lower back.
  • Koebner phenomenon (isomorphic response): The development of psoriatic lesions in areas of trauma or injury to the skin. This is also commonly seen in psoriasis.
  • Parakeratosis: Retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum, a histological hallmark of psoriasis.

Explanation of other options:

Pemphigus vulgaris (Option A): Pemphigus vulgaris is an autoimmune blistering disease affecting the skin and mucous membranes. It is characterized by flaccid bullae and a positive Nikolsky's sign (epidermal shearing with lateral pressure), but not Auspitz sign.

Pustular psoriasis (Option C): Pustular psoriasis is a severe form of psoriasis characterized by widespread pustules. While it is a type of psoriasis, the Auspitz sign is most classically associated with the scaling plaques of psoriasis vulgaris, although it might theoretically be elicited on any scaled area.

DLE (Option D): DLE stands for Discoid Lupus Erythematosus, a chronic cutaneous form of lupus characterized by coin-shaped, erythematous plaques with follicular plugging, scarring, and pigmentary changes, primarily on sun-exposed areas. It does not present with Auspitz sign.

Key Takeaways:

  • Auspitz sign is the appearance of pinpoint bleeding after removing psoriatic scales.
  • It is a characteristic clinical sign of Psoriasis vulgaris.
  • It occurs due to dilated capillaries in elongated dermal papillae beneath the thin epidermis.

question_text: A patient initially presented with the skin lesions shown in the accompanying image and subsequently developed arthritis. What is the preferred treatment for this clinical scenario?
explanation:
Explanation:

The combination of sharply demarcated, red papulosquamous plaques plus joint involvement (knee effusion, dactylitis) is most consistent with psoriatic arthritis. For moderate-severe psoriasis with associated inflammatory arthritis, conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic therapy such as methotrexate is a first-line systemic agent.

It improves both skin and joint disease and is widely used as the initial steroid-sparing, long-term treatment. (Oral small-molecule options such as apremilast are also used in certain cases.)

Explanation for other options:

PUVA (psoralen + UVA) (Option A): PUVA is an effective phototherapy for cutaneous psoriasis but does not treat the joint inflammation of psoriatic arthritis. It may be considered as a skin-directed therapy when systemic agents are contraindicated, but it is not the treatment of choice when significant arthritis is present.

Steroids(Option B): Systemic corticosteroids can suppress inflammation but are generally avoided as long-term therapy in psoriasis because abrupt withdrawal can precipitate severe flares (including erythroderma) and they do not provide disease modification for arthritis. Targeted use (e.g., intra-articular steroid injection) can be very helpful for a single symptomatic joint (effusion), but systemic steroids are not recommended as the primary disease-modifying treatment for psoriatic arthritis.

Infliximab(Option D): Infliximab (an anti-TNF biologic) is a highly effective option for both skin and joint disease, especially in severe or refractory cases. However, biologics are typically reserved for patients who have an inadequate response to, contraindication to, or intolerance of first-line conventional agents (like methotrexate), or when rapid, strong disease control is required.

Key takeaway:

Drug of choice for different types of psoriasis

question_text: Identify the disorder in which the following clinical picture is seen:
explanation:
Pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP) is a rare inflammatory papulosquamous disorder of unknown etiology. There are 6 distinct subtypes which occur in both children and adult which occur striking variation.

The classic sequence of signs begins with a diffuse fine scale seen on the scalp.

Within weeks to months, lesions increase , coalescing into patches and plaques that progress in a cephalocaudal manner appear.

Characteristic orange-red hyperkeratotic follicular papules are prominent both within the patches of erythema and within adjoining areas of uninvolved skin. Various terms including "nutmeg grater" or "exaggerated gooseflesh" have been used to describe these follicular-based papules.

Involved skin is often sharply demarcated from adjacent uninvolved skin producing a very characteristic phenomenon coined "islands of sparing" or "skip areas."

At times, the disease may even evolve in to diffuse orange-red erythroderma.

Another characteristic finding, also notable in children, is a unique red-orange waxy palmoplantar keratoderma (PPK) so-called "sandal-like" PPK

question_text: Which of the following best describes the pathophysiology of psoriasis?
option_a: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
option_c: Immune-mediated destruction of the thyroid gland
option_d: Defective T cell maturation in the thymus
explanation:
• Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells: This describes Type 1 diabetes, not psoriasis.
  • Hyperproliferation of keratinocytes: Psoriasis is characterized by the rapid turnover and proliferation of skin cells (keratinocytes), leading to thickened skin and scaling.
  • Immune-mediated destruction of the thyroid gland: This is seen in Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, not psoriasis.
  • Defective T cell maturation in the thymus: This is related to autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome, not psoriasis.

Key Takeaway: Psoriasis is primarily due to the hyperproliferation of keratinocytes.

Tag Line: Moderate

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding immunology of psoriasis is correct?
explanation:
Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease with a strong genetic predisposition and autoimmune pathogenic traits.

Epidermal dendritic cells(antigen-presenting cells) play a major role in the initial stages of disease, their activation in psoriasis involves the recognition of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), secreted by keratinocytes in response to injury and are characteristically overexpressed in psoriatic skin

Activated mDCs migrate into draining lymph nodes and secrete tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α, IL-23, and IL-12, with the latter two modulating the differentiation and proliferation of Th17 and Th1 cell subsets.

The TNFα-IL-23-Th17 inflammatory pathway characterizes plaque-type psoriasis

Th17 cytokines, namely IL-17, IL-21, and IL-22 activate keratinocyte proliferation in the epidermis.

The importance of these inflammatory cytokines has been proven by the specific cytokine inhibitors, which show strong anti-inflammatory action against psoriatic skin inflammation

question_text: A 30-year-old male develops the solitary, well-demarcated, dusky erythematous plaque shown on his trunk one week after taking an over-the-counter NSAID for a headache. He reports having a similar lesion in the exact same spot a year ago after taking the same medication. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The diagnosis is Fixed Drug Eruption (FDE). This is a classic Type IV hypersensitivity reaction to a medication. The key diagnostic features present in this case are:

  • Morphology: A well-demarcated, edematous, dusky erythematous or violaceous plaque.
  • Timing: Onset typically occurs within 1-2 weeks of the first exposure to the offending drug.
  • Pathognomonic Feature: The hallmark of FDE is its recurrence in the exact same location upon re-exposure to the causative agent. The lesion resolves after drug withdrawal, often leaving behind post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.

Common causative drugs include NSAIDs, sulfonamides, barbiturates, and tetracyclines.

Explanation of Other Options:

Psoriasis (Option A): Psoriasis typically presents as well-demarcated, erythematous plaques with a characteristic silvery scale, not a dusky, edematous plaque. It is a chronic autoimmune condition, not an acute drug reaction.

Erythema multiforme (Option B): The classic lesion of erythema multiforme is a "target" or "iris" lesion, which has three distinct concentric zones. The lesions are typically multiple and symmetrically distributed, most commonly on the acral surfaces (hands and feet).

Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) (Option D): SJS is a severe, life-threatening mucocutaneous reaction. It presents with widespread, coalescing, purpuric macules and blisters, leading to epidermal detachment, and is always accompanied by severe mucosal involvement (oral, ocular, genital).

Key Takeaways: Differentiating Drug Rashes

question_text: Which of the following is NOT a distinguishing feature of psoriatic arthritis when compared with other arthropathies?
explanation:
Explanation:

Psoriatic arthritis is an inflammatory arthropathy seen in association with psoriasis, characterized by features such as dactylitis, enthesitis, asymmetric oligoarthritis, and nail involvement.

Diarrhoea is not a feature of psoriatic arthritis; instead, it is more typically associated with enteropathic arthritis (linked to inflammatory bowel disease like Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis).

Explanation of Other Options:

Dactylitis (Option B): Also called "sausage digit," it is a hallmark feature of psoriatic arthritis caused by inflammation of flexor tendons and soft tissues.

Enthesitis (Option C): Inflammation at tendon/ligament insertion sites (e.g., Achilles tendon) is common in psoriatic arthritis.

Nail pitting (Option D): A classic dermatological feature of psoriasis; its presence supports the diagnosis of psoriatic arthritis.

Key Takeaways:

  • Psoriatic arthritis = dactylitis + enthesitis + nail pitting.
  • Diarrhoea → Enteropathic arthritis (IBD-related), not psoriasis.

question_text: What variant of Psoriasis is seen in the image below?
explanation:

It often has an acute onset and may evolve into chronic plaque psoriasis in some patients.

question_text: What is the name of the sign shown in this picture?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given image shows a linear erythematous lesion developing at the site of trauma, this phenomenon is called the Koebner phenomenon (isomorphic response).

  • Defined as the appearance of new lesions typical of a pre-existing dermatosis at sites of trauma.
  • Classically seen in psoriasis, but also occurs in lichen planus and vitiligo. (Mnemonic - LPV)
  • It's a pathergy like response where trauma triggers disease specific lesion.

Explanation of Other Options:

  • Auspitz sign (Option A): It's the Pinpoint bleeding spots which appear when psoriatic scales are removed, This due to exposure of dermal papillary vessels. Seen in psoriasis but not related to trauma-induced lesions.
  • Dermographism (Option B): It's a form of physical urticaria where stroking the skin produces a linear wheal and flare reaction.
  • Nikolsky sign (Option D): Epidermal detachment occurs when lateral pressure is applied to the skin. Seen in pemphigus vulgaris, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome.

Key Takeaways:

  • Koebner phenomenon = isomorphic response at trauma sites.
  • Seen in psoriasis, lichen planus, vitiligo.

question_text: A patient has a painless, growing lesion on the shoulder with a scar in the center. What is the likely diagnosis?

  • On diascopy, apple jelly nodules may be seen, which is a diagnostic clue.

Explanation of Other Options:

Basal cell carcinoma (Option B): Pearly nodules with rolled-out, beaded borders, no central scarring.

Tinea (Option C): It is a fungal infection with annular lesions with scaling and its pruritic in nature.

Psoriasis (Option D): It is a chronic disease, with characteristic inflammatory plaques, which produces silvery scales and are usually itchy with no central scar.

Key Takeaways:

  • Lupus vulgaris -> slowly progressive cutaneous TB with central atrophy/scarring.
  • Characteristic sign ->apple jelly nodules on diascopy.

question_text: Identify the phenomenon shown in the image
explanation:
• Isomorphic phenomenon, also known as Koebner's phenomenon, is the development of new lesions of an existing skin condition at sites of trauma, such as scratches, surgical incisions, or injury.
  • It is commonly observed in psoriasis, lichen planus, and vitiligo. When the skin experiences trauma, lesions appear in areas where the skin has been damaged, reflecting the underlying condition.

Explanation of the Incorrect Options:

  • (B) Reverse Isomorphic Phenomenon:
    • The reverse isomorphic phenomenon is not a widely recognized dermatologic term. There is no specific condition characterized by this phenomenon in dermatology.
  • (C) Gottron's Papule:
    • Gottron's papules are characteristic erythematous, scaly, raised lesions found on the extensor surfaces of the joints in dermatomyositis. They are not related to trauma or the development of lesions after injury.
  • (D) Nikolsky Sign:
    • The Nikolsky sign is a clinical sign where the skin shears off or blisters easily when slight pressure is applied, commonly seen in conditions like pemphigus vulgaris or toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN). It is not associated with trauma-induced lesion formation.

Key Takeaway:

Isomorphic phenomenon (Koebner's phenomenon) involves the development of new lesions of an existing skin condition at sites of trauma, commonly seen in psoriasis, lichen planus, and vitiligo.

question_text: Which of the following features is not typically linked with the condition depicted in the image below?
explanation:
Explanation:

Munro microabscesses are collections of neutrophils in the stratum corneum, which are characteristic of psoriasis, not lichen planus.

The image depicts lichen planus (LP), an idiopathic inflammatory disorder affecting both the skin and mucous membranes.

Key Clinical Features of Lichen Planus:

  • Skin lesions: Pruritic, purple, polygonal papules and plaques, often with fine white lines on the surface called Wickham's striae. Common sites include the volar wrists, lumbar region, and ankles.
  • Mucosal involvement: Frequently affects the buccal mucosa and tongue, and may rarely involve the genitalia, anus, or other mucous membranes.
  • Nail involvement: Can present as thinning of the nail plate, longitudinal ridging, linear depressions, or even complete nail loss (anonychia). Other changes include longitudinal melanonychia, subungual hyperkeratosis, hyperpigmentation, or onycholysis.

Histopathology:

  • Epidermal acanthosis: Irregular thickening of the epidermis.
  • Granular layer: Irregular thickening with compact hyperkeratosis.
  • Colloid (Civatte) bodies: Degenerated basal keratinocytes appearing as eosinophilic bodies.
  • Rete ridges: Often show a sawtooth pattern, sometimes with focal separation forming Max Joseph spaces.
  • Inflammatory infiltrate: Band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermo-epidermal junction.

Explanation for other options:

Wickham's Striae (Option A): These are fine, white, lacy lines seen on the surface of lichen planus papules. Most prominent on the buccal mucosa, but can also be seen on the skin lesions of the wrists, ankles, and lumbar region. Considered pathognomonic for lichen planus and helps differentiate it from other papular eruptions.

Epidermal Acanthosis(Option B): Refers to thickening of the epidermis due to increased keratinocyte proliferation. Histologically, lichen planus shows irregular acanthosis along with hypergranulosis and compact hyperkeratosis. This contributes to the characteristic appearance of the papular lesions.

Colloid Bodies (Civatte Bodies) (Option D): These are eosinophilic, apoptotic basal keratinocytes seen in the epidermis and papillary dermis. Represent basal cell degeneration due to the autoimmune attack on keratinocytes. Their presence on histology is a hallmark feature of lichen planus.

question_text: The patient exhibits a numbed region on the face, depicted in the image provided. Which nerve is most frequently affected in this particular condition?
explanation:
Explanation

  • In leprosy (Hansen's disease), Mycobacterium leprae often invades peripheral nerves, particularly the facial nerve.
  • Facial nerve damage produces weakness of the orbicularis oculi and other facial muscles, leading to inability to close the eyelids (lagophthalmos) and facial droop.
  • This motor loss explains the asymmetry and complications such as corneal ulceration and facial deformities.

Pathophysiology

  • M.leprae infects Schwann cells, causing segmental demyelination and axonal damage.
  • Motor branches of the facial nerve, especially the zygomatic and buccal branches, are vulnerable.
  • Chronic involvement causes progressive facial paralysis and trophic changes.

Clinical Features of Facial Nerve Involvement in Leprosy

  • Facial weakness with drooping of the mouth and eyelid.
  • Lagophthalmos due to orbicularis oculi paralysis.
  • Loss of facial expression, leading to characteristic deformity.
  • Secondary corneal damage from incomplete eye closure.

Facial Nerve: Function and Involvement

  • Normal function: Motor supply facial muscles, taste from anterior two-thirds of tongue, parasympathetic fibers to lacrimal and salivary glands.
  • In leprosy: Predominantly motor impairment; sensory branches less commonly affected.
  • Complications: Corneal ulceration, exposure keratitis, facial disfigurement.

Explanation of Incorrect Options

Abducens nuclei (Option A): This nerve controls lateral rectus muscle for eye abduction; not associated with facial weakness or numbness.

Optic nerve (Option C): Responsible for visual input; not involved in motor or sensory innervation of the face.

Trigeminal nerve (Option D): Governs facial sensation and mastication muscles, but leprosy more characteristically affects the facial nerve motor supply rather than pure sensory distribution alone.

Key TakeawayFacial nerve involvement is common in leprosy, leading to facial paralysis, lagophthalmos, and deformity-making it the most frequently affected cranial nerve in this condition.

question_text: A migrant labor presented with complains of urethral discharge one week after unprotected sexual intercourse, accompanied with painful micturition. What is the causative organism?
explanation:
• The patient presents with urethral discharge and painful micturition one week after unprotected sexual intercourse, which suggests a gonococcal infection.
  • The causative organism is Neisseria gonorrhoeae, which is responsible for gonorrhea.
  • Incubation period for gonorrhea is typically 3 to 10 days after exposure.
  • Most common site of infection in men is the urethra (80%), followed by the rectum (40%) and pharynx (10%-20%).
  • Symptoms of gonococcal infection usually include copious purulent urethral discharge, dysuria (painful urination), and perimeatal erythema (redness around the urethral opening).
  • The first-line treatment for uncomplicated urogenital, anorectal, and pharyngeal gonococcal infections is:
    • Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscular (IM) injection as a single dose.

Incorrect Options:

  • (A) Escherichia coli:
    • While coli is a common cause of urinary tract infections (UTIs), it is not typically associated with urethral discharge and painful micturition following sexual exposure. It is more commonly seen in cystitisor pyelonephritis.
  • (C) Ureaplasma urealyticum:
    • Ureaplasma urealyticum can cause urethritis, but it is less likely to cause copious purulent dischargecompared to Neisseria gonorrhoeae. It is typically associated with non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU) and can cause asymptomatic or mild symptoms.
  • (D) Trichomonas vaginalis:
    • Trichomonas vaginalis causes trichomoniasis, which is associated with vaginal discharge in women and urethral discharge in men, but it tends to present with a frothy, yellow-green discharge and is less commonly associated with the purulent discharge seen in gonorrhea.

Key Takeaway: The most likely cause of urethral discharge and painful micturition in this case is Neisseria gonorrhoeae, which causes gonorrhea. The incubation period is typically 3 to 10 days, and the treatment involves a single dose of ceftriaxone.

question_text: Which of the following is the most common side effect of dapsone:
explanation:
Explanation:

Dapsone (4,4′-diaminodiphenylsulphone) is well absorbed orally, widely distributed in tissues, and metabolized through acetylation and hydroxylation. The hydroxylamine metabolite has strong oxidizing properties that make red blood cells particularly vulnerable to oxidative injury. As a result, haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia occur to some degree in all patients receiving dapsone, although the severity varies.

Haemolytic anaemia is the most common adverse effect and is more pronounced in individuals with G6PD deficiency, where impaired protection from oxidative stress leads to increased erythrocyte destruction. Methaemoglobinaemia may accompany haemolysis and presents with lethargy, headache, and a cyanotic hue to the skin and mucous membranes.

Dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome, agranulocytosis, peripheral neuropathy, gastrointestinal upset, hepatic toxicity, and other rare reactions may occur, but these are significantly less common than haemolytic anaemia.

Therefore, hemolytic anemia is the most common and expected side effect of dapsone, making Option A correct.

question_text: Which is the most common nerve involved in leprosy?
explanation:
Explanation:

Two large cohort studies with systematic nerve examinations showed that the posterior tibial nerve is the most frequently affected nerve in leprosy, followed by the ulnar (Option B), median (Option D), lateral popliteal (common peroneal), and facial nerves. Posterior tibial nerve damage causes paralysis and contracture of the small foot muscles and anesthesia of the sole.

Ulnar and median nerve lesions in leprosy are usually low, producing weakness of the small hand muscles without deep flexor involvement and causing anesthesia of the corresponding halves of the hand. Isolated median nerve lesions are uncommon.

Common peroneal nerve (Option C) involvement results in difficulty with dorsiflexion and eversion of the foot and anesthesia along the outer border of the foot, predisposing to trauma and plantar ulceration.

Posterior tibial nerve damage is more serious, leading to paralysis and contracture of the small muscles of the foot along with anesthesia of the sole.

This pathogen affects the skin (dermal histiocytes) and the peripheral nerves (schwann cells).

M.leprae multiplies very slowly, requiring 12 to 14 days for generation.Thus doubling time is 12-14 days.

Although 37 °C is the standard incubation temperature used for most pathogens, M. leprae requires a low temperature for growth. Therefore, in humans it tends to preferentially parasitize cooler areas such as the skin, nasal mucosa and ears.

Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9th edition, Chapter 28, page 6

The reason for sparing of these zones has been attributed to the relatively high local temperature.

question_text: In lepromatous leprosy, globi consist of:
option_a: Macrophage cells laden with acid fast bacilli
option_b: Lipid laden macrophages and degenerated tissue
explanation:
Explanation:

In lepromatous leprosy, the dermis contains enormous numbers of acid-fast bacilli (AFB) located within foamy macrophages. These bacilli may occur singly or in clumps, and these clumps are known as globi. The infiltrate is composed of dense, uniform macrophages with AFB visible on Wade-Fite staining.

Lipid-laden macrophages (Option B): Although macrophages are described as foamy, the content attributes globi specifically to clusters of AFB, not to lipid degeneration.

Epitheloid cells with AFB (Option C): Epithelioid cells are not described in lepromatous leprosy; the infiltrate consists of foamy macrophages, not epithelioid granulomas.

Immunoglobulin-containing plasma cells (Option D): Plasma cells may be present in small numbers, but globi are not formed by plasma cells; they consist of bacilli-laden macrophages.

Key Takeaways:

Globi = clusters of macrophages loaded with AFB in LL leprosy.

question_text: In which of the following asymptomatic gonococcal infection is common?
explanation:
Gonorrhea, caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae,

Affects epithelium and commonly manifests as urethritis, conjunctivitis, cervicitis and proctitis. Gonorrhea involves incubation period of 3- 10 days

Undiagnosed and/or untreated gonorrheal urogenital infections can ascend through the upper urogenital tract and cause many severe reproductive complications, most commonly but not exclusively in women, such as endometritis, pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, and/or life-threatening morbidity via ectopic pregnancy.

However, females who either remain asymptomatic or have only minor symptoms may delay in seeking medical attention.

These minor symptoms may comprise of scant vaginal discharge that are issued from the inflamed cervix (without vaginitis or vaginosis per se) and dysuria that may be associated with gonococcal urethritis.

question_text: A farmer presents with foot swelling and discharging sinuses. Staining of the lesion shows Gram-positive filamentous structures.
explanation:
Explanation:

Nocardia brasiliensis causes actinomycetoma, presenting with swelling, sinuses, and granules, and appears as Gram-positive filamentous bacteria on stains.

  • Nocardia brasiliensis is a soil-dwelling aerobic actinomycete, commonly causing actinomycetoma; a chronic, granulomatous infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue. Farmers and those who walk barefoot are at higher risk.
  • Key clinical features of actinomycetoma include:
    • Painless swelling of the foot
    • Multiple discharging sinuses
    • Presence of sulphur granules (actually colonies of the bacteria)
    • Gram-positive, filamentous, weakly acid-fast rods on microscopy
    • Common in tropical/subtropical regions
  • Diagnosis is confirmed by Gram stain, acid-fast staining, culture, and biopsy.
  • Treatment includes trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) and prolonged antibiotics.

Explanation of other options:

Sporothrix schenckii (Option B): A dimorphic fungus causing sporotrichosis, typically follows a thorn prick and causes nodular lymphangitis, not discharging sinuses with filamentous Gram-positive organisms.

Staphylococcus aureus (Option C): Causes acute pyogenic infections, abscesses, or cellulitis. It is Gram-positive cocci in clusters, not filamentous organisms, and doesn't cause actinomycetoma.

Aspergillus (Option D): A septate hyaline fungus causing aspergillosis, especially in immunocompromised hosts. It is not Gram-positive and does not appear filamentous on Gram stain.

Standard WHO Multidrug Therapy (MDT) for adult leprosy management includes:

Always adhere to the WHO MDT blister pack guidelines to ensure compliance and avoid drug resistance.

question_text: A patient presents with a plaque on the face with central clearing and atrophy, and his chest X-ray demonstrates apical calcification. Which of the following can be used for the diagnosis of the underlying condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

A patient presenting with a skin lesion along with apical calcification on chest X-ray raises a strong suspicion for cutaneous tuberculosis, particularly in the setting of prior or latent pulmonary tuberculosis.

  • Cutaneous TB can manifest in several forms, including lupus vulgaris, which is often paucibacillary and challenging to confirm microbiologically.
  • While diagnosis may be suggested by clinical appearance and histopathology, the only definitive diagnostic methods for cutaneous TB are:
    • Tissue culture
    • Cytological smear
    • Detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA via PCR
  • Among these, PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) is especially valuable because it enables the rapid and specific detection of tuberculosis DNA, even in paucibacillary lesions such as lupus vulgaris, where conventional methods may fail.
  • PCR techniques utilize targets such as IS6110, MPB-64, or 16S rRNA genes, and have demonstrated good sensitivity and specificity in cutaneous TB, with overall sensitivities ranging from 73% to 100% in multibacillary cases.

Mantoux test (Option B) is a supportive test but not diagnostic, as it only indicates prior exposure or immune response to TB antigens and may be positive in latent TB, BCG vaccination, or other mycobacterial infections.

Slit skin smear test (Option C) is used to diagnose leprosy, not tuberculosis.

Probe test (Option D) is a clinical bedside test used to check for sinus tract depth or bone involvement, particularly in scrofuloderma, but it is not a diagnostic tool for identifying the pathogen.

question_text: A patient with a history of herpes labialis eruption one week back, now presents with lesions as on palms, soles and oral cavity. What is the diagnosis ?

Erythema multiforme (EM) is a cutaneous and mucosal Type 4 hypersensitivity reaction with characteristic target lesions triggered by certain antigenic stimuli.

The etiology of EM is

Most lesions appear in 48-72 hours and favor the extremities

Clinically, the typical lesion of the EM is the target lesion/bull's eye/iris lesion

Rounded well defined lesion with three concentric circles.

The peripheral ring is erythematous, ; the middle zone is pale oedematous, and the center is violaceous +/- blister.

question_text: A 17-year-old female presents for a three-day history of malodorous, watery vaginal discharge that is more noticeable after sexual intercourse. A bedside test revealed the following finding. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?

explanation:

  • (1) thin, white, and homogeneous vaginal discharge

  • (4) release of a fishy odour on adding alkali (10% KOH), also known as a positive whiff test.
  • Treatment regimens include oral metronidazole (500 mg twice daily for 5-7 days, or 2 g single dose); metronidazole 0.75% intravaginal gel once daily for five days; or clindamycin 2% intravaginal cream for seven days

question_text: A 65-year-old man with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus presents with a large, painful, and indurated inflammatory mass on the nape of his neck, as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• The image shows a large, deep-seated, erythematous, and suppurative lesion with multiple draining sinus tracts (pustules). The location on the posterior neck and the patient's history of uncontrolled diabetes are classic for a carbuncle.
  • A carbuncle is a deep infection of a contiguous group of hair follicles. It represents a coalescence of several furuncles, extending deep into the subcutaneous tissue.
  • The key differentiating feature is the presence of multiple pustular openings on the skin surface, through which pus drains from the interconnected abscesses below.

Explanation of Other Options:

Furuncle (Option A): A furuncle (or boil) is an infection of a single hair follicle. It typically presents as a single pustule or abscess, not a large, multiloculated lesion with multiple draining points.

Erythrasma (Option C): Erythrasma is a superficial bacterial infection of the skin caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum. It presents as a well-demarcated, reddish-brown patch in intertriginous areas (like the axilla or groin) and is not suppurative.

Cellulitis (Option D): Cellulitis is a diffuse, spreading infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue. While it presents with erythema, warmth, and pain, it is typically not associated with the formation of multiple, deep, draining pustules like a carbuncle.

question_text: Which organism is primarily responsible for causing erysipelas?
explanation:
Explanation:

Erysipelas is a superficial skin infection most commonly caused by beta-hemolytic streptococci. Among these, Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus) is the most frequent causative agent.

  • Erysipelas presents as a bright red, well-demarcated, raised, and warm plaque.
  • It commonly affects the face or lower limbs.
  • Disruption of the skin barrier, such as from trauma, insect bites, or existing dermatoses, can predispose individuals to erysipelas.
  • Prompt antibiotic treatment (e.g., penicillin) is essential to prevent complications.

Explanation of other options:

Staphylococcus aureus (Option A): While Staphylococcus aureus is a common cause of other skin and soft tissue infections like cellulitis, folliculitis, and impetigo, it is less typical for classical erysipelas.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Option B): Pseudomonas aeruginosa can cause skin infections, especially in specific circumstances like "hot tub folliculitis" or infections in burn patients and immunocompromised individuals, but it is not the primary cause of erysipelas.

Fungus (Option C): Fungal infections (mycoses) can cause various skin conditions, such as tinea infections (ringworm) or candidiasis. However, erysipelas is a bacterial infection, not a fungal one.

Key Takeaways:

  • Erysipelas is primarily caused by bacteria belonging to the Streptococcus
  • Streptococcus pyogenes is the most common specific species.

question_text: Find the treatment for the following condition given in image?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image shows a unilateral, grouped vesicular eruption arranged along a dermatome, which is a classical sign for Herpes Zoster (shingles) caused by reactivation of varicella-zoster virus (VZV).

  • Antiviral therapy is the treatment of choice.
  • Valacyclovir, a prodrug of acyclovir, has better oral bioavailability and is commonly used.
  • Early initiation (within 72 hours of rash onset) reduces acute symptoms and post-herpetic neuralgia

Explanation of Other Options:

  • Imipenem (Option B): A broad-spectrum carbapenem antibiotic used for severe bacterial infections; it has no role in treating viral infections like herpes zoster.
  • Carbapenem (Option C): Refers to a class of beta-lactam antibiotics (e.g., meropenem, ertapenem) used for resistant bacterial infections; not effective against VZV.
  • Penicillin (Option D): Active against many Gram-positive bacteria, but ineffective against viruses like VZV.

Key Takeaways:

  • Herpes Zoster = dermatomal vesicular eruption.
  • Treatment: antivirals (acyclovir, valacyclovir, famciclovir), best if started early.

question_text: A 6-year-old child presents with fever and a pleomorphic rash, as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The term "pleomorphic rash" refers to a rash that contains lesions in different stages of development simultaneously (e.g., macules, papules, vesicles, and crusts all present at the same time). This is a classic hallmark of chickenpox (varicella) caused by the varicella-zoster virus.

  • Chickenpox is highly contagious and usually affects children.
  • It often begins with a prodrome of fever, malaise, and loss of appetite before the rash appears.
  • The rash typically starts on the trunk and face and then spreads, accompanied by fever.
  • The vesicles are often described as "dewdrops on a rose petal."
  • The lesions are intensely itchy.
  • Complications can include bacterial superinfection of skin lesions, pneumonia, and encephalitis.
  • Vaccination has significantly reduced the incidence of chickenpox.

Explanation of other options:

Smallpox (Option A): Smallpox also presents with a rash, but its lesions are typically monomorphic (all lesions in the same stage of development) and tend to be concentrated on the face and extremities. Also, smallpox has been globally eradicated.

Measles (Option B): Measles presents with a maculopapular rash that typically starts on the face and spreads downwards, becoming confluent. It is usually preceded by a prodrome of fever, cough, coryza (runny nose), and conjunctivitis, along with Koplik spots (small white spots on the buccal mucosa). The rash is not pleomorphic.

Rubella (Option C): Rubella (German measles) causes a milder maculopapular rash that starts on the face and spreads rapidly downwards, often clearing by the third day. It is usually accompanied by low-grade fever and prominent postauricular and occipital lymphadenopathy. The rash is not pleomorphic.

Key Takeaways:

  • A pleomorphic rash (lesions in various stages of development simultaneously) in a child with fever is highly indicative of
  • This differentiates it from other common viral exanthems like measles and rubella, and the eradicated smallpox.

question_text: A patient presented with multiple painful blisters on an erythematous base on the trunk as shown in the image. Diagnosis?
explanation:
Herpes zoster (shingles) is caused by the reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus (VZV), which remains latent in the dorsal root ganglia after primary infection (chickenpox).

  • Clinical Features:
    • Pain and burning sensation along the affected dermatome.
    • Painful, grouped vesicles on an erythematous base distributed unilaterally along dermatomes.
  • Treatment:
    • Antiviral medications like acyclovir, famciclovir, or valacyclovir, administered within 72 hours of symptom onset to reduce complications and duration.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

  • (A) Herpes Simplex:
    • Usually presents as grouped vesicles on mucocutaneous junctions (e.g., lips or genital area). Does not follow a dermatome pattern and is recurrent in nature.
  • (C) Molluscum Contagiosum:
    • Caused by the poxvirus, presenting as multiple pearly, dome-shaped papules with central umbilication. It is painless and not vesicular.
  • (D) Chickenpox:
    • Caused by primary varicella-zoster virus infection, presenting as a polymorphic rash (vesicles, papules, and crusts) that is generalized and pruritic, often involving the trunk and extremities.

Key Takeaway: Herpes zoster presents as unilateral painful vesicles along a dermatome, distinguishing it from other conditions with vesicular or papular rashes.

question_text: A 10 year old child with a recent history of sore throat and fever, now presents with lesions all over the body as shown. Which of the following is correct about the diagnosis ?
explanation:
Urticaria is a vascular reaction of the skin marked by the transient appearance of smooth, slightly elevated papules or plaques (wheals) that are erythematous and that are often attended by severe pruritus. Individual lesions resolve without scarring in several hours. Lesions commonly last 20 minutes to 3 hours, disappear, and then reappear in other skin areas. Individual lesions usually fade within 24 hours or so, Urticaria has been reported with infectious diseases.

Viral infections associated with acute urticaria include acute viral syndromes, hepatitis (A, B, and C), Epstein-Barr virus, and herpes simplex virus. Streptococcal infection has been reported as the cause of 17% of acute urticaria cases in children. Urticaria has also been reported with chronic parasitic infections.

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 42, page 7

question_text: Tzanck cells refer to which type of cell?
explanation:
Explanation:

Tzanck cells/acantholytic cells are large, rounded keratinocytes with hypertrophic nucleus, hazy or absent nucleoli and abundant basophilic cytoplasm. The morphology of cells changes from polyhedral to rounded as they lose attachment from other epithelial cells.

Langerhans cells (Option A): Langerhans cells are antigen-presenting dendritic cells found in the epidermis. They have a characteristic "coffee-bean" nucleus and contain Birbeck granules on electron microscopy.

Multinucleated giant cells (Option C): Multinucleated giant cells are formed by the fusion of macrophages, commonly seen in granulomas (e.g., TB, sarcoidosis) or viral infections like

Leucocytes (Option D): Leucocytes (white blood cells) include neutrophils, lymphocytes, and macrophages. They may be present in inflammatory skin diseases but are not the defining cells on a Tzanck smear. They do not show the rounded "acantholytic" morphology characteristic of Tzanck cells.

question_text: What is the mechanism of action of imiquimod?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Imiquimod works by activating the innate and adaptive immune responses. Its primary mechanism is binding to Toll-like receptor 7 (TLR7) on immune cells, which leads to activation of nuclear factor kappa-B.
  • Imiquimod 5% cream is an FDA-approved treatment for external anogenital warts, actinic keratoses, and superficial basal cell carcinoma. It is classified as an immune response modifier rather than a direct antiviral or cytotoxic agent.
  • Imiquimod is an immune response modifier.
  • This activation results in the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including interferon-alpha, and recruitment of plasmacytoid dendritic cells to the site of application.
  • Through this mechanism, imiquimod induces a Th1-mediated immune response, enhancing antiviral activity against HPV and promoting apoptosis of abnormal or infected cells.
  • In addition to its antiviral properties, it demonstrates anti-tumoral activity, contributing to its efficacy in treating superficial skin cancers.

Key Takeaways:

  • Imiquimod is unique because it stimulates the immune system through TLR7 activation
  • imiquimod induces a Th1-mediated immune response.
  • Imiquimod works by activating the innate and adaptive immune responses.

question_text: A child presents with sores in the mouth and a rash on the hands and feet, as shown in the image. What is the causative organism?
explanation:
Explanation:

The classic presentation of sores in the mouth (herpangina) and a rash on the hands and feet is highly characteristic of Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease (HFMD). Coxsackievirus A16 is the most common causative agent of HFMD. Other enteroviruses, such as enterovirus 71, can also cause HFMD, sometimes with more severe neurological complications.


  • HFMD is a common viral illness in infants and children.
  • It is typically mild and self-limiting, resolving within 7-10 days.
  • Transmission occurs through direct contact with nasal discharge, saliva, stool, or fluid from blisters of an infected person.
  • There is no specific antiviral treatment; management is supportive, focusing on hydration and pain relief.
  • Oral lesions can be painful, leading to reduced fluid intake and potential dehydration.

Explanation of other options:

Pox virus (Option A): Poxviruses cause diseases like smallpox (eradicated) and molluscum contagiosum. Molluscum contagiosum causes discrete, flesh-colored, dome-shaped papules, but typically not widespread oral sores and a vesiculopapular rash on hands and feet.

HPV(Option B): Human Papillomavirus (HPV) causes warts (e.g., common warts, genital warts) but does not present with the typical oral sores and hand-foot rash of HFMD.

Herpes virus(Option C): Herpes simplex virus (HSV) causes oral cold sores (herpes labialis) or stomatitis, and can cause cutaneous lesions (e.g., herpes gladiatorum), but usually not the widespread hand and foot rash concurrent with distinct oral lesions seen in HFMD. While a severe primary HSV infection could cause extensive oral lesions, the specific pattern of hand-foot rash points away from typical HSV.

Key Takeaways:

  • Oral sores and a rash on the hands and feet characterize Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease (HFMD)
  • Coxsackievirus A16 is the most common causative agent of HFMD.

question_text: What is the likely diagnosis for a patient presenting with several painful vesicles on a red base, distributed along a dermatome on the trunk, as shown in the given image?
explanation:

Explanations of other options:

Herpes simplex (Option A): Herpes simplex is not the correct answer, as HSV usually manifests as recurrent vesicular eruptions on the lips (HSV-1) or genital area (HSV-2), and unlike herpes zoster, it does not appear in a dermatomal distribution.

Molluscum contagiosum (Option C): Molluscum contagiosum is not the right diagnosis, as it produces dome-shaped, umbilicated papules instead of vesicular lesions. It is a poxvirus infection, more frequently observed in children and immunocompromised patients.

Chickenpox (Option D): Chickenpox is not the correct diagnosis, as varicella typically shows vesicles at varying stages of development ("dew drop on a rose petal") that are spread diffusely over the body, rather than being restricted to a dermatomal pattern.

question_text: What condition is seen in the image below?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image depicts swelling of the foot with multiple discharging sinuses. This is characteristic of Mycetoma (Madura foot), a chronic, progressive, granulomatous disease of skin and subcutaneous tissues caused by either fungi (eumycetoma) or filamentous bacteria (actinomycetoma).

Hallmark triad:

  1. Swelling (tumefaction) of affected part.
  2. Multiple draining sinuses.
  3. Discharge containing coloured granules (representing colonies of causative organisms).

Common sites: foot > leg > hand. Disease is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions.

Pathogenesis of Mycetoma

Traumatic inoculation of fungi/actinomycetes → Chronic granulomatous inflammation → Sinus formation → Extrusion of coloured granules

Explanations Of Other Options:

Chromoblastomycosis (Option B): Chronic fungal infection with warty, verrucous plaques. No multiple draining sinuses with granules.

Tuberculosis verrucosa cutis (Option C): Caused by exogenous reinfection with M. tuberculosis. Presents as warty lesions on hands/feet, but not tumefaction with draining sinuses.

Cellulitis (Option D): Acute bacterial infection of dermis and subcutis. Redness, warmth, pain, swelling → but NO discharging sinuses or granules.

question_text: A farmer presents with a swollen foot exhibiting multiple draining sinuses, as shown in the accompanying image. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Mycetoma is a long-standing, granulomatous infection of the skin, subcutaneous tissue, fascia, and even bone, most frequently involving the foot or hand-hence the term Madura foot or maduramycosis. It is found worldwide, particularly in tropical and subtropical regions.

Etiology:

  • The condition is classified according to the causative organism:
  • Eumycetoma: Caused by true fungi.
  • Actinomycetoma: Due to filamentous bacteria (actinomycetes).
  • Botryomycosis: A similar chronic bacterial infection.

Pathogenesis & Clinical Features

  • Mode of infection: Follows traumatic implantation of organisms from soil or plant material, often via a thorn or splinter.
  • Classic triad:
    • Progressive swelling (tumefaction) of the affected area
    • Multiple draining sinuses
    • Discharge of "grains" or granules, which are compact colonies of the causative organism, typically 0.5-2 mm in size.
  • The colour of these grains varies with the specific pathogen.
  • It commonly affects the subcutaneous tissues of the feet, lower legs, hands, and other exposed sites.

Laboratory Diagnosis

  • Direct microscopy: Demonstration of characteristic grains in pus from draining sinuses or in biopsy specimens confirms the diagnosis.
  • Culture: Material should be cultured at both 25-30 °C and 37 °C.
    • Actinomycetes: Brain-heart infusion agar or blood agar
    • Fungi: Sabouraud agar without cycloheximide

Management

  • Eumycetoma: Requires combined medical and surgical treatment-wide excision or debridement along with prolonged antifungal therapy.
  • Actinomycetoma: Usually responds well to antibiotics such as rifampicin combined with sulfonamides or cotrimoxazole.

Explanation of other options:

Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) (Option B): SCC of the skin can present as a chronic ulcer, plaque, or nodular growth, sometimes arising on scars or areas of chronic inflammation. It may ulcerate and occasionally form a sinus, but it does not show the classic triad of tumefaction, multiple draining sinuses, and discharge of colored "grains." Histopathology reveals malignant keratinocytes with keratin pearls, which distinguishes it from infectious causes.

Nocardia Infection(Option C):Nocardia species can cause actinomycetoma, which is one subset of mycetoma. When used as a separate option here, however, it likely refers to pulmonary or disseminated nocardiosis, which typically presents with lung involvement (cough, nodules, cavitation) and may spread to the brain or skin. Isolated foot involvement with the classic mycetoma appearance and grains is more consistent with the broader category of mycetoma rather than primary nocardial disease.

Sporotrichosis(Option D): Caused by Sporothrix schenckii, this is a subcutaneous fungal infection usually contracted via plant material (e.g., rose thorns). The hallmark is a lymphocutaneous pattern: a painless nodule at the site of inoculation that ulcerates and is followed by secondary nodules along lymphatic channels ("sporotrichoid spread"). It does not produce multiple sinus tracts or colored granules, and extensive foot deformity is uncommon.

question_text: A farmer presents to you with swelling on foot and multiple discharging sinuses in the lower limb. Granules from the discharge were examined under the microscope, shown below. Which of the following is true regarding this condition?
option_a: Both bacteria and fungi can be causative
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The presentation described-chronic swelling of the foot, multiple discharging sinuses, and granules in pus-is typical of mycetoma.
  • Farmers and agricultural workers are commonly affected due to repeated trauma with soil contamination.
  • Mycetoma can be caused by both bacteria (Actinomycetoma) and fungi (Eumycetoma), making option A correct.
  • The granules seen under microscopy are diagnostic clues, with color varying by causative organism.

Mycetoma:

  • Actinomycetoma (bacterial):
    • Causative agents: Actinomyces, Nocardia.
    • Granule colors: white, yellow, or red.
    • Treatment: Long-term antibiotics.
  • Eumycetoma (fungal):
    • Causative agents: Madurella, Exophiala.
    • Granule colors: black or brown.
    • Treatment: Antifungal agents and sometimes surgical excision.
  • Pathology: Progressive granulomatous infection with discharging sinuses, leading to deep tissue and even bone involvement.
  • Spread: Direct extension and hematogenous spread, but not lymphatic.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

Undergoes lymphatic spread (Option B): Incorrect because mycetoma does not spread via lymphatics. It spreads by direct extension and hematogenous routes.

There is lymphocyte accumulation (Option C): Incorrect because mycetoma is a granulomatous disease characterized by neutrophils, macrophages, and giant cells rather than predominantly lymphocyte infiltration.

Involves only superficial tissues (Option D): Incorrect because mycetoma progressively extends into subcutaneous tissue, fascia, muscle, and bone, causing chronic deformity and disability if untreated.

Key Takeaway:
Mycetoma is a chronic granulomatous infection characterized by swelling, discharging sinuses, and granules. It can be caused by both bacteria (actinomycetoma) and fungi (eumycetoma), spreads by direct extension, and involves deep tissues including bone.

question_text: A 60-year-old woman presents with great toe infection showing discoloration and subungual hyperkeratosis, suggestive of onychomycosis. Which topical drug is recommended for toenail onychomycosis?

It is FDA-approved for the treatment of onychomycosis of the toenails caused by Trichophyton rubrum and Trichophyton mentagrophytes. Applied daily as a solution, it penetrates the nail plate effectively, making it suitable for localized disease.

question_text: A farmer presents with a solitary lesion on the foot as shown below. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

TB verrucosa cutis (warty tuberculosis) occurs due to exogenous inoculation of M. tuberculosis into the skin of individuals already sensitized to TB.

Lesions appear on trauma-prone sites such as the hands, knees, ankles, and feet, especially in people walking barefoot in contaminated environments.

It begins as a small indurated warty papule that slowly enlarges into a verrucous plaque with finger-like projections or serpiginous borders. It is typically solitary, asymptomatic, firm, purplish-red or brown, and slowly progressive.

This presentation, a solitary, warty, well-defined lesion on the foot, matches TBVC.

Mycetoma (Option A): Swelling + sinuses + discharging granules.

Sporotrichosis (Option B): Linear nodulo-ulcerative lesions in a lymphatic distribution.

Botryomycosis (Option D): Chronic suppurative Staphylococcus aureus infection, swelling, nodules, pus.

Key Takeaways:

TBVC = exogenous inoculation TB, solitary warty verrucous plaque on trauma-prone areas (hands, feet, knees, ankles), common in those walking barefoot.

question_text: Pityriasis versicolor is caused by:
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Pityriasis versicolor is a common, benign, superficial fungal infection of the skin.
  • It is caused by Malassezia, a dimorphic lipophilic yeast that is part of the normal skin flora.
  • The main species involved are Malassezia furfur and Malassezia globosa.
  • Under certain conditions, Malassezia converts to its pathogenic filamentous form, leading to the characteristic hypopigmented or hyperpigmented patches seen in pityriasis versicolor.
  • This condition is often seen in warm, humid climates and is treated with topical or systemic antifungals.

Explanation of Other Options

  • Option C - Trichophyton rubrum: A dermatophyte responsible for tinea corporis, tinea pedis, and onychomycosis.
  • Option D - Trichophyton mentagrophytes: Another dermatophyte causing tinea infections, especially tinea barbae and tinea pedis.

question_text: Which of the following is used as nail lacquer for treatment of onychomycosis?
explanation:
• Terbinafine is the drug of choice for onychomycosis (fungal nail infection). It is available as both oral medication and nail lacquer for topical application.
  • Its mechanism of action involves inhibiting squalene epoxidase, an enzyme crucial for fungal cell membrane synthesis, making it highly effective against dermatophytes.
  • Nail lacquers containing terbinafine provide direct application to the infected nail, ensuring localized treatment with minimal systemic side effects.

Explanation of the Incorrect Options:

  • (A) Fluconazole:
    • An azole antifungal, used systemically or topically for mucosal and systemic fungal infections but not commonly formulated as a nail lacquer.
  • (B) Nystatin:
    • Effective against Candida infections, particularly oral and cutaneous candidiasis, but not typically used for onychomycosis.
  • (C) Itraconazole:
    • Another azole antifungal used orally for onychomycosis but is not formulated as a nail lacquer. It is a second-line choice compared to terbinafine.

Key Takeaway:

Terbinafine is the most effective antifungal for onychomycosis, available in both oral and topical nail lacquer forms.

question_text: A patient presents with the history of thorn prick while working in his garden. The lesion gradually spread up to his shoulder in a linear manner. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Sporotrichosis, also known as "rose gardener's disease" is caused by Sporothrix schenckii.
  • The infection is mainly through thorn pricks or plant material and It spreads along the lymphatics.
  • The characteristic presentation is the appearance of nodular lesions spreading in a linear fashion along lymphatic channels called the Sporotrichoid pattern.

Other diseases that show Sporotrichoid Pattern:

  • Mycobacterium marinum
  • Nocardia brasiliensis
  • Atypical mycobacteria (e.g., chelonae, M. abscessus)
  • Leishmania species

Asteroid Bodies are also seen in Sarcoidosis but are formed inside giant cells, its host derived and made of collagen.

The asteroid bodies In sporotrichosis is fungus-associated (yeast cell at the center).

Explanation of Other Options:

Abscess (Option A):It is a Pus-filled lesion and is caused by bacterial, the lesion here follows a nonlinear pattern

Furuncle (Option B): It usually presents as boils, nonlinear and is caused by S.aureus.

Lymphangitis (Option C): It's a non-nodular lesion and usually presents with fever, it is caused by bacteria.

Key Takeaways:

  • Sporotrichosis = "rose gardener's disease."
  • Shows sporotrichosis spread or linear spread of nodules along lymphatics.

question_text: A woman presents with foul-smelling vaginal discharge. On examination, the cervix appears normal, and the whiff test is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Bacterial vaginosis is caused by an imbalance of normal vaginal flora, with overgrowth of Gardnerella vaginalis and anaerobes, and reduction of lactobacilli. The hallmark features include:

  • Thin, foul-smelling, grey-white vaginal discharge.
  • Positive whiff test (fishy odor after adding KOH, due to volatile amines).
  • Normal-appearing cervix, which helps distinguish it from trichomoniasis.
  • Microscopy shows clue cells (vaginal epithelial cells covered with bacteria).

Explanation of Other Options:

Candidiasis (Option A): Presents as Thick, curdy white discharge with intense itching. The cervix/vaginal mucosa will inflamed and whiff test negative.

Trichomoniasis (Option B): Presents with frothy, yellow-green discharge with strawberry cervix and motile trichomonads on microscopy.

Chlamydial infection (Option D): Often presents with mucopurulent cervicitis and a friable cervix , the discharge is not typically foul-smelling.

Key Takeaways:

  • Whiff test + foul-smelling discharge + normal cervix = BV.
  • Amsels criteria is the diagnostic criteria used.

question_text:
Which of the following are cause chronic urticaria:
1. Idiopathic
2. Antibodies against mast cells
3. Drugs
4. Pseudo-allergies
5. Infections
explanation:
Chronic urticaria (CU) is defined by recurrent episodes occurring at least twice a week for 6 weeks.

Females are more commonly affected than males.

Establishing the cause of CU is difficult and at times almost impossible.

Various etiologies

  1. Physical urticaria accounts for about 15% of urticaria cases, and is triggered by exogenous mechanical stimuli
  2. Auto-immune : 30-50% patients with CU have circulating functional auto antibodies against the high-affinity IgE receptor (FCeRIa) on mast cells or against IgE. Also, urticaria has been associated with a number of autoimmune diseases like systemic lupus erythematosus, cryoglobulinemia.
  3. Infectious agents reported to cause urticaria include hepatitis B virus, Streptococcus and Mycoplasma species, Helicobacter pylori, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, herpes simplex virus, chronic parasitic infections, H pylori.
  4. Drugs : aspirin, other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, opioids, ACE inhibitors, and alcohol.
  5. Pseudoallergy to food ingredients.
  6. Most cases of CU are considered idiopathic.

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 42, page 9

question_text: Identify the condition shown below.
explanation:
Explanation:

The given image depicts warty lesions in the anogenital region suggestive of condyloma acuminata.

  • Genital warts (condyloma acuminata) are caused by Human Papillomavirus (HPV), most commonly strains 6 and 11.
  • Characteristic features include:

question_text:
A patient had recurrent oral ulcers and painful superficial eruptions in the genital area. A biopsy of the vesicular lesions was done.

What is the best treatment option for this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Painful grouped vesicular lesions in the genital area that rupture to form multiple tender ulcers are characteristic of genital herpes (HSV infection).
  • Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells due to cell-to-cell fusion (syncytia formation) and acantholysis of keratinocytes.

The drug of choice is oral Acyclovir (200 mg five times daily or 400 mg three times daily for 7-10 days).

  • Alternative antivirals include valaciclovir and famciclovir.

Genital Herpes:

This is caused by HSV-2 (most cases), HSV-1 increasing in young adults and transmitted through sexual contact (asymptomatic viral shedding).

Clinical features

  • Primary infection: Painful grouped vesicles/ulcers on genitalia, dysuria, tender inguinal lymphadenopathy, fever/malaise.
  • Recurrent infection: Usually milder, shorter, often preceded by tingling/burning prodrome.
  • Severity: Prior HSV-1 infection attenuates severity of HSV-2 primary infection.

Complications

  • Radiculoneuropathy: Sacral paraesthesia, urinary retention, constipation, impotence.
  • Meningism: Headache, neck stiffness; HSV DNA detectable by CSF PCR.
  • Encephalitis: Rare but serious.
  • Chronic verrucous HSV (esp. in HIV): Ulcers may persist, thicken, mimic neoplasia.

Treatment

  • First-line: Oral acyclovir, valaciclovir, or famciclovir (reduce duration & severity). Analgesia for pain.
  • Severe/atypical (HIV, verrucous, resistant): High-dose oral/IV acyclovir or valaciclovir ± cidofovir or imiquimod.

Explanation of other options:

Corticosteroids (Option B): Used in autoimmune blistering disorders (pemphigus, pemphigoid), not viral infections.

Penicillin (Option C): Drug of choice for syphilis, not herpes.

Azithromycin (Option D): Used in bacterial STIs like chlamydia, not viral herpes.

question_text: A patient presents with a generalized rash over the body, a greyish patch over the anal area, and characteristic hair changes as shown in the image. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical triad of generalized rash, perianal condyloma lata, and moth-eaten alopecia is characteristic of secondary syphilis caused by Treponema pallidum.

  • Secondary syphilis, caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum, typically occurs 6-12 weeks after the primary chancre heals.
  • It is characterized by systemic dissemination of the organism and presents with:
    • Generalized symmetrical maculopapular rash, often involving the palms and soles.
    • Condyloma lata - greyish, flat moist papules commonly seen in the perianal and genital region.
    • Moth-eaten alopecia - a patchy, non-scarring hair loss seen on the scalp.
  • These findings, especially when seen together, are highly suggestive of secondary syphilis.
  • Diagnosis is confirmed by serologic tests (e.g., VDRL/RPR and TPHA/FTA-ABS).
  • Treatment involves intramuscular benzathine penicillin G, which is the drug of choice.

Explanation of other options:

Staphylococcus aureus (Option A): Typically causes pustular or abscess-forming skin lesions like impetigo or folliculitis; it does not cause systemic rash with alopecia or perianal lesions as seen in syphilis.

Malassezia furfur (Option C): Causes pityriasis versicolor, which presents with hypopigmented or hyperpigmented macules, not generalized rash or hair loss.

Microsporum canis (Option D): A dermatophyte that causes tinea capitis with patchy scalp hair loss, but it does not cause perianal lesions or generalized body rash.

question_text: A 28 year old sexually active male presents with scanty mucoid discharge from the urethra. Gram stain from the discharge is shown below. The patient is suffering from?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • More than 5 polymorphonuclear leucocytes per oil immersion field on a smear of intraurethral swab specimen is one of the diagnostic feature of Non gonococcal urethritis
  • Non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU) presents with scanty mucoid or purulent urethral discharge or sometimes may be completely asymptomatic.
  • Sexually transmitted urethritis in males may be gonococcal or nongonococcal.
  • Gonococcal urethritis (GCU) usually presents with severe dysuria and profuse mucopurulent urethral discharge and perimeatal erythema.
  • Gram staining of the pus taken from the external urethral meatus, in case of GCU revels numerous pus cells and gram-negative reniform intracellular diplococci.
  • Gonococcal urethritis (option A) produces copious, thick purulent discharge.
  • Dhaat syndrome (option C) is a psychological condition involving anxiety over semen loss.There is no urethral discharge on Gram stain.
  • Syphilis (option D) causes a painless chancre, but not produce urethral discharge

Key Takeaways:

  • More than 5 polymorphonuclear leucocytes on a smear of intraurethral swab specimen is one of the diagnostic feature of Non gonococcal urethritis
  • Non gonococcal urethritis (NGU) presents with scanty mucoid or purulent urethral discharge

question_text: An 8-day-old newborn of consanguineous parents presents with blisters and skin peeling at sites of pressure or handling. A previous sibling had a similar condition that resulted in death. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Epidermolysis bullosa (EB) refers to a group of inherited blistering disorders in which even minor trauma leads to skin fragility, blistering, and erosions. Symptoms typically begin at birth or in the early neonatal period.

Consanguinity, recurrence in siblings, and fatal outcomes strongly suggest an autosomal recessive form, commonly seen in junctional or dystrophic EB. Warm environments and friction worsen blistering.

  • EB is classified into three main types:
    • Epidermolysis bullosa simplex (EBS)
    • Junctional EB (JEB)
    • Dystrophic EB (DEB)
  • Bullous pemphigoid (Option A): Autoimmune blistering disorder seen in elderly, not neonates. Not associated with consanguinity or family history.
  • Letterer-Siwe disease (Option B): Aggressive form of Langerhans cell histiocytosis in infants.
  • Congenital syphilis (Option C): Presents with pemphigus syphiliticus (bullous lesions). No relation to consanguinity or recurrent fatal blistering in siblings.

question_text: What is the condition shown in the image?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given image shows condyloma acuminatum, also known as Genital warts. These are benign growths on the skin or mucous membranes of the anogenital region, caused by certain types of Human Papillomavirus (HPV), primarily HPV types 6 and 11. They typically appear as flesh-colored to pinkish, soft, verrucous (warty) papules or nodules that can be solitary or confluent.

  • Human Papillomavirus (HPV): The causative agent. Low-risk HPV types (6, 11) cause most genital warts, while high-risk types (16, 18) are associated with an increased risk of anogenital cancers.
  • Transmission: Primarily through skin-to-skin contact during sexual activity.
  • Vaccination: HPV vaccines (e.g., Gardasil 9) are highly effective in preventing infection with the HPV types that cause most genital warts and many cancers.

Explanation of other options:

Bowen disease (Option B): Bowen disease is a form of squamous cell carcinoma in situ of the skin. It can occur on genital skin (erythroplasia of Queyrat on mucous membranes), but it is a precancerous condition, not benign warts.

Condyloma lata (Option C): Condyloma lata are moist, broad, flat-topped, grayish-white lesions seen in secondary syphilis. They are highly infectious but are distinct from the verrucous lesions of condyloma acuminata (genital warts).

Hemorrhoids (Option D): Hemorrhoids are swollen veins in the rectum or anus. They are not sexually transmitted and are not skin growths, but rather vascular structures that can cause itching, bleeding, and discomfort.


Key Takeaways:

  • Genital warts are medically known as condyloma acuminata.
  • They are caused by Human Papillomavirus (HPV), typically low-risk types 6 and
  • Condyloma lata are a manifestation of secondary syphilis and are distinct from genital warts.

question_text: The presence of painless lesions on the vulva, as shown in the image, is most suggestive of which condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The probable diagnosis is Condylomata acuminata.

These painless, verrucous, cauliflower-like growths on the vulva are characteristic of genital warts, a sexually transmitted infection caused primarily by human papillomavirus (HPV) types 6 and 11. Lesions can also appear on the perineum, perianal skin, and other genital mucosa.

Management

  • Topical therapy: Podophyllin resin 20-25% (applied for about 6 hours and then washed off), or podofilox (podoflox) 0.5% solution.
  • Chemical cautery: Trichloroacetic or bichloroacetic acid applied at intervals.
  • Other treatments: Intralesional interferon for refractory lesions.
  • Prevention: Prophylactic HPV vaccination-Cervarix (0, 1, 6 months) or Gardasil (0, 2, 6 months)-provides strong protection against oncogenic HPV strains and partial protection against types 6 and 11.

Explanation for other options:

Genital herpes(Option A): Caused by herpes simplex virus type 2 (occasionally type 1). Presents with clusters of painful vesicles or ulcers accompanied by burning, itching, or dysuria. Lesions tend to be recurrent and often accompanied by systemic symptoms during primary infection.

Gonococcal vulvovaginitis(Option C): Infection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae typically causes purulent, foul-smelling vaginal discharge. External genitalia are painful, swollen, and erythematous, and dysuria is common. Unlike HPV warts, lesions are not verrucous or exophytic.

Condyloma lata(Option D): Represents secondary syphilis due to Treponema pallidum. Lesions are broad-based, moist, smooth, and flat or slightly raised plaques, pink to gray-white in colour. They occur in warm, intertriginous areas such as the perineum or inner thighs and are highly infectious, but lack the cauliflower-like appearance of HPV warts.

question_text: All are true regarding secondary syphilis except :
explanation:
Secondary syphilis presents with a variety of symptoms.

The cutaneous manifestations are also varied

A diffuse mucocutaneous rash (generally coppery red, non-pruritic and bilaterally symmetrical), coppery brown scaly macules on palms and soles are seen.

Most often, the lesions are macular, discrete, reddish brown, and 5 mm or smaller in diameter; however, they can be pustular, annular, or scaling. Vesicular rash is typically absent.

Generalized non-tender lymphadenopathy is typical, especially epitrochlear LN.

Mucosal - condyloma lata, mucous patches, snail track ulcers - they contain a high load of spirochetes, these lesions are highly contagious.

Hair - patchy non-scarring alopecia (Moth-eaten alopecia)

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 29, page 12

question_text: A patient suffering from secondary syphilis was administered injection Benzathine penicillin 2.4 mIU IM stat by the treating doctor. He came in next day with sudden fever, arthralgia and increased number of lesions on the body. What is the diagnosis here ?
explanation:
Jarisch Herxheimer reaction (JHR) is a transient clinical phenomenon that occurs in patients infected by spirochetes who undergo antibiotic treatment.

More specifically, the reaction occurs within 24 hours of antibiotic therapy for spirochetal infections, including syphilis, leptospirosis, Lyme disease.

It is a type 3 hypersensitivity reaction to breakdown products of the spirochete after the use of antibiotics.

JHR is thought to be caused by an acute inflammatory reaction due to increase in cytokines - interleukin-6, interleukin-8, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha, which result in the development of body aches, fevers, rashes, nausea and vomiting, and flushing, along with other symptoms.

The symptoms usually begin 2 hours from the administration of the antibiotic and resolve within 24 hours

Along with systemic symptoms, exacerbation of skin lesions is seen.

JHR is an acute, self-limiting condition and it is important to identify JHR and to distinguish it from allergic reactions and sepsis, which can be life-threatening.

Mild reactions are self-limiting and often resolve spontaneously within 24 hours. The patient should be treated for symptoms with antipyretics and kept under observation.

More severe cases may need steroids

In pregnant women treated for syphilis, the reaction incidence nears 40%. Fetal monitoring is imperative in these patients as recurrent variable decelerations are often seen.

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 29, page 26

question_text: A truck driver presented with complains of painless genital ulcer after unsafe intercourse. The motility of the causative organism can be best checked by which microscope?
explanation:
• The patient presents with painless genital ulcer and inguinal swelling, which is characteristic of primary syphilis.
  • Syphilis is caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum, a spirochete.
  • In primary syphilis, the chancre (ulcer) is usually painless and often appears 10 to 90 days after exposure. The ulcer is often indurated and has serum oozing, which contains a large number of Treponema pallidum spirochetes.
  • Dark field microscopy is the best method to observe these spirochetes in the lesion's fluid. It provides a direct examination and allows for the identification of Treponema pallidum due to its motility, which is visible under the microscope. This technique provides immediate results, which are especially useful in diagnosing syphilis.

Explanation of the Incorrect Options:

  • (A) Electron microscope:
    • While an electron microscope can provide highly detailed images of bacteria and viruses, it is not typically used for diagnosing syphilis. It is expensive, not commonly available in clinical settings, and is not necessary for visualizing Treponema pallidum, which can be observed using a dark field microscope.
  • (C) Fluorescent microscope:
    • Fluorescent microscopy is used for detecting organisms labeled with fluorescent markers or those that naturally fluoresce, but it is not the primary tool for diagnosing syphilis. While fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption tests may be used for syphilis diagnosis, dark field microscopy is preferred for directly visualizing the spirochete in lesions.
  • (D) Light microscope:
    • A light microscope can be used to observe a wide range of organisms, but Treponema pallidum is difficult to see using standard light microscopy due to its small size and lack of natural staining. Dark field microscopy provides better contrast and visibility of spirochetes in the lesion.

Key Takeaway: For the diagnosis of syphilis and the detection of Treponema pallidum, dark field microscopy is the best diagnostic tool as it allows direct observation of the motile spirochetes in the ulcer's exudate, offering an immediate and reliable diagnosis.
