Due to its many protean clinical manifestations, it has been named the "great imitator and mimicker."

T. pallidum is the only treponemal agent that causes venereal disease.

Regional lymphadenopathy is common and consists of rubbery lymph nodes.

The chancre oozes serum, which is teeming with treponema

question_text: All of the following are true about latent syphilis except
explanation:
Latent syphilis is a stage at which the features of secondary syphilis have resolved, though patients remain seroreactive

They are asymptomatic during the latent phase, and the disease is detected only by serologic tests

Latent syphilis is divided into early latent and late latent. The distinction is important because treatment for each is different.

The early latent period is the first year after the resolution of primary or secondary syphilis.

Late latency syphilis is not infectious

About one third of untreated latent syphilis patients go on to develop tertiary syphilis, whereas the rest remain asymptomatic

question_text: The most frequent and important sign of early congenital syphilis is ___
explanation:
Congenital syphilis (CS) is caused by transmission of the spirochete Treponema pallidum from the mother to the fetus, resulting in a multitude of clinical presentations

congenital syphilis differs from syphilis in adults in that T. pallidum is released straight into the bloodstream of the fetus causing spirochetemia with spread to most organs including the bones, kidney, spleen, liver, and heart. This leads to widespread inflammation throughout these organ systems leading to a variety of clinical manifestations.

While CS can cause severe illness and fetal demise, most neonates born with CS are asymptomatic at birth.

However, in untreated infants clinical manifestations usually appear by three months of age and commonly include:

  • Rhinitis:One of the first clinical presentations, usually in the first week of life. Copious, persistent white discharge is noted, which contains spirochetes that can be visualized under darkfield microscopy.
  • Hepatomegaly:This is the most common finding and may occur with splenomegaly. Biopsy of the liver followed by darkfield microscopy may reveal the spirochete. Liver function tests may be abnormal and Jaundice may or may not be present.
  • Generalized Lymphadenopathy:Generalized, non-tender lymphadenopathy is also a common finding.
  • Rash:Rash usually appears one to two weeks after rhinitis. Small red or pink colored maculopapular lesions may be commonly seen on the back, buttocks, posterior thigh and soles of the feet. Vesicular rash can also be seen (Syphilitic pemphigus). The rash progresses to desquamation and crusting

Maternal screening for syphilis in early pregnancy is of prime importance in preventing CS, and it is considered the standard of care in the India

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 29, page 28

question_text: Fitz hugh Curtis syndrome is seen following all these infections except
explanation:
Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome (FHCS), or perihepatitis, is a chronic manifestation of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID).

It is complication of PID caused by Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae, though other bacteria such as Bacteroides, Gardnerella, E. coli and Streptococcus, mycobacterium tuberculosis, have also been found to cause Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome on occasion. It is described as an inflammation of the liver capsule, without the involvement of the liver parenchyma, with adhesion formation accompanied by right upper quadrant pain.

A final diagnosis can be made through laparoscopy or laparotomy via direct visualization of violin string-like adhesions between liver capsule and anterior abdominal wall.

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, chapter 30, page 4

question_text: Which is/are true in secondary syphilis :
explanation:
Secondary syphilis appears 2 to 8 weeks after the disappearance of the primary chancre and has multiple systemic manifestations that can involve any system and body part.

Secondary syphilis presents with a variety of symptoms, such as malaise, sore throat, headache, weight loss, low-grade fever, pruritis, and muscle aches, in addition to the dermatologic manifestations.

The cutaneous manifestations are also varied

A localized or diffuse mucocutaneous rash (generally coppery red, non-pruritic and bilaterally symmetrical), coppery brown scaly macules on palms and soles are seen, with generalized non-tender lymphadenopathy is typical.

Mucosal - condyloma lata, mucous patches, snail track ulcers - they contain a high load of spirochetes, these lesions are highly contagious.

Hair - patchy non-scarring alopecia (Moth-eaten alopecia)

question_text: Which of the following is not seen in late congenital syphilis?
explanation:
If there is a failure to diagnose congenital syphilis early, persistent inflammation may lead to scarring and gumma formation. Clinical findings in late CS includes:

  • Skin and mucous membrane gummas and perioral fissures/scarring
  • Facial changes including frontal bossing, saddle nose, prominent maxilla
  • Anterior bowing of the shin called saber shins.
  • Hutchinson teeth which are hypoplastic notched permanent teeth, most commonly of the upper central incisors
  • Sensorineural hearing loss
  • Eye involvement may lead to interstitial keratitis, secondary glaucoma, and corneal scarring

Hutchinson triad - Hutchinson teeth, interstitial keratitis, and sensorineural hearing loss

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 29, page 31

question_text: How do the borders of a basal cell carcinoma typically appear?
explanation:
Explanation:

Basal cell carcinoma is the most common skin malignancy.

  • Its hallmark clinical feature is pearl like nodules with rolled-out, beaded borders.
  • The edge is translucent and with telangiectasia as the disease progress the lesion may ulcerate, producing the classic "rodent ulcer."

Explanation of Other Options:

Punched out edge(Option B): Typical of Syphilis and trophic ulcer.

Sloping edge (Option C): Seen in healing ulcers or venous ulcers.

Everted edge (Option D): Characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma, not basal cell carcinoma.

question_text: Which condition typically presents with a bubo?
explanation:
Explanation:

Lymphogranuloma venereum is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis L1-L3 serovars.

  • Is associated with inguinal or femoral lymphadenopathy.
  • In the secondary stage, lymph nodes enlarge, become tender, and may coalesce to form buboes.
  • They can rupture and form sinus tracts. This is a hallmark of LGV.

Explanation of Other Options:

Gonorrhoea (Option B): Presents with urethritis and purulent discharge, no bubo.

Syphilis (Option C): Primary stage shows painless chancre, lymphadenopathy is firm and rubbery, no bubo is seen.

Donovanosis (Option D): Causes beefy red ulcerogranulomatous growth due to Klebsiella granulomatis, no lymph node involvement and no bubo formation

question_text: A woman with multiple sexual partners presents with painless irregular ulcers and inguinal swelling. What is the diagnosis ?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Syphilis is a bacterial infection caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum. It often presents with painless, irregular ulcers (chancre) at the site of inoculation and inguinal swelling due to regional lymphadenopathy.
  • Primary syphilis typically appears 10 to 90 days after exposure and presents as a painless, indurated ulcer that may ooze serum teeming with treponema.
  • Regional lymphadenopathy is common in syphilis and presents as rubbery lymph nodes.
  • The diagnosis can be confirmed using dark field microscopy, which directly visualizes the spirochetes from the mucosal lesion.
  • Treatment: The treatment of choice is Benzathine penicillin 2.4 million IU.

Incorrect Answers:

  • B. Chancroid: Chancroid is caused by Haemophilus ducreyi and typically presents with painful ulcers and suppurative inguinal lymphadenopathy. It is not associated with painless ulcers as in syphilis.
  • C. Lymphogranuloma inguinale: Lymphogranuloma inguinale, caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, presents with painless genital ulcers but is more often associated with inguinal lymphadenopathy that may progress to buboes, not as a painless, irregular ulcer like in syphilis.
  • D. Granuloma inguinale: Granuloma inguinale, also called donovanosis, is caused by Klebsiella granulomatisand presents with painless, beefy-red ulcerative lesions that grow over time but does not typically involve inguinal swelling as prominently as syphilis.

Key Takeaway:

  • Syphilis presents with painless, indurated ulcers (chancre) and inguinal lymphadenopathy. It is diagnosed through dark field microscopy to detect the spirochetes and is treated with Benzathine penicillin.

question_text: A patient has an ulcer with overhanging or undermined edges in the neck region as shown in the image. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

An ulcer with "overhanging" or "undermined" edges in the context of lymphadenopathy, particularly in the neck region, is a classic description of a scrofuloderma, which is a cutaneous manifestation of underlying tuberculosis, often originating from a caseating tubercular lymph node. The necrotic material from the lymph node can break through the skin, forming an ulcer with characteristic bluish-red, unhealthy, and often undermined edges, with purulent or caseous discharge. This is also commonly referred to as a "cold abscess" due to the lack of acute inflammatory signs.

  • Scrofuloderma: A form of cutaneous tuberculosis that results from direct extension of tuberculosis from underlying structures (like lymph nodes or bone) to the overlying skin.
  • Caseous Necrosis: A distinct form of necrosis characteristic of tuberculosis, appearing as a cheese-like material.
  • Cold Abscess: An abscess that develops slowly and is relatively painless, lacking the cardinal signs of acute inflammation (heat, redness, pain, swelling).

Explanation of other options:

Malignant cervical lymphadenopathy (Option B): While malignant lymph nodes can ulcerate, the description of "overhanging or undermined edges" is not typically a hallmark feature of ulceration due to metastatic cancer. Cancer ulcers often have rolled or everted edges (e.g., basal cell carcinoma) or irregular, indurated borders.

Syphilis (Option C): Syphilitic ulcers (chancres in primary syphilis, gummas in tertiary syphilis) can occur, but the specific description of undermined edges, especially in the context of a lymph node breaking through the skin, is not typical for syphilis. Chancres are usually clean-based and firm, and gummas can be destructive but have different characteristics.

Extragenital syphilitic chancre

Reactive lymphadenopathy (Option D): Reactive lymphadenopathy is an enlargement of lymph nodes due to an infection or inflammation. While the nodes can become quite large, they typically do not spontaneously ulcerate through the skin to form an ulcer with undermined edges unless there is a secondary infection or a very severe, specific pathology (like Bartonella henselae in cat-scratch disease, which can sometimes fistulize but typically not with the "undermined" characteristic.

Key Takeaways:

  • Ulcers with undermined or overhanging edges in the neck, associated with lymphadenopathy, are highly suggestive of
  • Scrofuloderma is a form of cutaneous tuberculosis, often from underlying tubercular lymph nodes.
  • It is often described as a "cold abscess."

question_text: A 45-year-old male with a history of multiple sexual partners presents with painful genital ulcers and painful Buboes. What is the most probable diagnosis based on these symptoms and history?
explanation:
Explanation:


  • Chancroid caused by Hemophilus ducreyi presents with a painful ulcer and painful inguinal lymphadenopathy.
  • The ulcer bleeds on touch, and the organisms show a school of fish appearance on the gram stain.

Chancroid:

  1. Cause: Hemophilus ducreyi
  2. Incubation period: 3-7 days
  3. Primary lesion: Pustules which progressed to form a genital ulcer called a soft chancre-non indurated and painful.
  4. Inguinal lymph node: unilateral painful bubo with a concomitant genital ulcer.
  5. Gram stain: school of fish/ railroad appearance
  6. Culture: Muller-Hinton agar
  7. Treatment: Azithromycin 1g stat

Explanation of other options:

LGV (Option B):

Caused by specific serovars of Chlamydia trachomatis. While it presents with painful inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes), the primary lesion is usually a small, transient, often painless ulcer or papule that may go unnoticed.

Herpes genitalis (Option C):

Caused by Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV). It typically presents with multiple, painful vesicles that ulcerate and then crust over. While the ulcers are painful, the associated lymphadenopathy is usually bilateral, tender, and non-suppurative, not the prominent, painful buboes seen in chancroid or LGV.

Syphilis (Option D):

Caused by Treponema pallidum. The primary lesion is a chancre, which is typically a single, painless ulcer with a clean base and raised, firm borders. The associated regional lymphadenopathy is usually bilateral, firm, and painless.

Key Takeaways:

question_text: A 40-year-old truck driver, currently on treatment for a genital lesion, presents with generalized symmetrical erythematous papular eruptions over the trunk, back, and palms/soles as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The history of a prior genital lesion (chancre) followed by systemic rash strongly supports secondary syphilis.

The image shows multiple erythematous papulosquamous lesions over trunk and back. This is highly characteristic of secondary syphilis, caused by systemic dissemination of Treponema pallidum.

Other features which can also be found in this condition are mucous patches, condyloma Lata, generalized lymphadenopathy, and constitutional symptoms.

Explanation of Other Options:

  • Drug Eruption (Option B): May mimic syphilitic rash, but usually appears after drug intake, often itchy, and typically spares palms/soles.
  • Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) (Option C): Severe mucocutaneous reaction with widespread epidermal necrosis and detachment, not discrete papules.
  • Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) (Option D): Severe hypersensitivity reaction with targetoid lesions, mucosal erosions, systemic toxicity; not the symmetrical papulosquamous eruption seen here.

Key Takeaways:

  • Secondary syphilis rash is bilateral, symmetrical, papulosquamous, and involves palms & soles.
  • Always look for associated systemic signs and history of primary chancre.

question_text: A sexually active patient presents with painful lesions on the penis
explanation:
Explanation:

Herpes genitalis presents as painful grouped vesicles or ulcers on an erythematous base, commonly caused by HSV-2.

  • Herpes genitalis is a sexually transmitted infection (STI) most often caused by Herpes Simplex Virus type 2 (HSV-2) and occasionally by HSV-1.
  • It is the most common cause of painful genital ulcers.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Painful vesicles or ulcers on the genitalia
    • Vesicles rupture to form shallow, painful ulcers with an erythematous base
    • Often associated with fever, dysuria, inguinal lymphadenopathy in primary infection
    • Lesions may recur due to latency in dorsal root ganglia
    • Diagnosis: Tzanck smear (shows multinucleated giant cells), PCR, viral culture, or serology

Explanation of other options:

Chancroid (Option B): Caused by Haemophilus ducreyi; presents with painful ulcers but these are deep, soft, non-indurated, often with ragged edges and painful inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes), usually unilateral.

Syphilis (Options C): Caused by Treponema pallidum; primary chancre is painless, indurated, and clean-based. Also associated with painless lymphadenopathy.

Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV)(Option D): Caused by Chlamydia trachomatis (serovars L1-L3); painless transient genital ulcer followed by painful inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes) weeks later.

question_text: Which of the following organisms is transmitted through walking barefoot on soil?
explanation:
Explanation:

Madurella mycetomatis causes eumycetoma (Madura foot). It is acquired through traumatic inoculation of fungal elements present in soil into the skin and subcutaneous tissue, this happens usually while walking barefoot. The condition is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions.

This disease presents as a chronic, progressive, granulomatous disease of the foot, with swelling, sinus tract formation, and discharge of characteristic granules.

Explanation of Other Options:

Curvularia (Option B): A dematiaceous fungus causing phaeohyphomycosis and occasionally keratitis, but not typically associated with barefoot soil inoculation.

Nocardia brasiliensis (Option C): A filamentous bacterium (not a true fungus), causes actinomycetoma, also acquired from soil, but its prevalence is lower compared to Eumycetoma.

Aspergillus fumigatus (Option D): A ubiquitous airborne fungus causing allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, aspergilloma, and invasive aspergillosis; transmission is usually via inhalation, not barefoot exposure.

Key Takeaways:

  • Madurella mycetomatis → Madura foot via barefoot soil contact.
  • Presents with classical triad swelling(tumor), sinus tracts, and granules.

question_text: Among the following sexually transmitted diseases, which one is most strongly associated with drug resistance?
explanation:
Explanation:

Gonorrhoea, caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, is the STD most notorious for developing antimicrobial resistance.

Over time, it has acquired resistance to sulfonamides, penicillins, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, and in some cases even to third-generation cephalosporins.

Presently, the recommended treatment is Inj Ceftriaxone 1g i.v.

The emergence of multidrug-resistant gonorrhea ("super gonorrhea") is a significant global public health concern.

Key Takeaways:

  • Gonorrhea = most resistant STD pathogen.
  • Current DOC: Inj ceftriaxone 1g I.v

question_text: The following sign is seen In which sexually transmitted infection?
explanation:
• Both men and women who acquire lymphogranuloma venereum can develop inguinal lymph node involvement.
  • A groove sign is caused by proliferation of inguinal and femoral lymph nodes separated by the inguinal ligament.
  • This presentation is seen in about 20% of patients.
  • Many patients with lymphogranuloma venereum also have deep pelvic node involvement

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 30, page 18

question_text: A 28 year old sexually active male presents with scant mucoid discharge from the urethra. Gram stain from the discharge is shown below. The patient is suffering from?
explanation:
• Sexually transmitted urethritis in males may be gonococcal or nongonococcal.
  • Gonococcal urethritis (GCU) usually presents with severe dysuria and profuse mucopurulent urethral discharge and perimeatal erythema.
  • Nongonococcal urethritis (NGU) on the other hand presents with scanty mucoid or purulent urethral discharge or sometimes may be completely asymptomatic.
  • Gram staining of the pus taken from the external urethral meatus, in case of GCU revels numerous pus cells and gram-negative reniform intracellular diplococci.
  • In case of NGU only pus cells are seen . More than 5 polymorphonuclear leucocytes per oil immersion field on a smear of intraurethral swab specimen is also diagnostic of NGU (in the image in the question - only PMNs)

REFERENCE: Rooks textbook of dermatology, chapter 31

question_text: True about grey kit used in syndromic management of STI
option_a: It is used only in males
option_c: It is used for genital ulcer
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The grey kit is one of the standardized kits used in the syndromic management of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) according to NACO guidelines. This kit is specifically designed for the management of urethral, cervical, and anorectal discharge.
  • According to NACO, the grey kit is designated as Kit 1, not Kit 3. Kit 3 refers to another syndrome-specific treatment kit used for genital ulcers.
  • Can be given either to male or female
  • The grey kit contains two tablets only:
    • Azithromycin 1 g, taken as a single stat dose, which is effective against Chlamydia trachomatis and other common bacterial pathogens causing discharge.
    • Cefixime 400 mg, also taken as a single stat dose, which is effective against Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

Key Takeaways:

  • Grey kit is Kit 1 in the NACO syndromic management system.
  • It is intended for urethral, cervical, or anorectal discharge in both males and females.
  • The kit contains two tablets: Azithromycin 1 g stat and Cefixime 400 mg stat.
  • It is not used for genital ulcers.

Reference:

NACO guidelines for Syndromic Management of STI

https://naco.gov.in/sites/default/files/National%20Technical%20Guidelines%20on%20STI%20and%20RTI_Final.pdf

question_text: Which of the following statements is false about disseminated gonococcal infection?
option_a: It occurs as a result of direct spread by ascending infections
option_b: Classic presentations is with a dermatitis - arthritis syndrome
option_c: Skin lesions are small, tender and maculopapular
explanation:
DGI occurs when the sexually transmitted pathogen Neisseria gonorrhoeae invades the bloodstream and spreads to distant sites in the body, leading to clinical findings such as septic arthritis, polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, petechial/pustular skin lesions, bacteremia, or, on rare occasions, endocarditis or meningitis.

The classic triad of features consists of dermatitis, tenosynovitis and migratory polyarthritis

DGI is uncommon and thought to occur in 0.5-3% of untreated gonorrhea cases.

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, chapter 30, page 5

question_text: Malignant pustule is seen in:
explanation:
1. Anthrax is an acute disease caused by the bacteria Bacillus anthracis gram-positive, spore-forming bacillus.
  2. Cutaneous Anthrax is known as Malignant pustule.

Clinical Features

  1. Malignant pustule: A form of anthrax infection that begins as papule that becomes a vesicle and breaks down into an ulcer covered with eschar, with a discharge of toxins; symptoms of septicemia are severe with vomiting and high fever and profuse sweating; the infection is often fatal.
  2. In more than 95% of cases of endemic disease, spores are transmitted from infected animals or their products by means of skin abrasions

Treatment

ciprofloxacin, doxycycline, erythromycin, vancomycin or penicillin.

  1. In possible cases of inhalation anthrax, early antibiotic prophylaxis treatment is crucial to prevent possible death.

question_text: Recurrent genital ulcer is caused by:
explanation:
Genital herpes

  • MC ulcerative STI among adolescents, is a chronic, lifelong viral infection
  • Two sexually transmitted HSV types have been identified, HSV-1 and HSV-2
  • Majority of cases of recurrent genital herpes are caused by HSV-2, which is also called HHV2

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 25, page 20

explanation:
Trachomatis isolates exist as 15 serovariants.

Trachoma - ocular tropic strains (A, B, Ba, and C)

Genitourinary tract tropic (D, E, F, G, H, I, J, and K) strains Invasive lymphogranuloma venereum (L1, L2, and L3)

question_text: A 40-year-old woman, back from a trip to United States presents with complaints of malaise, headache, rash, and fever. She went hiking in a local park with her family seven days ago. A rash is noted on her right upper extremity was seen. What is the recommended treatment for this patient's condition?
explanation:
• Lyme disease is caused by the spirochete bacterium, Borrelia burgdorferi.
  • It is transmitted after a bite by the Ixodes deer tick.
  • The most common presenting sign of Lyme disease is a circular expanding rash called erythema chronicum migrans. Other early symptoms of Lyme disease include headache, muscle pain, fever, and malaise.
  • A 10-day-course of doxycycline is recommended for patients with early, localized disease.

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 33

question_text: A 30-year-old female presents with multiple painful, red ulcerated lesions on the vulva and bilateral lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presence of multiple painful genital ulcers with bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy is characteristic of chancroid, distinguishing it from other genital ulcer diseases.

  • Chancroid is a sexually transmitted infection caused by Haemophilus ducreyi, a Gram-negative facultative anaerobic coccobacillus
  • It presents with painful, non-indurated genital ulcers that have undermined edges and a necrotic or purulent base
  • The ulcers may develop from red papules that progress to pustules before ulcerating
  • Bilateral or unilateral painful inguinal lymphadenitis is common and may lead to fluctuant buboes that can rupture
  • Autoinoculation may result in multiple or "kissing" ulcers on adjacent skin surfaces
  • Vulval ulcers in females are often painful and associated with visible lymph node enlargement
  • Chancroid has a short incubation period of 3-10 days and may follow recent sexual contact in endemic areas

Explanation of Other Options:

Granuloma inguinale (Option B) (donovanosis) typically causes painless beefy-red ulcers without lymphadenopathy.

Lymphogranuloma venereum (Option C) (LGV) often begins with a transient painless ulcer followed by tender lymphadenopathy

Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Option D) causes cervicitis or urethritis rather than ulcerative lesions on the vulva

question_text: Which of the following is not considered as a sexually transmitted infection?
explanation:
• Bacterial vaginosis is not considered as an STI. It is usually caused by imbalance between aerobic and anaerobic flora of the vagina.
  • However it is mostly seen in sexually active women, with new partner or multiple partners.
  • It is rare in virgins.

REFERENCE: Rooks textbook of dermatology, chapter 31

question_text: A sexually active woman presents with foul-smelling, watery vaginal discharge. What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
Explanation:

Trichomonas vaginalis infection typically causes foul-smelling, thin, watery vaginal discharge, often accompanied by vulvar irritation and itching.

  • Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the protozoan parasite Trichomonas vaginalis.
  • It is one of the most common causes of malodorous, frothy, yellow-green vaginal discharge in women.
  • Key clinical features include:
    • Thin, foul-smelling, watery or frothy discharge
    • Strawberry cervix (punctate hemorrhages on cervix)
    • Vaginal pruritus and irritation
    • Dyspareunia and dysuria may also be present
  • Diagnosis:
    • Wet mount microscopy: Motile, flagellated protozoa
    • NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test) is highly sensitive
    • Vaginal pH typically > 4.5
  • Treatment:
    • Metronidazole (2g single dose or 500 mg BID x 7 days)
    • Treat sexual partners simultaneously to prevent reinfection

Explanation of other options:

Gardnerella vaginalis (Option A): Causes bacterial vaginosis, which presents with thin, grey-white discharge with fishy odor (especially after intercourse). Discharge is usually not watery or frothy, and clue cells are seen on microscopy.

Candida albicans (Option B): Causes thick, white, curd-like (cottage cheese) discharge, with intense itching. The discharge is typically odorless, not foul-smelling.

Lactobacillus (Option D): This is part of the normal vaginal flora and plays a protective role by maintaining acidic pH. It is not a pathogen.

question_text: In which infection is the following clinical picture seen?
explanation:
'saxophone penis' is a typical deformity of penis arising secondary to diseases causing chronic lymphatic obstruction in bilateral inguinal region

Secondary lymphedema is predominantly caused in India by filariasis and sexually transmitted infections like lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV)

The causative agent of LGV is Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1-L3. It is a lymphotropic organism which initiates the disease process primarily in the lymphatic channels, leading to thrombolymphangitis and perilymphangitis. LGV causes bilateral inguinal bubo in one-third of cases and 'saxophone penis' after LGV is well known.

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 30, page 18

question_text: A 8 year old boy presents with a mild painful swelling over scalp since 3 months. He gives the history of having a pet dog at home. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
• Tinea capitis is a fungal infection of the scalp, caused by dermatophyte fungi like Trichophyton and Microsporum
  • Kerion is a severe inflammatory form of tinea capitis, where the immune system has a hypersensitivity reaction against the dermatophytes.
  • The presentation typically includes:
    • Red, boggy swelling on the scalp, which is non-tender to mildly tender.
    • The scalp may be studded with pustules.
    • There is easy pluckability of hair due to the weakened hair follicles.
    • Regional lymphadenopathy (swelling of lymph nodes) is often present.
  • In this case, the history of a pet dog is important, as zoophilic dermatophytes (those transmitted from animals, particularly dogs) are a common cause of kerion.
  • Diagnosis can be confirmed by KOH scraping, which identifies the presence of fungal elements.
  • Treatment of choice is Griseofulvin, an oral antifungal that is effective against dermatophyte infections.

Explanation of the Incorrect Options:

  • (A) Furuncle:
    • A furuncle is a boil or deep skin abscess caused by Staphylococcus aureus. It is typically painful and fluctuant, but it is not associated with scalp fungal infections or lymphadenopathy like kerion.
  • (C) Dissecting cellulitis:
    • Dissecting cellulitis is a chronic inflammatory skin condition of the scalp, often affecting young adults, characterized by abscess formation and scarring. It is not caused by a fungal infection and does not typically present with the features of kerion like pustules or hair pluckability.
  • (D) Abscess:
    • An abscess is a localized collection of pus due to infection, commonly caused by bacteria like Staphylococcus aureus. While an abscess may present with swelling, it is not associated with fungal infections or the typical features of kerion.

Key Takeaway: Kerion is the most likely diagnosis in this case, given the scalp swelling, mild tenderness, and history of pet dog exposure suggesting a zoophilic dermatophyte infection. The management involves oral antifungal therapy with Griseofulvin.

question_text: Which of the following infections also require treatment of the male partner?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Trichomoniasis, is a protozoal infection caused by Trichomonas vaginalis.
  • Both symptomatic women and their male partners must be treated simultaneously. This is done to prevent reinfection.
  • The male partner is usually asymptomatic and can act as a reservoir.

Explanation of Other Options:

Candidiasis (Option A): Not sexually transmitted; male partner treatment is not necessary unless symptomatic.

Bacterial Vaginosis (Option B): An imbalance of vaginal flora, not an STI; partner treatment is not recommended.

Herpes (Option D): The recurrence of herpes is from the ganglia not from male partner. Male doses not act as a reservoir.

question_text: Which of the following organisms is NOT associated with urethritis in men?
explanation:
Explanation:

Urethritis refers to inflammation of the urethra. Symptoms are dysuria, urethral discharge, and itching or burning sensation.


Gardnerella vaginalis is primarily associated with bacterial vaginosis in women. It is not considered a pathogen responsible for male urethritis.

Presently, the recommended treatment is Inj Ceftriaxone 1g i.v.

Key Takeaways:

  • Gardnerella vaginalis → BV in women, not urethritis in men.
  • gonorrhoeae → gonococcal urethritis.
  • Trichomonas & Mycoplasma → nongonococcal urethritis.
  • Always consider both gonococcal and nongonococcal causes when evaluating male urethritis.

question_text: What is the genetic defect in the disease shown below?
explanation:
Harlequin ichthyosis (HI), also known as 'ichthyosis fetalis', is an extremely rare autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis (ARCI) affecting the ABCA12 gene.

Neonates affected by HI are typically born prematurely and encased in markedly thickened, hardened stratum corneum. This casing cracks and results in yellow plaque-like "armor" plates separated by deep longitudinal and transverse erythematous fissures encompassing the entirety of the body

Edematous hands and feet are often enveloped in a mitten-like casing from hardened scales. Furthermore, severe bilateral ectropion (out turning of the eyelids) involving upper and lower eyelids exposes the conjunctiva leaving the cornea at risk for abrasions and desiccation. The nose may appear flattened

Reference: Rook's dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 65, Page 7

question_text: A chronic alcoholic develops an itchy, eczema-like rash on the neck and back of the hands. Which nutritional deficiency is most likely?
explanation:
Explanation:

Pellagra is caused by deficiency of niacin (Vit B3). It classically presents with symptoms such as dermatitis, diarrhoea, and dementia(classical triad). The dermatitis is photosensitive type and is seen on exposure to sun in sites such as the neck (Casal's necklace), dorsum of hands, and forearms. Chronic alcoholics are more predisposed to this condition due to poor nutrition and impaired niacin metabolism.

Explanation of Other Options:

Vitamin B1 (Option B): Deficiency leads to beriberi or Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome,

Vitamin D (Option C): Deficiency causes rickets or osteomalacia, bone-related disease.

Vitamin C (Option D): Deficiency leads to scurvy, presenting with bleeding gums and perifollicular hemorrhages.

question_text: Ash leaf maculae is found in:
explanation:
Various skin manifestations are included in the major criteria for the diagnosis of tuberous sclerosis.

Hypomelanotic/Ash leaf macules are the most common dermatological manifestation.

These are present in approximately 90% of patients and manifest as lighter patches of skin.

Most easily detectable by examination under Wood's

Light, are frequently present on the trunk or limbs.

They are a valuable physical sign as they may be found at birth or in early infancy, some years before other signs of the disease develop, and may suggest the correct diagnosis in infants with convulsions

Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9th edition, Chapter 80, page 11

question_text: In which disorder the following condition seen?
explanation:
Periungual fi bromas (Koenen tumours) appear at or after puberty as smooth, firm, flesh-coloured growths emerging from the nail folds.

Seen in Tuberous sclerosis

Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9th edition, Chapter 80, page 11

question_text: Defective DNA repair is associated with :
explanation:
The basic defect in xeroderma pigmentosum(XP) is in nucleotide excision repair (NER), leading to deficient repair of DNA damaged by UV radiation.

Reference: Rooks textbook of Dermatology, 9th edition, Chapter 78, page 1

question_text: Which nutritional deficiency is associated with an pruritic eczematous rash on neck and dorsum of hand in chronic alcoholics ?
explanation:
Pellagra - niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency

The pellagra syndrome has historically been characterized by the 4 D's: Dermatitis, Diarrhea, and Dementia leading to Death

  • The characteristic skin rash has a typical photosensitive distribution with welldefined borders, and is mostly observed on the face, the neck - forming the so-called Casal's necklace-, the dorsa of the hands and the extensor surface of the forearms.
  • Gastrointestinal involvement - intractable diarrhea, stomatitis and glossitis,
  • neurocognitive impairment - apathy, memory loss (dementia)
  • Niacin deficiency should especially be suspected in - corn/maize eaters, chronic alcoholism, malnutrition, malabsorption, hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis;, drugs like isoniazid, ethionamide, 6-mercaptopurine and estrogens, carcinoid syndrome

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology 9th edition, chapter 63, page 15

question_text: Granular layer is absent in:
explanation:
• Ichthyosis vulgaris: There is little to no granular layer and stratum corneumn thickness is increased(hyperkeratosis)

Reference: Rook's dermatology, 9th Edition, Chapter 65, Page 3

question_text: This is a characteristic rash of which disease?
explanation:
Dermatomyositis is an idiopathic inflammatory myopathy with characteristic cutaneous findings that occur in children and adults

Persons with dermatomyositis often present with skin disease as one of the initial manifestations,

  • Characteristic, possibly pathognomonic cutaneous features: Heliotrope rash, Gottron papules
  • Characteristic but not pathognomonic features: violaceous erythema or in a photosensitive distribution, violaceous erythema on the extensor surfaces of hands and arms (Gottron sign), and periungual telengiectasia
  • Violaceous erythema involving the anterior chest is referred to as the "V-neck sign" whereas involvement of the upper back and shoulders is referred to as the "shawl sign" and lateral thigh(Holster sign)
  • B/L Proximal muscle weakness
  • Muscle fatigue/weakness when climbing stairs, walking, rising from a seated position, combing hair, or reaching for items above shoulders

question_text: Erythema multiforme is seen in?
explanation:
Erythema multiforme (EM) is a self-limiting hypersensitivity reaction of the skin and mucosa. It is characterized by the formation of target lesions and is triggered by several factors, including infections, medications, and autoimmune conditions.

  • Triggers:
    • Idiopathic: Most common cause.
    • Infections:
      • Herpes simplex virus (most common infectious trigger).
      • Mycoplasma pneumoniae (second most common).
    • Drugs:
      • Antimalarial drugs, NSAIDs, and antibiotics are common drug triggers.
    • Connective Tissue Disorders (CTD):g., systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
    • Malignancies: Leukemia and other cancers.
    • Food Additives: Rarely implicated.
  • Typical Lesion:
    • Target or Bulls-Eye Lesion:
      • Central dusky/purple zone.
      • Middle pale area.
      • Peripheral erythematous ring.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

  • (A) Celiac Disease:
    • More commonly associated with dermatitis herpetiformis, not erythema multiforme.
  • (B) ITP (Idiopathic Thrombocytopenic Purpura):
    • Presents with petechiae, purpura, and mucosal bleeding due to low platelet counts, not hypersensitivity reactions.
  • (D) Leukemia:
    • Although malignancies like leukemia can rarely trigger erythema multiforme, antimalarial drugs are a more common cause.

Key Takeaway:

Erythema multiforme is a hypersensitivity reaction most commonly triggered by infections and drugs, with characteristic target lesions as a diagnostic hallmark.

question_text: A patient has multiple skin tumors and a defective DNA repair system caused by double-strand breaks. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Ataxia-Telangiectasia (A-T) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by a defect in the ATM gene, which plays a crucial role in responding to DNA double-strand breaks. This leads to genomic instability, impaired cell cycle control, and increased susceptibility to various cancers, including skin tumors. The classic triad includes cerebellar ataxia, oculocutaneous telangiectasias, and immunodeficiency. The defective DNA repair, particularly concerning double-strand breaks, is a hallmark of this condition.

  • ATM gene: Ataxia-Telangiectasia Mutated gene, a serine/threonine protein kinase involved in DNA damage response, especially double-strand breaks.
  • Clinical features of A-T: Progressive cerebellar ataxia (usually starting in early childhood), oculocutaneous telangiectasias, immunodeficiency (predisposing to infections), increased risk of malignancies (leukemias, lymphomas, solid tumors including skin cancers), and radiation hypersensitivity.
  • Laboratory findings: Elevated alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), chromosomal instability, impaired cellular and humoral immunity.

Explanation of other options:

Xeroderma Pigmentosum (Option A): This is also a DNA repair disorder, but it primarily involves defective nucleotide excision repair (NER), leading to extreme photosensitivity and a very high risk of skin cancers (basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, melanoma) due to UV damage. While it involves skin tumors, the specific defect mentioned (double-strand breaks) points away from XP.

Bloom Syndrome (Option B): This is characterized by defective DNA helicase (BLM gene), leading to genomic instability and increased sister chromatid exchanges. Patients present with short stature, photosensitivity, characteristic facial features, and an increased risk of various cancers, but the primary defect isn't specifically double-strand break repair in the same way as A-T.


Fanconi Anemia (Option D): This is a heterogeneous disorder caused by defects in DNA interstrand cross-link repair (FANC genes). It presents with bone marrow failure, congenital malformations, and an increased risk of acute myeloid leukemia and solid tumors, but the primary DNA repair defect is different from what's described.

Key Takeaways:

  • Defective DNA repair is a common underlying mechanism for many genetic disorders involving skin and cancer predisposition syndromes.
  • Specific types of DNA repair defects (e.g., nucleotide excision repair, double-strand break repair, interstrand cross-link repair) are associated with different syndromes.
  • Ataxia-Telangiectasia is characterized by a defect in double-strand break repair (ATM gene) and predisposes to various cancers, including skin tumors.

question_text: A 60-year-old person presented with an ulcer on the medial canthus. The ulcer has rolled-out beaded margins. Histopathology of the same showed nesting cells with a peripheral palisading pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

An ulcer on the medial canthus with rolled-out margins is a classic presentation of Basal Cell Carcinoma. This is confirmed by a microscopic description showing nesting cells with peripheral palisading.

Explanation of Other Options:

Melanoma (Option C)

Melanoma, also redundantly known as malignant melanoma, is a type of skin cancer that develops from the pigment-producing cells known as melanocytes.

A: Asymmetry.

B: Border. Melanoma borders tend to be uneven and may have scalloped or notched edges.

C: Colour. Multiple colours are a warning sign.

D: Diameter: if the size of the lesion is 6 mm or larger.

E: Evolving. Any change in size, shape, colour or elevation, or any new symptom in it, such as bleeding, itching or crusting, may be a warning sign of melanoma.

Nevus (Mole) (Option D)

A nevus (mole) is a benign growth of melanocytes. It usually appears as a small, round, brown or black spot. Unlike BCC, a nevus does not ulcerate or have rolled-out beaded margins. Additionally, nevus cells do not show the palisading pattern seen in basal cell carcinoma.

Key Takeaway:

Basal cell carcinomaappears as a pearly nodule with rolled borders and visible telangiectasias, often with a central ulcer, on sun-exposed skin. Microscopically it shows nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading.

question_text: What pattern of inheritance is seen in Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), which is commonly associated with multiple cafe-au-lait spots?
explanation:
Explanation:

Neurofibromatosis type 1 (von Recklinghausen disease) is a neurocutaneous syndrome caused by mutations in the NF1 gene on chromosome 17q11.2. The condition is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, with variable expressivity.
Key cutaneous features:

  • Café-au-lait macules (≥6, >0.5 cm in children or >1.5 cm in adults).
  • Axillary/inguinal freckling.
  • Multiple cutaneous neurofibromas.

Other features: Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas), skeletal abnormalities, and risk of malignancies (e.g., malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour).


NF1 Pathogenesis

NF1 gene mutation → ↓Neurofibromin (tumour suppressor protein) → ↑RAS pathway activity → Cell proliferation → Neurofibroma formation + pigmentary changes

Explanation of other Options:

X-linked Dominant (Option A): NF1 is not linked to the X chromosome. X-linked dominant conditions: Incontinentia pigmenti, Rett syndrome.

X-linked Recessive (Option B): Again, NF1 gene is on chromosome 17, not X-linked.
X-linked recessive dermatoses: Hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia, Fabry disease.

Autosomal Recessive (Option D): NF1 is not recessive. Autosomal recessive neurocutaneous disorder: Xeroderma pigmentosum.

Cushing syndrome (Option D): Cushing's syndrome can lead to proximal muscle weakness from steroid-induced myopathy, but it does not feature the distinctive skin rash characteristic of dermatomyositis.

question_text:
A 40-year-old asymptomatic patient presents with a progressive skin lesion over the neck and chest. There is no systemic involvement noted. What investigations are to be done in this patient?

1. KOH
2. Skin biopsy
3. Chest X-ray
4. HIV test
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical description suggests lupus vulgaris, a chronic, progressive paucibacillary form of cutaneous tuberculosis occurring in a previously sensitised individual.

  • Lesions are slow-growing plaques with raised margins and central atrophy; on diascopy they show apple-jelly nodules.

Investigations to be taken include:

  • Skin biopsy (diagnostic - shows tuberculoid granulomas with epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells, and caseous necrosis).
  • Chest X-ray (important since 10-20% of patients have associated pulmonary TB; cutaneous involvement may also be secondary to a pulmonary focus).

Explanation of other investigations:

(Investigation 1): This is more suggestive of a non-infective dermatosis (like cutaneous TB, leprosy,) rather than a superficial fungal infection. So, KOH is not necessarily taken.

(Investigation 4): HIV testing is not routinely indicated here unless there are other risk factors or clinical suspicion of immunosuppression.

Key Takeaways:

  • Lupus vulgaris = most common form of cutaneous TB, chronic plaque with central atrophy and apple-jelly nodules on diascopy.
  • Biopsy is essential for histopathological confirmation (tuberculoid granulomas with Langhans giant cells).
  • Chest X-ray is mandatory to rule out pulmonary TB (present in 10-20%).

question_text: An image shows the characteristic skin findings of phrynoderma, described as plugged keratotic papules. Which of the following should be done next?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image described shows plugged keratotic papules, which are characteristic of phrynoderma-a cutaneous manifestation of vitamin A deficiency and potentially other nutritional deficiencies.

  • Phrynoderma is often associated with vitamin A deficiency, which also causes ocular symptoms.
  • Ocular signs may include:
    • Night blindness
    • Conjunctival xerosis
    • Corneal ulcerations
  • These symptoms may be subclinical or underreported, so it is crucial to actively assess ocular involvement.
  • Early detection of ocular involvement helps in prompt management and prevention of vision loss.

Treatment

  • First-line Management:
    • Nutritional correction.
    • Vitamin supplementation.
    • Treatment of underlying causes (e.g., malabsorption, anorexia).
  • Vitamin A Dosing (Oral):
    • Age ≥8 years and adults:
      • 100,000 units/day for 3 days
      • Then 50,000 units/day for 2 weeks
      • Then 10,000 units/day for 2 months
    • Oral administration is preferred over parenteral.

Vitamin D3 status (Option B): Checking vitamin D3 status is not directly relevant in the context of phrynoderma, as vitamin D deficiency is more commonly associated with musculoskeletal symptoms

Deep tendon reflexes (Option C): Assessing deep tendon reflexes evaluates neurological function, which is not typically affected in phrynoderma

Vitamin B12 status (Option D): Measuring vitamin B12 levels may be relevant in cases of general malnutrition, but it is less immediately necessary than assessing for ocular involvement, which is a known and significant complication of vitamin A deficiency.

question_text: Scabies, an infection of the skin caused by Sarcoptes scabies, is an example of:

Public Health Classification of Water Borne Diseases

  • Water borne diseases: Caused by the ingestion of water contaminated by human or animal faeces or urine containing pathogenic bacteria or viruses. Cholera, Typhoid, Amoebic and bacillary dysentery, Viral hepatitis, Leptospirosis, Giardiasis
  • Water washed diseases: Diseases due to lack of water, Poor personal hygiene favours spread. Scabies, Skin sepsis & ulcers, Yaws, Trachoma, Conjunctivitis, Flea/ Lice/ Tick- borne diseases
  • Water based diseases: Caused by parasites found in intermediate organisms living in water, Infecting agents spread by contact or ingestion of water. An essential part of life cycle of agent takes place in aquatic animal Schistosomiasis, Dracunculiasis
  • Water related diseases: Transmitted by insect vectors which breed in water. Yellow fever, Dengue, Encephalitides, Filariasis, Malaria, Onchocerciasis, Trypanosomiasis, Sleeping sickness

question_text: Diagnosis of the lesion associated with itching and scaling
explanation:
• Tinea corporis (also known as ringworm) is a fungal infection caused by dermatophytes, such as Trichophyton, Microsporum, and Epidermophyton.
  • The typical presentation involves annular lesions with a scaling border, sometimes with vesicles or pustules in the center.
  • The most common causative organism is Trichophyton rubrum, which is responsible for most cases of tinea corporis and tinea cruris (jock itch).
  • The condition often causes itching and can spread easily through direct contact or contaminated surfaces.

Explanation of the Incorrect Options:

  • (A) Granuloma annulare:
    • A chronic, non-infectious skin condition presenting with ring-shaped, raised, red or skin-colored lesions. It does not typically cause itching or scaling as prominently as tinea.
  • (C) Pyoderma granulosum:
    • A rare, inflammatory skin condition that causes painful, red, ulcerated lesions, often seen in association with systemic conditions like inflammatory bowel disease or leukemia. It is not characterized by scalingor itching.
  • (D) Ichthyosis vulgaris:
    • A genetic skin disorder that leads to dry, scaly skin. While it causes scaling, it does not present with the characteristic annular lesions or vesicles/pustules seen in tinea corporis. It tends to affect the extensor surfaces rather than the areas typical for tinea.

Key Takeaway:

Tinea corporis is characterized by itchy, annular lesions with a scaling border and is caused by dermatophytes, commonly Trichophyton rubrum.

question_text: A neonate presents with a growing skin lesion, as shown in the image provided. The mother reports that the lesion has been increasing in size daily. What is the appropriate management?
option_c: Immediate Biopsy due to Malignancy Risk
explanation:
Explanation:

The bright red, raised, "strawberry-like" lesion in the given image represents Infantile Hemangioma.The described presentation of a reddish lesion on the cheek that appeared after birth and rapidly grew in the first few weeks fits the classic course of an infantile hemangioma.

Infantile hemangiomas are the most common benign vascular tumors in infancy. These lesions typically appear after birth, often within the first few weeks of life, and undergo a period of rapid growth followed by a gradual regression over several years.

Most cases of infantile hemangiomas undergo spontaneous involution over time, though some may require treatment with oral steroids or propranolol.

Explanation:

Excision and Laser Therapy (Option B)

Surgical excision and laser therapy are not first-line treatments for typical infantile hemangiomas. These are reserved for complicated cases where there is functional impairment, significant cosmetic disfigurement, or failure to regress.

Immediate Biopsy due to Malignancy Risk (Option C)

Immediate biopsy is not indicated. Infantile hemangiomas are benign and usually follow a predictable course of proliferation and involution without malignant transformation. Biopsy is unnecessary unless the diagnosis is uncertain or there are atypical features suggesting a different pathology.

Cryotherapy (Option D)

Cryotherapy is not appropriate for managing infantile hemangiomas. It can damage surrounding healthy tissues and is not effective for treating vascular tumors of infancy.

Key takeaway:

Infantile hemangiomas are benign vascular tumors that appear shortly after birth, rapidly grow for months, and then spontaneously regress over several years. They are often recognized by their characteristic bright red, raised "strawberry-like" appearance.

question_text: The skin color in humans is influenced by all except:
explanation:
Many factors influence the color of human skin, but the pigment melanin is by far the most important.

The amount of melanin in the skin, the amount of UV exposure, genetics, the quality of melanosomes, and pigments present in the skin all play a role in racial variation.

Melanin is produced by melanocytes in the skin.

Melanin has 2 forms, eumelanin (black-brown) and pheomelanin (yellow-reddish). eumelanin is primarily found in dark-skinned people, while light-skinned persons are more likely to develop phaeomelanin.

Furthermore, the size and number of melanosomes vary by the person and are even more significant in determining human skin color than the proportions of the 2 types of melanin. The degree of transfer of melanin into keratinocytes and its efficiency also play a role in determining skin color.

The number of melanocytes is constant across all races and gender and doesn't play a role in skin color.

Reference: Rooks textbook of dermatology, 9th edition, chapter 88, page 8

question_text: A patient presented with a single skin lesion on arm with loss sensation and ulnar nerve enlargement. Histopathology shown below. What is the diagnosis and antigen test status?
option_a: Tuberculoid leprosy with Antigen test positive
option_b: Tuberculoid leprosy with Antigen test negative
option_c: Lepromatous leprosy with positive antigen test
option_d: Borderline leprosy with negative antigen test
explanation:
Explanation:

Tuberculoid leprosy is characterized by strong cell-mediated immunity, localized lesions, nerve involvement, and a positive lepromin (antigen) test.

Histopathology reveals granulomas with well-formed epithelioid cells and Langhans giant cells, with no visible acid-fast bacilli.

Tuberculoid Leprosy (TT)

  • Tuberculoid leprosy (TT) is part of the Ridley-Jopling classification of Hansen's disease.
  • It reflects a strong immune response to Mycobacterium leprae
  • It is characterized by:
    • Asymmetric nerve involvement (e.g., ulnar thickening)
  • Histology: Well-formed granulomas with epithelioid cells and Langhans giant cells
  • Clinical features:
    • Few well-demarcated hypopigmented or erythematous plaques
    • Loss of sensation over lesions
    • Nerve thickening (e.g., ulnar, common peroneal)
    • Paucibacillary (very few or no bacilli seen on skin smear)
  • Histopathology:
    • Well-formed granulomas
    • Epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells
    • Dense lymphocytic infiltrate
    • No acid-fast bacilli (AFB)
  • Lepromin test: Positive (due to good T-cell immunity)
  • Lepromin Test Overview
    • It is a skin test for measuring cell-mediated immunity to Mycobacterium leprae.
    • Positive in tuberculoid and borderline tuberculoid forms.
    • Negative in lepromatous and borderline lepromatous forms.

question_text: What is the diagnosis in a patient suffering from ulcerative colitis who presents with an ulcer on the anterior leg as shown in the image below?
explanation:
Explanation:

Pyoderma gangrenosum is a rare, inflammatory, ulcerative skin condition that is frequently associated with systemic diseases, particularly inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) like ulcerative colitis. It typically presents as rapidly enlarging, painful ulcers with violaceous, undermined borders, often on the lower extremities. The anterior leg is a common site. It is a diagnosis of exclusion and often requires a biopsy to rule out other causes, though the biopsy itself is non-specific.

  • Pyoderma gangrenosum is an extraintestinal manifestation of IBD, meaning it occurs outside the gastrointestinal tract.
  • The ulcers can be very painful and may have a cribriform (sieve-like) scarring pattern upon healing.
  • Treatment often involves systemic corticosteroids or other immunosuppressants. Local wound care is also crucial.
  • Unlike other ulcers, debridement can worsen pyoderma gangrenosum (a phenomenon called pathergy).

Explanation of other options:

Venous ulcer(Option B): Venous ulcers typically occur on the medial malleolus, are associated with signs of chronic venous insufficiency (edema, hyperpigmentation, lipodermatosclerosis), and are usually less painful than pyoderma gangrenosum.

Tubercular ulcer(Option C): Tubercular ulcers are rare extrapulmonary manifestations of tuberculosis. They are usually chronic, indolent, and less acutely inflammatory than PG. They would require specific diagnostic tests for tuberculosis.

Chancroid(Option D): Chancroid is a sexually transmitted infection caused by Haemophilus ducreyi, presenting as painful genital ulcers. It would not typically present as a non-genital ulcer on the anterior leg, nor is it associated with ulcerative colitis.

Key Takeaways:

  • Pyoderma gangrenosum is a painful, ulcerative skin condition strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease, including ulcerative colitis.
  • It often appears on the lower extremities, commonly the anterior leg, with characteristic violaceous, undermined borders.

• Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) is a potentially life-threatening condition characterized by extensive exfoliation of the epidermis and mucous membrane.

  • Steven-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) shows the same disease process and is considered to be in the same spectrum of drug-induced epidermolysis. The main difference is the extent of skin detachment. TEN usually involves more than 30% of the total body surface area, while SJS affects less than 10%.

question_text: The correct statement regarding urticaria pigmentosa is :

Mastocytosis is a disorder characterized by mast cell accumulation, commonly in the skin, bone marrow, gastrointestinal (GI) tract, liver, spleen, and lymphatic tissues.

Urticaria pigmentosa (UP) is the most common cutaneous mastocytosis in children, but it can form in adults as well. It is considered a benign, self-resolving condition that often remits in adolescence.

UP is caused by several activating mutations in the KIT gene

UP has small, monomorphic tan to brown macules or papules distributed mainly on the trunk and classically spares the central face, palms, and soles.

Darier's sign is the formation of a wheal upon stroking or rubbing skin lesions and suggests the diagnosis of cutaneous mastocytosis. The wheal forms due to the release of mast cell mediators, which can contribute to the systemic symptoms that may occur after stroking the lesion.

The hallmark finding histologically for UP is having an increased amount of mast cells in the dermis. Mast cell nuclei are rounded with surrounding ample cytoplasm, producing a "fried egg" appearance.

question_text: Patient presented with redness, swelling, and characteristic skin nodules that are tender and painful under an ongoing treatment for leprosy. What is the next best management?

  • ENL is an immune complex-mediated vasculitis involving small- to medium-sized vessels, triggered by antigen release from dying bacilli during therapy.

  • A biopsy is not routinely required for diagnosis unless the presentation is atypical. (Option D ruled out)
  • Increasing the drug dose may worsen the reaction, and stopping treatment is inappropriate. (Option C ruled out)

question_text: Which of the following is not true regarding Type 2 Lepra reaction?

Leprosy reactions can occur at any time before, during, or after the treatment.

Type 2 reaction or erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL) occurs in patients with high bacilli load as in patients with LL leprosy)

question_text: Neurofibromatosis type 1 is a hereditary condition commonly associated with multiple café-au-lait spots on the skin. Which pattern of inheritance is seen in this?

Neurofibromin, a GTPase-activating protein, normally inhibits the rat sarcoma (RAS) pathway.

question_text: What is the most likely diagnosis of a 6-year-old with an intensely itchy skin lesions as shown below?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Scabies in humans and other animals is caused by mites of the family Sarcoptidae, which includes Sarcoptes scabiei, the scabies mite, Notoedres cati, a mange mite of cat and Trixacarus caviae, a mange mite of rodents.
  • Transmission of scabies occurs mainly via skin-to-skin contact and, less frequently, via fomites within a patient mite-contaminated environment
  • Very common in children, scabies is characterized by intense nocturnal pruritus.
  • Unlike adult infestations, in children with scabies, the face and neck are frequently involved.
  • Clinical features:
    • Itching is the most obvious manifestation of scabies, usually sparing the face in adult classical scabies.
    • It is generally worst at night and when the patient is warm.
    • The onset occurs 3-4 weeks after the infection is acquired.
    • Typical locations of lesions are the finger webs, the flexor surfaces of the wrists, the elbows, the axillae, the buttocks and genitalia and the breasts of women.
    • The typical lesions of scabies are burrows, which appear as slightly raised brownish tortuous lesions.
  • Examination findings include serpiginous white lines indicating mite burrowing and are typically located in intertriginous areas. Erythematous papules can form as a type IV hypersensitivity reaction to the mite, eggs, or excrement.
  • Treatment:
    • Topical treatment includes 5% permethrin, 1% ivermectin, 1% lindane, 10-25% benzyl benzoate, 0.6% esdepallethrine (bioallethrin), 10% crotamiton and 6-33% precipitated sulphur.
    • Oral ivermectin is neurotoxic for many parasites, including mites, binding specifically to their chloride-glutamate and GABA receptors.

question_text: Identify the condition shown in the image
explanation:
• Discoid Lupus Erythematosus (DLE) is a chronic form of cutaneous lupus erythematosus primarily affecting photo-exposed areas like the face, scalp, and ears.
  • The lesions are typically erythematous plaques with adherent white scaling, and they may have keratotic plugging, which blocks hair follicles. The carpet tack sign or tin tack sign refers to the appearance of keratotic plugs in the lesion, which is characteristic of DLE.
  • These lesions are chronic and may last for years, growing slowly over time.
  • Treatment generally includes topical glucocorticoids or intralesional glucocorticoids, and in extensive cases, hydroxychloroquine (a systemic antimalarial) may be used.

Explanation of the Incorrect Options:

  • (B) SLE (Systemic Lupus Erythematosus):
    • SLE is a systemic autoimmune disease that can affect multiple organs. Although cutaneous manifestations(such as the butterfly rash) are common in SLE, the lesions seen in SLE are not typically the same as those in DLE, and SLE usually involves systemic symptoms like fatigue, fever, and joint pain.
  • (C) Rosacea:
    • Rosacea presents with erythema, telangiectasia, and pustules on the face, often involving the cheeks, nose, and forehead. It is not associated with scarring, keratotic plugging, or photoexposed areas in the same way as DLE.
  • (D) Vitiligo:
    • Vitiligo is a condition where depigmented patches of skin appear due to the loss of melanocytes. Unlike DLE, it is not typically characterized by scarring, keratotic plugging, or erythematous plaques.

Key Takeaway:

Discoid Lupus Erythematosus (DLE) presents with erythematous plaques, keratotic plugging, and scarring in photo-exposed areas, such as the face, and is treated with topical glucocorticoids and systemic hydroxychloroquine in extensive cases.

question_text: A 20-year-old presented with a non-progressive hypopigmented skin lesion that has been present since birth. It shows white accentuation under Wood's lamp examination, and diascopy is inconclusive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical scenario here points to the diagnosis of nevus depigmentosus.

Definition:

  • Nevus depigmentosus is a rare, congenital, stable hypomelanosis.

Clinical Presentation:

  • Lesions appear as off-white macules with irregular, serrated, feathered, or geographic margins.
  • Commonly located on the trunk, lower abdomen, and proximal extremities.
  • It can appear in dermatomal or quasi-dermatomal distribution.
  • Facial involvement may lead to social embarrassment.

Course:

  • Stable throughout life; lesions do not change in size or distribution.
  • Primarily limited to the skin, but rare associations with:
    • Neurological abnormalities
    • Limb hypertrophy

Diagnosis - Commonly Used Clinical Criteria:

  • Leukoderma present at birth or with early onset
  • No change in the distribution of the lesion over time
  • Normal texture and sensation in the affected area
  • No hyperpigmented border around the lesion

Treatment:

  • Generally, no effective treatment exists.
  • However, suction blister grafting has shown success in individual cases.

Vitiligo (Option A) is unlikely because it is an acquired, progressive condition characterized by complete melanocyte loss, and it typically does not present at birth.

Nevus anemicus (Option C) is a vascular anomaly where the lesion disappears with diascopy due to vasoconstriction; since diascopy is inconclusive in this case, it is not consistent with nevus anemicus.

Indeterminate leprosy (Option D) is ruled out because it is acquired, may be progressive, and often involves sensory loss, none of which is present in this case.

Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3657231/#

question_text: All are true about skin except:
option_a: Both dermis & ectoderm are derived from ectoderm
option_b: Skin accounts for total of 15% of body weight
option_c: Most of the cells in skin are keratinocytes derived from ectoderm
option_d: Dermis is made up pf type 1 and type 3 collagen in 8:1 ratio
explanation:
• The statement that "both dermis and ectoderm are derived from ectoderm" is incorrect.
    • Epidermis (including keratinocytes, melanocytes, and Merkel cells) is derived from the ectoderm.
    • Dermis and Langerhans cells originate from the mesoderm.
    • Hence, the dermis is not ectodermal in origin.

Explanation of the Incorrect Options:

  • (B) Skin accounts for 15% of total body weight:
    • True. Skin is the largest organ of the body, weighing approximately 4-5 kg, which accounts for about 15% of the body weight.
  • (C) Most of the cells in the skin are keratinocytes derived from ectoderm:
    • True. Keratinocytes are the predominant cell type in the epidermis, forming the outermost protective layer, and are derived from the ectoderm.
  • (D) Dermis is made up of type I and type III collagen in an 8:1 ratio:
    • True. The dermis is primarily composed of type I (80%) and type III collagen (10%), with a ratio of 8:1. This ratio increases with age due to decreased type III collagen.

Key Takeaway:

The epidermis originates from the ectoderm, whereas the dermis originates from the mesoderm. This distinction is fundamental to understanding the embryological development of the skin.

question_text: A patient presents with the following lesion. Skin biopsy from the lesion shows non-caseating granulomas with epithelioid histiocytes and multinucleate giant cells in the superficial epidermis with prominent peripheral lymphocytes. What will be the therapy given?
explanation:
Explanation:

Disease is lupus vulgaris. Reddish brown fleshy plaque with central scarring and active serpiginous margins. Diascopy shows apple-jelly nodules.

Histopathology: typical tubercles with/without caseation, epithelioid histiocytes and multinucleate giant cells with peripheral lymphocytes. With diagnosis of cutaneous TB, treatment is anti-tubercular therapy.

Management of cutaneous tuberculosis, including warty tuberculosis and lupus vulgaris, are treated with standard multidrug antituberculosis therapy.

Biopsy findings of non-caseating granulomas with epithelioid histiocytes and multinucleate giant cells and the context of cutaneous tuberculosis indicate that therapy is anti-tubercular.

Isoniazid monotherapy is discouraged because of possible drug resistance and coexisting tuberculosis at other sites.

Key Takeaways: Cutaneous TB (lupus vulgaris), confirm by histology/clinical and treat with antitubercular therapy.

question_text:
Which of the following statements about Hailey-Hailey disease are true?
1. Corticosteroids are not effective
2. It is caused by a defect in the ATP2C1 gene
3 It follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern
4. It commonly affects flexural areas
5. It is also known as benign familial pemphigus
explanation:
Explanation:

Hailey Hailey disease (Benign familial pemphigus) is an autosomal dominant inherited blistering disorder caused by mutations in the ATP2C1 gene, which encodes a calcium pump in the Golgi apparatus.

Clinically, it presents with recurrent vesicles and erosions predominantly in flexural areas such as the neck, axillae, groin, and perineum. Topical and systemic steroids may help but are not consistently effective, especially in severe disease.

Histology reveals extensive acantholysis of keratinocytes, giving the epidermis a characteristic "dilapidated brick wall"appearance with suprabasal cleft formation. The dyskeratotic cells show intact nuclei and well-preserved cytoplasm.

question_text: A gardener from Himachal Pradesh presents with nodulo-ulcerative lesions on the upper limb and axillary lymphadenopathy. Microscopy of the aspirate is provided. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Sporotrichosis, also known as "rose gardener's disease" is caused by Sporothrix schenckii.
  • The infection is mainly through thorn pricks or plant material and It spreads along the lymphatics.
  • The characteristic presentation is the appearance of nodular lesions spreading in a linear fashion along lymphatic channels called the Sporotrichoid pattern.

Other diseases that show Sporotrichoid Pattern:

  • Mycobacterium marinum
  • Nocardia brasiliensis
  • Atypical mycobacteria (e.g., M. chelonae, M. abscessus)
  • Leishmania species

Asteroid Bodies are also seen in Sarcoidosis but are formed inside giant cells, its host derived and made of collagen.

The asteroid bodies In sporotrichosis is fungus-associated (yeast cell at the center).

Explanation of Other Options:

Chromoblastomycosis (Option A): Is a chronic infection with warts and verrucous lesions and presence of sclerotic (Medlar) bodies on microscopy; not nodulo-ulcerative with lymphatic spread.

Coccidomycosis (Option C): Endemic to Southwestern USA, presents with pulmonary infection or disseminated disease; not typical in India and rarely shows sporotrichoid spread.

Histoplasmosis (Option D): Caused by Histoplasma capsulatum; presents with systemic features and hepatosplenomegaly; skin lesions are secondary and not linear nodular.

Key Takeaways:

  • Sporotrichosis = Rose gardener's disease.
  • Sporotrichoid pattern (linear lymphatic spread) is pathognomonic.

question_text: A 30-year-old patient presents with a scaly, red plaque on the forearm. A skin biopsy is performed, and histology shows keratinocytes connected by numerous desmosomes, as given in the image, under the microscope. Which layer of the epidermis is most likely being described?
explanation:
• Stratum spinosum is also called the prickle cell layer because the cells are held together with spiny projections of the intercellular attachments called desmosomes between keratinocytes.
  • The spiny appearance is due to the shrinking of the microfilaments between desmosomes that occurs during the process of H&E staining.

Stratum basale (Option A): The deepest epidermal layer containing mitotically active basal keratinocytes and melanocytes.

Stratum granulosum (Option C): A layer where keratinocytes begin keratinisation and accumulate keratohyalin granules.

Stratum corneum (Option D): The outermost layer of dead, flattened, keratinised cells, providing a waterproof barrier.

Reference: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page Number: 6.

question_text:
Which of the following statements about skin structure and embryology are correct?
1. The epidermis can regenerate from the hair bulb and sebaceous glands
2. The stratum corneum is the outermost cellular layer
3. The epidermis is of ectodermal origin
4. The dermis and hypodermis are of endodermal origin
explanation:
Explanation:

The epidermis can regenerate from the hair bulb and sebaceous glands because stem cells are located in the interfollicular region, base of sebaceous glands, and bulge area of hair follicle. (Statement 1 is true)

  • The stratum corneum is the outermost layer but it is anucleated and non-cellular, hence the outermost cellular layer is stratum granulosum. (Statement 2 is false) 
  • The epidermis develops from ectoderm. (Statement 3 is true) 
  • The dermis and hypodermis are mesodermal in origin (neural crest contribution in face and frontal scalp). (Statement 4 is false)

Key Takeaways:

  • Epidermis → ectoderm, dermis/hypodermis → mesoderm (neural crest in face).
  • Stem cell niches: interfollicular region, sebaceous gland base, bulge area of hair follicle.
  • Stratum granulosum is the outermost cellular layer.

question_text: A patient suffering from inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis) with recurrent bloody diarrhea develops an extremely painful, rapidly expanding ulcer on the lower leg with violaceous, undermined borders and a necrotic base. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The image shows ulcer with violaceous margins, undermined edges - in a patient with IBD (recurrent bloody diarrhoea)
  • The most common associated systemic disorders include rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, and other autoimmune and inflammatory conditions.
  • In addition, pyoderma gangrenosum has an association with both solid tumors and hematologic malignancies.
  • Pyoderma gangrenosum (PG) is a rare non-infectious, autoinflammatory neutrophilic dermatosis commonly associated with underlying systemic disease.
  • In 2004, diagnostic criteria were proposed but have not been confirmed.
  • According to this proposal, both major criteria and two of the minor criteria are required to make the diagnosis.
  • Clinical phenotype classification:
    • Classic ulcerative
    • Peristomal
    • Pustular
    • Bullous
    • Vegetative (granulomatous superficial)
    • Extracutaneous
    • Atypical
  • Treatment response (rapid response to systemic steroid treatment)
  • Sweet syndrome (Option D): Sweet syndrome is an inflammatory neutrophilic dermatosis characterised by tender, tumid, red, dermal nodules and plaques with a predilection for the arms, upper body and face.
  • Erythema nodosum (Option A) occurs in up to 15% of CD patient and 10% of UC patients and responds when treatment for bowel inflammation is given. The lesions are red, tender nodules are found on the anterior surface of the lower legs, ankles, calves, thighs.
  • Erythema marginatum (Option B) is seen with rheumatic fever.
